teile.einleitung: The Food and Agriculture Organization, FAO for short, is a specialised agency of the UN. It fights hunger and helps to use farming, fishing and forests sustainably.
wichtigste: The FAO was founded in 1945 at a conference in Quebec in Canada.
Its Latin motto is “Fiat panis”, meaning “Let there be bread”.
Together with the WHO it runs the Codex Alimentarius.
Since 2019 Qu Dongyu from China has been Director-General (as of 2025).
Its database FAOSTAT is freely available.
It issues worldwide warnings about desert locusts.

abschnitte.text: The FAO was founded in October 1945 at a conference in **Quebec** in Canada. Its first seat after that was in Washington; later it moved to Rome. Its motto is **“Fiat panis”**, meaning “Let there be bread”. It appears in the logo and shows the aim: everyone should have enough to eat.

Together with the World Health Organization WHO, the FAO publishes the **Codex Alimentarius**. This is a collection of international rules for food. They are meant to make sure that food is safe and traded fairly. Many countries base their own laws on them.

In the database **FAOSTAT**, the FAO collects figures on harvests, livestock and nutrition from almost all countries. The data are freely available. The FAO also runs a worldwide **monitoring service** for desert locusts. Swarms of these insects can destroy whole harvests, so the FAO warns the countries affected early.

Since August 2019 the Director-General of the FAO has been **Qu Dongyu** from China (as of 2025). Before that he was Vice-Minister of Agriculture in China. The FAO also looks after international years on important topics. For example, 2023 was the **International Year of Millets**. Millet is a nutritious cereal that also grows in dry conditions.

gewusst: The FAO was founded in Canada, but today it has its seat in Rome.
Millet is one of the cereals that can cope well with drought.

teile.einleitung: When a new state comes into being, the question arises: do the other states accept it? In international law this confirmation is called **recognition**. It helps decide whether a state can open embassies, conclude treaties and join international organisations.
wichtigste: According to the three-element theory, a state needs territory, a people and state authority.
Having its own currency is not one of these features.
According to the declaratory theory, recognition only confirms a state that already exists.
A distinction is made between formal de jure recognition and de facto recognition.
Territories conquered by annexation are usually not recognised.
Switzerland recognised Kosovo in February 2008, shortly after its declaration of independence.

abschnitte.text: According to the **three-element theory**, a state needs three things: a **territory** with borders, a **people** who live there, and effective **state authority**, that is, a government that is actually in control. Its own currency is not necessary. Liechtenstein, for example, pays with the Swiss franc and is still a state. Size does not matter either.

Lawyers have long argued about exactly what recognition does. According to the **declaratory theory**, a state already exists as soon as it meets the three features. Recognition only confirms this. The **constitutive theory**, on the other hand, holds that a state only comes into being when other states recognise it. Today most experts tend to follow the declaratory view.

**De jure recognition** is formal and legally final. With **de facto recognition**, a state accepts the actual balance of power without fully confirming it. For example, it works with a government in practice but does not send an ambassador. In this way states can keep up contacts without committing themselves legally.

In a **secession**, a territory breaks away from its state and wants to become independent. One example is Kosovo, which broke away from Serbia in 2008. Switzerland was among the first states to recognise Kosovo. Quite different is an **annexation**, that is, the forcible incorporation of a foreign territory. It breaches the ban on the use of force in the UN Charter and is therefore not recognised by most states.

Some territories have their own government but are hardly recognised at all. A well-known example is **Taiwan**. The People's Republic of China regards Taiwan as part of its territory. That is why only a few states officially recognise Taiwan. But many others, including Switzerland, have unofficial relations, for example for trade and culture.

gewusst: Switzerland basically recognises states and not individual governments.
Liechtenstein is a state in its own right even though it has no currency of its own.

teile.einleitung: ECOWAS is the Economic Community of West African States. It was founded in 1975 to link the economies of the countries in the region. Later it also worked for peace and democracy.
wichtigste: ECOWAS was founded on 28 May 1975 with the Treaty of Lagos.
Its Commission has its seat in Abuja, the capital of Nigeria.
In 1990 the ECOWAS force ECOMOG intervened in Liberia.
In 2017 ECOWAS made sure that power in the Gambia was handed over to the election winner.
Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger left in January 2025.
The planned shared currency is to be called the Eco.

abschnitte.text: On **28 May 1975**, **15 West African states** signed the founding treaty in **Lagos** in Nigeria. The aim was **economic integration**: trade was to become easier, and people were to be able to travel and work more freely. In French, ECOWAS is called **CEDEAO**, because English, French and Portuguese are spoken in West Africa. The **Commission** of ECOWAS has its seat in **Abuja**, the capital of Nigeria. The Community's court is also there.

ECOWAS also became active in conflicts. In **1990** it sent the force **ECOMOG** into the civil war in **Liberia**. It was one of the first peacekeeping missions by a regional economic organisation in Africa. In January **2017** it intervened in **the Gambia**: President Yahya Jammeh did not want to step down after losing an election. Under pressure from ECOWAS troops he left the country, and the election winner **Adama Barrow** took office.

Not all countries have stayed. **Mauritania** left in **2000** and later signed an association agreement. In **Mali**, **Burkina Faso** and **Niger**, military governments took power. ECOWAS demanded a return to democracy and imposed sanctions. The three countries announced their withdrawal in January 2024, which took effect in **January 2025**. Back in 2023 they had founded the **Alliance of Sahel States**, which they expanded into a confederation in **Niamey** in July 2024.

For decades ECOWAS has been planning a **shared currency** called the **Eco**. It is meant to make trade between the members easier. However, its introduction has been postponed several times because the countries' economies are very different. Today several members already share the **CFA franc**, while others have their own currencies, such as the Nigerian naira.

gewusst: With a shared ECOWAS passport, citizens of the member states can travel more easily within the region.
Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa and the largest member of ECOWAS.

teile.einleitung: **Article 50** of the Treaty on European Union sets out how a state can leave the EU. For a long time it was only theory. It was used for the first time only with **Brexit**, the departure of the United Kingdom.
wichtigste: Article 50 was added to the EU treaties with the Treaty of Lisbon.
After notice of withdrawal is given, there are two years for negotiations unless the deadline is extended.
The United Kingdom triggered the procedure on 29 March 2017.
In the 2016 referendum about 52 per cent voted to leave.
The withdrawal took effect on 31 January 2020.
A state that wants to rejoin must go through the normal procedure under Article 49.

abschnitte.text: Article 50 was added to the EU treaties with the **Treaty of Lisbon**, which came into force in 2009. A state informs the European Council that it wants to leave. Then both sides negotiate a **withdrawal agreement**. Two years after the notice, the EU treaties no longer apply to that state, even without an agreement. The European Council, together with the state, can unanimously extend the deadline.

On 23 June 2016 people in the United Kingdom voted on the EU. Just under **51.9 per cent** chose “Leave”, that is, withdrawal. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, by contrast, there were majorities for remaining. On **29 March 2017** Prime Minister **Theresa May** handed over the notice of withdrawal. With this, Article 50 was triggered for the first time.

On the EU side, the Frenchman **Michel Barnier** led the negotiations. The border on the island of Ireland was especially disputed, because no hard border was to be created there. A fallback arrangement, the **backstop**, was replaced in 2019 by the Northern Ireland Protocol. After several extensions of the deadline, the United Kingdom left on **31 January 2020**. A transition period still applied until the end of 2020.

In December 2018 the **European Court of Justice** decided an important question in the Wightman case. A state may **withdraw its notice on its own** up until it leaves, if it decides so democratically. Once a state has left, Article 50 paragraph 5 applies: rejoining is treated like any other accession under **Article 49**.

Long before Article 50, one territory left the European Communities: **Greenland**. It belonged to them as part of Denmark and voted to leave in 1982, mainly because of fisheries policy. The departure took effect from 1985. Since then Greenland has been an overseas territory associated with the EU.

gewusst: Until Brexit, Article 50 had never been used.
Because of the extensions, the withdrawal procedure took almost three years instead of two.

teile.einleitung: On 1 May 2004, ten countries joined the European Union at once. It was the biggest enlargement in the EU's history. Most of the new members were in Central and Eastern Europe.
wichtigste: On 1 May 2004 ten countries became EU members.
This made the EU grow from 15 to 25 members.
The Treaty of Accession was signed in Athens on 16 April 2003.
The new members included Poland, the three Baltic states, Malta and Cyprus.
Romania and Bulgaria did not join until 2007.
In 2007 Slovenia became the first of the new countries to introduce the euro.
Switzerland supported the new members with an enlargement contribution of one billion francs.

abschnitte.text: On **1 May 2004**, **ten countries** became members of the EU at the same time. The number of members rose from **15 to 25**. The newcomers were **Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania**, **Poland**, the **Czech Republic**, **Slovakia**, **Hungary**, **Slovenia** and the island states of **Malta** and **Cyprus**. The countries had signed the **Treaty of Accession** in **Athens** on 16 April 2003, with the Acropolis as a backdrop.

Until 1989, many of the new members had belonged to the **Eastern Bloc** and had been led by communist governments. The three **Baltic states** had even been part of the **Soviet Union** until 1991. The **Czech Republic** and **Slovakia** had together formed Czechoslovakia until 1993, which split peacefully. For many people, joining was therefore a sign that the division of Europe had been overcome.

The most populous new member was **Poland**, with about 38 million inhabitants at the time. The smallest was **Malta**. Malta and Cyprus lie in the Mediterranean and used to be British colonies. **Romania** and **Bulgaria** were not yet ready in 2004 and did not join until **2007**.

When they joined, the new countries did not automatically get the euro. First they had to meet certain economic conditions. **Slovenia** managed it first and paid with the euro from **1 January 2007**. Other countries followed later. In 2025 Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary still had their own currencies.

Switzerland was affected too, because it is closely linked to the EU through **bilateral agreements**. In 2006 Swiss voters approved the **Eastern Europe Cooperation Act**. The **enlargement contribution** of one billion francs is based on it. With it Switzerland funded projects in the new member states to reduce economic and social differences in Europe.

gewusst: With the 2004 enlargement, around 75 million people joined the EU at a stroke.
Malta is still the smallest member state of the EU today.

teile.einleitung: Extreme poverty means that people do not have enough money for the bare necessities such as food, water or shelter. The World Bank measures it with a worldwide poverty line.
wichtigste: The World Bank sets the international poverty line.
Since 2025 it has been 3 US dollars a day.
About 830 million people live in extreme poverty (as of 2025).
Most of them live in Africa south of the Sahara.
In 1990 it was over 40 per cent of people; in 2025 it was about 10 per cent.

abschnitte.text: The **World Bank** calculates the **international poverty line**. Anyone who has less money than this to live on per day counts as extremely poor. In 2025 the World Bank raised the line from 2.15 to **3 US dollars a day**. The amount is **adjusted for purchasing power**. This means taking into account how much you can buy with the money in each country. In a poor country, many things are cheaper than in Switzerland.

Using the new line, about **830 million** people live in extreme poverty (as of 2025). That is about one person in ten. Roughly seven in ten of them live in **Africa south of the Sahara**. According to the World Bank, there are especially many in the **Democratic Republic of the Congo**. In the past, most extremely poor people lived in East and South Asia.

In 1990 over **40 per cent** of the world's population lived in extreme poverty. By 2025 the share had fallen to about **10 per cent**. The reasons include economic growth in countries such as China and India. Even so, much remains to be done, especially in countries with wars and conflicts.

**Absolute poverty** threatens survival, because the bare necessities are missing. **Relative poverty** is measured against the prosperity of your own country. Someone is relatively poor if they have clearly less than most people. There is poverty in Switzerland too. According to the Federal Statistical Office, about 8 per cent of the population counted as poor in 2022, about 700,000 people. The line is based on the guidelines of the **SKOS**, the Swiss Conference for Social Welfare.

gewusst: Since 1990 the share of extremely poor people in the world has fallen to about a quarter of what it was.
A dollar can buy much more in a poor country than in Switzerland, which is why calculations use purchasing power.

teile.einleitung: The Bürgenstock Conference was an international meeting about peace in Ukraine. It took place on 15 and 16 June 2024 at the Bürgenstock Resort high above Lake Lucerne. Switzerland was the host.
wichtigste: The conference took place on the Bürgenstock on 15 and 16 June 2024.
Switzerland organised the meeting at Ukraine's request.
It was based on President Zelensky's ten-point peace formula.
Three topics were dealt with: nuclear safety, food security and humanitarian questions.
At first about 80 states signed the final communiqué.
Russia was not invited.

abschnitte.text: Since 2022 Russia has been waging war against Ukraine. Ukraine wanted a large conference on peace. To prepare for it, **national security advisers** met several times, most recently in January 2024 in **Davos** on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum. After that, Switzerland announced that it would organise a summit. It took place on **15 and 16 June 2024** at the **Bürgenstock Resort** in the canton of Nidwalden.

About a hundred delegations from states and organisations attended. For the USA, **Vice-President Kamala Harris** came; President Biden did not take part in person. **Russia** was not invited, and China stayed away. The talks were based on President **Zelensky**'s **peace formula** with **ten points**. On the Bürgenstock, however, only three of them were dealt with.

At the end there was a **final communiqué**, that is, a joint declaration. It demanded that the **Zaporizhzhia** nuclear power station be operated safely and under full Ukrainian control. It called for free shipping for food. All **prisoners of war** were to be released through a complete exchange, and Ukrainian children who had been taken away were to return.

At first **80 states** and four European organisations signed. By autumn 2024 the number of states had risen to 89. Some participants such as **India**, Saudi Arabia and South Africa did not sign. Among other things, they demanded that Russia should also be included in future. **Iraq**, Jordan and Rwanda later withdrew their signatures. Brazil only took part as an observer. Opinions on the success of the conference differed.

gewusst: The Bürgenstock lies above Lake Lucerne and has been a well-known hotel complex for more than a hundred years.
As a neutral country, Switzerland often offers its “good offices”, that is, help with talks between states.

teile.einleitung: **Egypt** lies in the north-east of Africa. The country is famous for the pyramids, the Nile and the Suez Canal. Thousands of years ago the pharaohs ruled here; today Egypt is a republic.
wichtigste: The capital and largest city of Egypt is Cairo.
Cairo lies on the Nile, one of the longest rivers in the world.
The pyramids of Giza stand near Cairo.
People in Egypt speak Arabic.
Egypt is a republic with a president at its head.
People pay with the Egyptian pound.
The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean with the Red Sea.

abschnitte.text: Most of Egypt is **desert**. Only along the **Nile** is the land fertile. That is why almost all Egyptians live close to the river or in its delta on the Mediterranean. Without the Nile, farming would hardly be possible in Egypt. In the south, the **Aswan Dam** holds back the river to form a large lake.

**Cairo** is the capital of Egypt. The government and parliament work there. Cairo is the largest city in the Arab world. In Arabic it is called **“al-Qahira”**, which means “the victorious”. The city has old mosques, busy markets and a lot of traffic.

On the edge of Cairo stand the **pyramids of Giza**. They are more than 4500 years old and were tombs of pharaohs. The largest is the **Pyramid of Khufu**. Next to the pyramids lies the great **Sphinx**, a figure with a lion's body and a human head. Every year visitors come from all over the world, including from Switzerland.

Egypt is a **republic**. At its head is a **president**, no longer a pharaoh as in ancient Egypt. The official language is **Arabic**. Most people are Muslims, but there is also a large Christian community, the **Copts**. People pay with the **Egyptian pound**; some notes show ancient temples.

The **Suez Canal** opened in 1869. It connects the **Mediterranean** with the **Red Sea**. In this way ships travelling between Europe and Asia do not have to sail all the way round Africa. The canal is one of the most important shipping routes in the world. The fees paid by ships bring Egypt a lot of money.

gewusst: The Pyramid of Khufu was the tallest structure in the world for more than 3000 years.
The Nile flows from south to north and enters the Mediterranean in a large delta.

teile.einleitung: A delegation is a group of people who represent a country or an organisation at meetings. At the UN, every member country sends a delegation to the sessions. Delegates speak and negotiate on behalf of their country.
wichtigste: A delegation is a group that represents a country at meetings.
It is led by a head of delegation.
In the UN General Assembly, each country's delegation has one vote.
Delegates act on the instructions of their government.
Switzerland sends delegations to many international conferences.
The Swiss Parliament also has delegations, for example to the Council of Europe.

abschnitte.text: The word **delegation** comes from the Latin word delegare, which means to send as a representative or to entrust. A delegation is a group of envoys who speak for someone else. The individual members are called **delegates**. They do not represent their own opinion but the position of their country or organisation.

In the UN **General Assembly** in New York sit the delegations of all the member states. Each country has one vote there, whether it is large or small. A delegation often consists of diplomats, experts and sometimes also ministers. It is led by the **head of delegation**, who gives the speeches and decides in votes.

Before a conference, the delegation receives instructions from its government about which goals to pursue. During the sessions the delegates listen, give speeches and negotiate with other countries. They often meet in breaks for talks to find compromises. Afterwards they report to their government on what has been achieved.

Switzerland sends delegations to many meetings, for example to climate conferences or UN conferences in Geneva and New York. They are usually put together by the Department of Foreign Affairs. At some meetings, representatives of cantons, science or organisations are also included. Switzerland also has **youth delegates**, young people who bring the concerns of young people to the UN.

The Swiss Parliament also has delegations, for example the delegation to the **Council of Europe** in Strasbourg. In companies and clubs, too, people speak of delegations when a group is sent to a meeting. In everyday life, to delegate also means to hand over a task to someone else. A teacher can, for example, delegate a task to the class representatives.

begriffe.erklaerung: People who speak on behalf of a country or a group.
The person who leads a delegation.
The assembly of all the UN member states.
The task that a delegation receives from its government.

gewusst: Tens of thousands of people from almost every country in the world take part in large climate conferences.
In the UN General Assembly, a small country like Liechtenstein has exactly the same voting right as China.

t17qk0xx.t: Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, SDC for short, is the federal office responsible for Swiss development aid. It supports projects in poorer countries and helps in disasters and wars. In this way Switzerland wants to help ensure that fewer people have to live in poverty.
wichtigste: The SDC supports projects in poorer countries.
It belongs to the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA).
Its headquarters is in Bern.
The SDC provides both long-term development cooperation and humanitarian aid.
The Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit, which sends experts in disasters, is part of the SDC.
The SDC works together with aid organisations, UN organisations and governments.

abschnitte.text: The **SDC** is a directorate, that is, a large division, of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs. Its roots go back to 1961, when the Confederation founded a service for technical cooperation. Its present name dates from 1996. Its headquarters is in Bern, and it has offices in many partner countries.

A large part of the work is long-term **development cooperation**. The SDC supports, for example, schools, vocational training, clean drinking water, farming and health services. It follows the principle of **help for self-help**: the people on the ground should later be able to shape their future themselves. That is why projects often last many years.

In earthquakes, floods or wars, the SDC provides **humanitarian aid**. It supplies, for example, water, shelter, medicines or food. The **Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit** is made up of experts who can travel quickly to crisis areas. The Swiss Rescue chain also includes search dogs that find people buried after earthquakes.

The SDC does not work alone. It works together with Swiss aid organisations such as Helvetas or Caritas and supports **UN** organisations. In promoting the economy, it works closely with the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO). The money for this is approved by Parliament as part of the strategy for international cooperation.

The Federal Constitution requires Switzerland to help relieve need and poverty in the world. Through the SDC, Switzerland shows **solidarity** with other countries. At the same time the work helps to prevent conflicts and to tackle global problems such as climate change. How much money Switzerland should spend on this is debated again and again in politics.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large division in a department of the federal administration.
Quick help for people in need, for example after a disaster.
Support that enables people to help themselves later.
The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, which deals with the Confederation's economic questions.

gewusst: After a severe earthquake, Swiss Rescue can fly abroad with rescue teams and dogs within a few hours.
The SDC is also active in Eastern Europe, for example in reconstruction in Ukraine.

teile.einleitung: An embargo is a ban on trading with a particular country, either completely or only in certain goods. Countries use embargoes to put pressure on a country's government without going to war.
wichtigste: With an embargo, trade with a country is banned completely or partly.
An arms embargo bans the delivery of weapons.
The word comes from the Spanish “embargar”, which means “to seize”.
Only the UN Security Council can decide on embargoes that apply to all UN members.
The USA has kept up a trade embargo against Cuba since 1962.
In Switzerland, the Federal Council puts sanctions into effect with the Embargo Act.

abschnitte.text: With an **embargo**, a country or a group of countries bans trade with a particular country. The ban can cover **all goods** or only some. An **arms embargo**, for example, bans delivering weapons and military equipment to a country. This is meant to stop conflicts from being stirred up further. Embargoes are a kind of **sanction**, meaning a punishment measure against countries.

The word comes from **Spanish**: **embargar** means “to seize” or “to hinder”. In the past, an embargo was mainly used to hold **foreign ships** in port, so that they could no longer transport goods. Today it is mostly about bans on imports and exports or on money transactions.

Only the **UN Security Council** can decide on embargoes that **all member states** must keep to. The General Assembly can only make recommendations. In 1977 the Security Council imposed a binding **arms embargo on South Africa**, where **apartheid** ruled at the time. After **Iraq invaded Kuwait** in August 1990, the UN decided on a comprehensive embargo against Iraq.

In **1962** the **USA** imposed a comprehensive trade embargo on **Cuba**. It is one of the longest-lasting embargoes in history. In 1973, Arab oil-exporting countries stopped deliveries to several Western countries; this was called the **oil embargo**. Whether embargoes achieve their aim is disputed: sometimes it is mainly the ordinary people of a country who suffer.

In 1990 Switzerland adopted the embargo against Iraq, even though it was not yet a **UN member** at the time. Since **2003** there has been the **Embargo Act**. With it, the **Federal Council** can adopt sanctions of the UN and of important trading partners such as the **EU**. How far Switzerland supports sanctions is debated again and again in politics because of its **neutrality**.

gewusst: Because of the oil crisis in 1973, Switzerland had three car-free Sundays, when the roads were almost empty.
An embargo can also cover just certain technologies, for example a ban on delivering particular computer chips.

teile.einleitung: The United Nations Development Programme, UNDP for short, helps countries to reduce poverty and develop well.
wichtigste: The UNDP was founded in 1965.
Its headquarters is in New York.
It works in around 170 countries and territories.
Since 1990 the Human Development Report has been published every year.
It contains the Human Development Index, HDI for short.
The HDI measures health, education and income.

abschnitte.text: The UNDP is a programme of the **UN**. It was created in 1965 by merging two older UN programmes for technical assistance. Its headquarters is in **New York**, near the UN headquarters. But it works in around 170 countries and territories. There it helps, for example, with building up administrations, with elections or with protecting the environment.

The **Human Development Index** (HDI) compares the countries of the world. It measures three areas: **health** through life expectancy, **education** through years of schooling and **income** per person. In this way it shows more than just how rich a country is. The value lies between 0 and 1. From 0.800 upwards, this is called very high human development. Switzerland is among the countries with the highest values.

The index appears in the **Human Development Report**, which the UNDP has published every year since 1990. The Pakistani economist **Mahbub ul Haq** led the first report. The Indian economist **Amartya Sen** worked with him. Do not confuse it: the World Development Report comes from the World Bank.

In 2015 the UN countries adopted the **2030 Agenda** with 17 **Sustainable Development Goals**. The UNDP helps many countries to reach these goals. It also runs the **UN Volunteers programme** (UNV). This places volunteers in UN projects and has its seat in Bonn.

gewusst: The HDI shows that a rich country is not automatically ahead in health and education too.
The UN Volunteers programme has its seat not in New York but in Bonn.

teile.einleitung: **Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation**, **APEC** for short, is a forum of countries around the Pacific Ocean. They want to make trade and economic cooperation easier. It includes large economic powers such as the USA, China and Japan.
wichtigste: APEC was founded in Canberra in 1989.
It has 21 member economies around the Pacific.
Instead of states, it speaks of economies so that Taiwan and Hong Kong can also take part.
The Secretariat has been in Singapore since 1993.
Since 1993 the heads of state and government have met every year.
Since 1998 there has been a freeze on new members.

abschnitte.text: The idea came from the Australian Prime Minister **Bob Hawke**. On his initiative, ministers from twelve countries met in **Canberra**, the capital of Australia, in 1989. This is how APEC began. It is not an alliance with fixed treaties but a **forum** in which the members cooperate voluntarily.

APEC deliberately speaks of **member economies**. In this way **Taiwan** and **Hong Kong** can also take part. Taiwan takes part as “Chinese Taipei”, Hong Kong as “Hong Kong, China”. The term economy avoids the delicate question of who is recognised as a state. In 1998 **Russia, Peru and Vietnam** joined. Since then APEC has had **21 members** and is not admitting any new ones for the time being.

In 1994 the leaders met in **Bogor** in Indonesia. They set themselves the goal of free trade and free investment. The industrialised countries were to reach it by **2010** and the developing countries by **2020**. These Bogor Goals shaped APEC's work for a long time. They were not fully reached, but many customs duties were lowered.

In 1993 US President **Bill Clinton** invited the heads of state and government to **Blake Island** near Seattle. Since then there has been a summit every year. The chair changes every year between the members. For 2026 China took over the chair from South Korea and chose **Shenzhen** as the summit venue. The host country is supported by the **Secretariat in Singapore**.

gewusst: For a long time, participants at APEC summits wore clothing in the style of the host country for a group photo.
Switzerland is not a member, because APEC only includes countries around the Pacific.

teile.einleitung: The Bilaterals I are a package of seven agreements between Switzerland and the European Union. They were signed in 1999 and regulate important areas such as work, trade and transport.
wichtigste: The Bilaterals I consist of seven agreements.
They were signed on 21 June 1999.
On 21 May 2000 the people voted yes with 67.2 per cent.
The agreements came into force on 1 June 2002.
Because of the **guillotine clause**, all seven agreements are linked.
The agreements include the free movement of persons.

abschnitte.text: In 1992 the Swiss people rejected joining the **European Economic Area** (EEA). But Switzerland still wanted to work closely with the EU. That is why it negotiated separate agreements for particular areas. Such agreements between two partners are called **bilateral**, that is, two-sided. The first package is called the Bilaterals I.

The package includes seven agreements: **free movement of persons**, technical barriers to trade, public procurement, agriculture, land transport, air transport and research. **Public procurement** is about contracts that municipalities, cantons and public companies award to firms. The agreement on **technical barriers to trade** makes sure that a product such as a machine only has to be tested once. The air transport agreement opens the European market to Swiss airlines.

The seven agreements are linked to each other. If one falls away, for example because it is terminated, all the others fall away too. This rule is called the **guillotine clause**. The EU wanted to make sure in this way that Switzerland did not keep only the parts it liked. That is why votes on individual agreements are so important.

A **referendum** was called against the agreements. On 21 May 2000, 67.2 per cent voted yes. After that, all the EU states still had to agree, so the agreements only applied from 1 June 2002. The free movement of persons was introduced step by step. For the 15 old EU states, the quotas were dropped in June 2007. The **limitation initiative**, which wanted to end the free movement of persons, was rejected by the people in September 2020 with about 62 per cent.

gewusst: Thanks to the research agreement, Swiss universities could take part in large European research programmes.
The land transport agreement regulates, among other things, how lorries may travel through Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Conference on Disarmament in Geneva is an international meeting at which states negotiate on limiting and controlling weapons. It is the only permanent body in the world that is meant to negotiate new disarmament treaties for all states. It meets in the Palais des Nations, the seat of the UN in Geneva.
wichtigste: The Conference on Disarmament negotiates on limiting and controlling weapons between states.
It is based in Geneva.
It has existed in its present form since 1979.
Decisions are made by consensus, that is, only if no member is against them.
Important results are the Chemical Weapons Convention and the treaty banning nuclear tests.
For many years the states have hardly been able to agree on new negotiations.

abschnitte.text: **Disarmament** means that states have fewer weapons, or no longer have dangerous weapons at all. This applies above all to **weapons of mass destruction** such as nuclear, chemical and biological weapons. Disarmament is meant to make wars less likely and to protect people. For everyone to keep to it, treaties and checks are needed.

The Conference on Disarmament is based in the **Palais des Nations** in Geneva. It was created in its present form in 1979, but there had already been similar committees before. Today it has 65 member states, including all the countries with nuclear weapons and also Switzerland. It works closely with the United Nations but is independent.

The conference follows the **consensus principle**. This means a decision is only made if no state objects. This makes sure that all the important states agree. The disadvantage is that a single country can block everything.

The conference's predecessors prepared the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968. The conference itself negotiated the **Chemical Weapons Convention**, which was signed in 1993 and bans chemical weapons. In 1996 came the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. These treaties are regarded as great successes of disarmament.

Since the end of the 1990s the conference has hardly been able to agree on new negotiations. The reasons are tensions between great powers and the consensus principle. Even so, the diplomats continue to meet regularly so as to keep talking. For Switzerland, Geneva as a place of disarmament is an important part of its role as a **host state**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Reducing or abolishing weapons.
A decision that nobody objects to.
Weapons that can kill a great many people at once, such as nuclear weapons.
A written agreement between states that they must keep to.

gewusst: In front of the Palais des Nations in Geneva stands the Broken Chair, a giant chair with a broken leg that commemorates the victims of landmines.
The Conference on Disarmament is the only permanent body in the world that is meant to negotiate general disarmament treaties.

teile.einleitung: The Dayton Agreement ended the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995. It was negotiated in the USA and set out how the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be organised after the war.
wichtigste: The agreement was negotiated near Dayton in the US state of Ohio in November 1995.
It was signed in Paris in December 1995.
It was signed by Alija Izetbegović, Franjo Tuđman and Slobodan Milošević.
The US diplomat Richard Holbrooke led the negotiations.
Since then Bosnia and Herzegovina has consisted of the Federation and the Republika Srpska.
The state presidency has three members.
A High Representative oversees implementation.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 1990s **Yugoslavia** broke apart. In **Bosnia and Herzegovina** there were mainly three ethnic groups: **Bosniaks**, **Croats** and **Serbs**. From 1992 to 1995 there was a war there in which a great many people died or had to flee. Many international attempts at mediation failed at first.

In November 1995 the warring parties met at **Wright-Patterson Air Force Base**, an air force base near **Dayton** in the US state of Ohio. The secluded military base allowed talks away from the public eye. The US diplomat **Richard Holbrooke** led the negotiations doggedly and put a lot of pressure on all sides. He is regarded as the **architect** of the agreement. It was signed in **Paris** in December 1995.

Three presidents signed: **Alija Izetbegović** for Bosnia and Herzegovina, **Franjo Tuđman** for Croatia and **Slobodan Milošević**, the Serbian President, for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Bosnian Serbs were involved through Milošević. Tuđman led Croatia from 1990 to 1999.

Since Dayton, Bosnia and Herzegovina has consisted of two **parts**, also called entities. The **Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina** is mainly inhabited by Bosniaks and Croats, the **Republika Srpska** mainly by Serbs. Both have their own governments. At the head of the state is a **state presidency with three members**: one each for Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs. The chair rotates regularly.

The international community oversees implementation. The **High Representative** has wide-ranging powers: he can pass laws and remove politicians from office. From December 1995 the NATO force **IFOR**, with about 60,000 soldiers, secured the ceasefire. Other missions followed later. To this day the political system is complicated, and the ethnic groups often argue about the country's future.

gewusst: The negotiations in Dayton lasted about three weeks, and the delegations were hardly allowed to leave the military base during that time.
The constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is an annex to the Dayton Agreement.

t19e0bhp.t: Relations between China and the USA

teile.einleitung: The USA and the People's Republic of China are the two largest economies in the world. Their relations swing between close cooperation in trade and fierce competition for power and technology.
wichtigste: In 1971 “ping-pong diplomacy” opened the way to rapprochement.
Since 1 January 1979 the USA has had official relations with the People's Republic of China.
In December 2001 China joined the World Trade Organization WTO.
From 2011 President Obama shifted the focus of US foreign policy to Asia (“Pivot to Asia”).
Since 2022 the two countries have argued especially about advanced computer chips.
In February 2023 a Chinese high-altitude balloon strained relations.

abschnitte.text: After the People's Republic of China was founded in 1949, the USA had no official relations with the government in Beijing for a long time. In 1971 the American **table tennis team** travelled to China at its invitation. This visit went down in history as **ping-pong diplomacy**. In 1972 President Richard Nixon visited China. On **1 January 1979** the USA established official **diplomatic relations** with Beijing and broke off official relations with the government in Taipei on Taiwan.

In the decades that followed, trade grew strongly. In December **2001** China became a member of the **World Trade Organization WTO**. After that China rose to become the largest exporting nation in the world. Many goods sold in the USA are made in China. That is why the two countries are closely intertwined economically.

As China rose, worry grew in the USA about its position in the world. From **2011** Barack Obama's government focused its foreign and military policy more strongly on Asia; this was called the **Pivot to Asia**. The political scientist Graham Allison coined the term **Thucydides Trap**: it warns that war can threaten when a rising power challenges an established one. Other experts consider this comparison exaggerated.

**Semiconductor technology** is especially disputed. In October 2022 the USA restricted the export of advanced **computer chips**, and of the machines used to make them, to China. In this way it wanted to slow down China's progress in artificial intelligence and military technology. With the **CHIPS and Science Act** of 2022, the USA is also supporting chip factories and research at home with about 52 billion dollars. China criticises these measures as an obstacle to its development.

In February 2023 a **Chinese high-altitude balloon** crossed North America for several days. The USA classified it as a **spy balloon** and shot it down off its east coast. China, on the other hand, spoke of a weather balloon that had drifted off course. Because of this, the US Secretary of State postponed a planned trip to China. The case shows how quickly mistrust can arise between the two countries.

gewusst: A table tennis visit helped two great powers to approach each other again after more than 20 years.
Thucydides was a historian in ancient Greece who, about 2400 years ago, described the war between Athens and Sparta.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Chancellor is the head of government in Germany. He decides in which direction politics goes. He is elected by parliament, the Bundestag.
wichtigste: The Federal Chancellor leads the German government.
He is elected by the **Bundestag**, not directly by the people.
Since May 2025 **Friedrich Merz** of the CDU has been Federal Chancellor (as of 2026).
The first Federal Chancellor was **Konrad Adenauer**, from 1949.
**Angela Merkel** was the first woman Federal Chancellor, from 2005 to 2021.
The head of state is the **Federal President**.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Chancellor** is the head of the German government. He chooses the **ministers** and sets the broad lines of policy. Alongside him there is the **Federal President**. He is the head of state and represents Germany but does not lead the government. The Federal Chancellor works in the **Chancellery** in **Berlin**, very close to the Reichstag building.

In Germany the people elect the **Bundestag**, that is, parliament. The members of the Bundestag then elect the Federal Chancellor. Usually this needs a **coalition**, that is, several parties working together. The Bundestag can also vote a chancellor out, but only if it elects a new one at the same time.

The first Federal Chancellor was **Konrad Adenauer**. He was elected in 1949 and stayed in office for 14 years. **Angela Merkel** was in office from 2005 to 2021 and was the first woman to hold the office. After her, **Olaf Scholz** of the SPD governed from December 2021 to May 2025. Since May 2025 **Friedrich Merz** of the CDU has been Federal Chancellor (as of 2026).

Switzerland also has a **Federal Chancellor**. But this person is not the head of government. The Swiss Federal Chancellery is the **staff office of the Federal Council** and supports the government in its work. Switzerland has no single head of government: the **Federal Council**, with seven members, leads the country together. **Austria** too has a Federal Chancellor as head of government.

gewusst: Angela Merkel and Helmut Kohl were both Federal Chancellor for 16 years.
Until 1999 the German government was in Bonn; then it moved to Berlin.

teile.einleitung: The **Nagorno-Karabakh conflict** is a dispute between **Armenia** and **Azerbaijan** in the South Caucasus. It was about a territory that belonged to Azerbaijan under international law but where mostly Armenians lived. The conflict lasted more than 30 years and led to several wars.
wichtigste: Under international law, Nagorno-Karabakh belonged to Azerbaijan.
From 1988 the Armenian majority wanted to join Armenia.
The first war ended in May 1994 with a ceasefire.
From 1992 the OSCE Minsk Group mediated.
The second war in autumn 2020 lasted 44 days.
After an offensive in September 2023, almost the entire Armenian population fled.

abschnitte.text: In the **Soviet Union**, Nagorno-Karabakh was an **autonomous region** within Azerbaijan. But most of its inhabitants were Armenians. From **1988** they demanded to join Armenia. This led to a conflict that turned into war after the Soviet Union broke up.

The first war ended in **May 1994** with a **ceasefire**. After that, Armenian forces controlled Nagorno-Karabakh and surrounding Azerbaijani areas. Hundreds of thousands of people had been driven out on both sides. From 1992 the **Minsk Group** of the OSCE, led by the USA, Russia and France, was to mediate. In about 30 years it did not achieve a lasting solution.

In Nagorno-Karabakh the Armenians declared their own republic. From 2017 it called itself the **Republic of Artsakh**, after an old Armenian name for the region. It was not recognised by any member of the UN, not even by Armenia. Under international law the territory remained part of Azerbaijan.

In autumn 2020 the second war broke out. It lasted **44 days**, from 27 September to 10 November, when Russia brokered a ceasefire. Azerbaijan won back large areas. From December 2022 Azerbaijan blocked the **Lachin corridor**, the only road to Armenia. After a short offensive in September 2023, almost the entire Armenian population fled, more than 100,000 people. The Republic of Artsakh was dissolved as of 1 January 2024.

In **August 2025** the heads of state **Ilham Aliyev** and **Nikol Pashinyan** met at the **White House** in Washington. With US President Donald Trump mediating, they signed a joint peace declaration. It includes a planned transport route through the Armenian province of Syunik. Whether this will lead to a lasting peace is still open.

gewusst: Not even Armenia itself officially recognised the Republic of Artsakh as a state.
During the blockade of the Lachin corridor, food and medicines were in short supply in Nagorno-Karabakh for months.

teile.einleitung: **Australia** is a country and at the same time a whole continent. It lies on the other side of the Earth, far away from Switzerland. It is known for kangaroos, vast deserts and its special capital **Canberra**.
wichtigste: The capital of Australia is Canberra.
Canberra was newly planned because Sydney and Melbourne were arguing.
The city plan was designed by Walter Burley Griffin.
In Australia voting in elections is compulsory.
The head of state is King Charles III (as of 2026).
The coat of arms shows a kangaroo and an emu.

abschnitte.text: When Australia became a single country in 1901, **Sydney** and **Melbourne** both wanted to be the capital. A compromise was found: a completely **new city** was built between the two. This is how **Canberra** came about. Today Canberra is the seat of the government and parliament.

There was a **competition** for the best city plan for Canberra. In 1912 it was won by the architect **Walter Burley Griffin** from the USA, together with his wife **Marion**. Then the city was built on almost empty land. In the middle is an artificial lake named after Griffin.

In Australia **voting is compulsory**. All adult citizens must go and vote. Anyone who does not vote without a good reason has to pay a small **fine**. That is why a great many people vote in Australia. In Switzerland, by contrast, voting is voluntary; only the canton of Schaffhausen has compulsory voting.

Australia is a **monarchy** and belongs to the Commonwealth. The head of state is the British King **Charles III**, who is also King of Australia (as of 2026). But the country is governed by parliament and the Prime Minister. On top of **Parliament House** in Canberra stands a huge steel flagpole flying a large Australian flag.

Australia's **coat of arms** is held by a **kangaroo** and an **emu**. Both animals are typical of Australia. Kangaroos hop on their strong back legs, and emus are large running birds that cannot fly. Many other animals, such as koalas and platypuses, live only on this continent.

gewusst: The lake in the middle of Canberra is called Lake Burley Griffin, after the city's architect.
Canberra is the capital, but Sydney and Melbourne are much bigger.

teile.einleitung: The 1.5 degree target is a goal of worldwide climate policy. The warming of the Earth is to be limited as far as possible to 1.5 degrees Celsius above the pre-industrial level. This is meant to prevent the worst effects of climate change.
wichtigste: The Paris Agreement of 2015 calls for efforts to limit warming to 1.5 °C.
The pre-industrial level is taken to be the average of the years 1850 to 1900.
The small island states fought especially hard for the target.
Net CO2 emissions would have to reach zero around 2050.
In 2024, for the first time, a whole calendar year was above 1.5 °C.
Switzerland wants to reach net zero by 2050, as set out in the Climate and Innovation Act.

abschnitte.text: Since industrialisation began, people have burned a lot of coal, crude oil and natural gas. This produces **greenhouse gases** such as **CO2**, which warm the Earth. The **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change IPCC** compares today's temperatures with the **pre-industrial level**. As an approximation, the average of the years **1850 to 1900** is used, because before that there were hardly any widespread measurements. The greater the warming, the more frequent heatwaves, droughts and heavy rain become.

In 2015 almost all the countries of the world agreed on the **Paris Agreement**. Article 2 calls for warming to be kept **well below 2 °C** and for efforts to be made to limit it to **1.5 °C**. The **Alliance of Small Island States**, AOSIS for short, fought especially hard for this. For low-lying islands, even a warming of 2 °C threatens their existence because of rising sea levels. Their motto was “1.5 to stay alive”.

According to a special report by the IPCC in 2018, worldwide CO2 emissions would have to fall by about 45 per cent by 2030 compared with 2010. Around **2050** they would have to reach **net zero**. Net zero means that no more CO2 is emitted than is removed from the air again. The synthesis report of 2023 gives a reduction in **greenhouse gases** of about **43 per cent** by 2030 compared with 2019.

According to the World Meteorological Organization, **2024** was about **1.55 °C** above the pre-industrial level. Even so, the target is not automatically considered missed. It refers to a **long-term average** over about 20 years, because individual years vary, for example because of **El Niño**. If warming rises above 1.5 °C for a while and later falls again, this is called **overshoot**. For this, more CO2 would have to be removed from the air than is emitted. Some damage could still remain.

In Switzerland warming is stronger than the worldwide average. The **glaciers** are melting very visibly. On **18 June 2023** voters approved the **Climate and Innovation Act** with about 59 per cent voting yes. It states that Switzerland should reach net zero by **2050**. How quickly and by what means this should happen is still being debated in politics.

gewusst: Half a degree's difference sounds small, but according to the IPCC, at 2 °C many more people would be affected by extreme heat than at 1.5 °C.
The abbreviation IPCC stands for “Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change”.

teile.einleitung: The euro is the shared money of many countries of the European Union. Since 2002, millions of people from Portugal to Finland have paid with the same coins and banknotes. After the US dollar, the euro is the second most important currency in the world.
wichtigste: The euro is the shared money of many countries of the European Union.
Its sign is €, and its abbreviation is EUR.
Coins and banknotes have existed since 1 January 2002.
Since 2026, 21 EU countries have used the euro; Bulgaria was the latest to join.
One euro has 100 cents.
The European Central Bank in Frankfurt am Main is responsible for the euro.
Switzerland does not have the euro; it pays with the Swiss franc.

abschnitte.text: The **euro** is a **currency**, meaning a money system that several countries use together. The countries with the euro form the **eurozone**. Since 2026 it has had 21 countries, for example Germany, France, Italy, Austria and, since the start of 2026, Bulgaria. Some EU countries such as Denmark, Sweden or Poland have kept their own currency.

The euro was first introduced on 1 January 1999 as book money, meaning for transfers and bank accounts. On 1 January 2002 the coins and banknotes came into circulation. Old currencies such as the German mark, the French franc and the Italian lira disappeared. The basis was the Maastricht Treaty of 1992.

There are eight **euro coins**, from 1 cent to 2 euros. The front is the same everywhere; each country designs the back itself, for example with coats of arms, buildings or rulers. The banknotes go from 5 to 500 euros and show windows, gateways and bridges from different periods. The 500-euro note has not been newly issued since 2019, but it is still valid.

The **European Central Bank** (ECB) has its seat in Frankfurt am Main. It makes sure that the euro stays stable and that prices do not rise too fast. To do this it sets, among other things, the **key interest rate**. The banknotes are put into circulation by the central banks of the euro countries.

Switzerland is not in the EU and so has its own **franc**. Even so, the euro is very important for Switzerland, because it trades a lot with the euro countries. The **exchange rate** shows how many francs you get for one euro. In many shops near the border and at railway stations you can also pay in euros, but the change is often given in francs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The official money of a country or a group of countries.
All the countries that use the euro as their money.
The price of one currency in another currency, for example how many francs one euro costs.
The bank of a country or a currency that issues the money and keeps prices stable.

gewusst: Some countries outside the EU also use the euro, for example Monaco, San Marino, the Vatican, Andorra, Montenegro and Kosovo.
The euro sign € recalls the Greek letter epsilon and has two horizontal lines that are meant to stand for stability.
The euro banknotes do not show real buildings but invented examples of architectural styles.

teile.einleitung: A diplomatic mission is the official representation of a country in another country or at an international organisation. The best-known form is the embassy. It is like a piece of home abroad that keeps up contacts and helps fellow citizens.
wichtigste: An embassy is the representation of one country in another country.
It is headed by an ambassador.
A consulate deals mainly with fellow citizens, passports and visas.
At international organisations such as the UN there are permanent missions.
The premises of an embassy are specially protected.
Switzerland has about 170 representations worldwide.

abschnitte.text: A **diplomatic mission** is an office of a state abroad. It represents its country's government towards the host country. The most important form is the **embassy**, which is usually in the host country's capital. The Vatican calls its embassies nunciatures.

The embassy maintains the political relations between two countries. It promotes cooperation in the economy, science and culture. It watches what is happening in the host country and reports to the government at home. It also protects the interests of its own citizens.

A **consulate** is a representation that deals mainly with practical matters. It issues passports and visas and helps fellow citizens who, for example, have lost their passport or fallen ill. Large countries often have consulates in several towns. Many embassies also have their own consular section.

At international organisations such as the UN, states have **permanent missions**. Geneva is one of the most important places in the world for this, because almost every state has a mission there. Switzerland itself has permanent missions to the UN in New York and in Geneva. These diplomats work together with representatives from all over the world.

Switzerland has about 170 representations worldwide, that is, embassies, consulates and missions. They belong to the **Department of Foreign Affairs** in Bern. For Swiss people abroad there is also a helpline that can be reached round the clock. Anyone who gets into difficulty abroad can turn to the nearest Swiss representation.

begriffe.erklaerung: The official representation of a country in the capital of another country.
A representation that mainly helps fellow citizens and issues passports and visas.
Permission to enter another country.
A country's representation at an international organisation.

gewusst: Sometimes several countries share an embassy building to save costs.
As a protecting power, Switzerland sometimes takes on tasks for foreign countries that have no embassy of their own in the host country.

teile.einleitung: The eurozone, also called the euro area, includes all the countries of the European Union that have the euro as their currency. It is one of the largest economic areas in the world.
wichtigste: The shared currency is the euro, divided into 100 cents.
The euro has existed as book money since 1999 and as cash since 2002.
Since 1 January 2026, 21 countries have belonged to it.
Croatia introduced the euro in 2023, Bulgaria in 2026.
Thanks to an exemption, Denmark does not have to introduce the euro.
Switzerland has never introduced the euro.

abschnitte.text: The **euro** is the shared currency of the eurozone. It is divided into 100 cents. It has existed as **book money**, meaning in accounts, since 1999. On **1 January 2002** the banknotes and coins came into circulation. The European Central Bank is responsible for monetary policy.

On 1 January 2023 **Croatia** introduced the euro, replacing the kuna. On 1 January 2026 **Bulgaria** followed as the 21st country. This means 21 of the 27 EU countries have the euro. The other EU countries must in principle introduce it as soon as they meet the conditions. Only **Denmark** has secured the right in a treaty to keep its krone.

A country must meet certain **convergence criteria** to introduce the euro. These include low inflation and sound public finances. The criteria were laid down in the **Maastricht Treaty**. The finance ministers of the euro countries meet regularly in the **Eurogroup**, usually once a month.

Some microstates use the euro even though they are not in the EU, for example **Vatican City**. On the basis of an agreement, it may even mint its own coins. **Switzerland** is almost completely surrounded by euro countries, but it has the **Swiss franc**. Liechtenstein also uses the franc. Near the border, many shops accept euros all the same.

gewusst: Vatican City mints its own euro coins, even though it does not belong to the EU.
On 1 January 2026 Bulgaria became the 21st euro country.

teile.einleitung: The **Élysée Palace** stands in the middle of Paris. It is the official residence of the French president. This is where France's head of state works and receives guests from all over the world.
wichtigste: The Élysée Palace is in Paris.
It is the official residence of the President of France.
The grand avenue of the Champs-Élysées is very close by.
In 2026 Emmanuel Macron is President of France.
Since 2002 the president has been elected for five years.
You can visit the palace on the Heritage Days in September.

abschnitte.text: The Élysée Palace was built in the 18th century as a **town mansion** for a nobleman. Later various famous people lived there, including **Napoleon**. Since the 19th century the palace has been the **official residence** of the French presidents. It has a large garden and many splendid halls.

The palace is in the centre of **Paris**, the capital of France. Very close by runs the **Avenue des Champs-Élysées**, one of the most famous streets in the world. The palace and the street have almost the same name. It comes from the “Elysian Fields”, a place in the Greek myths.

The official title of the head of state is **“président de la République”**, meaning President of the Republic. The president is elected directly by the people. Since 2002 a term of office has lasted **five years**; before that it was seven years. **Emmanuel Macron** has been president since 2017 and has been elected twice. The French flag in **blue, white and red** flies on the palace.

Normally you cannot visit the Élysée Palace, because people work here. On the **European Heritage Days** in September, however, the palace opens its doors. Then many people queue to see the halls. Switzerland also has such days, when buildings that are normally closed are open.

gewusst: Unlike the President of the Swiss Confederation, who changes every year, the French president stays in office for five years.
The name Élysée recalls the Elysian Fields, a place for happy souls in the Greek myths.

teile.einleitung: Brasília is the capital of Brazil. The city was planned from scratch on empty land and built in just a few years. It was opened in 1960.
wichtigste: Brasília is the capital of Brazil, not Rio de Janeiro or São Paulo.
The city was opened on 21 April 1960.
Before that, Rio de Janeiro was the capital.
Seen from above, the city plan by **Lúcio Costa** looks like an aeroplane.
The architect **Oscar Niemeyer** designed many buildings.
The city lies on the artificial **Lake Paranoá**.

abschnitte.text: For a long time **Rio de Janeiro** on the coast was the capital of Brazil. But the government wanted the **interior of the country** to grow too and to get more people and work. That is why a completely new capital was built, almost in the middle of the country. Under President **Juscelino Kubitschek**, Brasília was built in only a few years. The city was opened on **21 April 1960**.

abschnitte.titel: A city plan like an aeroplane
abschnitte.text: The urban planner **Lúcio Costa** drew the city with two large axes that cross each other. From above the plan looks like an **aeroplane** or a bird. The residential districts lie in the “wings”. Ministries and other important buildings stand along the long axis. Wide roads were meant to make car traffic easier.

The Brazilian architect **Oscar Niemeyer** designed many of the city's buildings. They include the **cathedral** and the **parliament**. His buildings often have round, curving shapes and a lot of white concrete. On the **Square of the Three Powers**, the parliament, the government and the supreme court stand close together. In Portuguese it is called “Praça dos Três Poderes”.

For the new city a river was dammed. This created the artificial **Lake Paranoá** on the edge of Brasília. It was meant to make the climate more pleasant and to provide space for leisure. Brasília lies on a high plateau, much higher than the coastal cities. Because of its special planning, the city is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: Brasília is one of the world's large cities that were only founded in the 20th century.
Switzerland too has its embassy in Brazil in Brasília.

teile.einleitung: The civil war in Syria began in 2011 and lasted more than 13 years. It forced millions of people to flee, within the country and abroad. In December 2024 the ruler Bashar al-Assad was overthrown.
wichtigste: The war began in 2011 with protests in the town of **Daraa**.
Syria was ruled from 1970 by **Hafez al-Assad** and from 2000 by his son **Bashar**.
**Turkey** took in the most refugees from Syria.
**Lebanon** took in an especially large number of people compared with its population.
In 2015 many refugees came to Central Europe via the **Balkan route**.
In December 2024 Bashar al-Assad was overthrown and fled to Russia.

abschnitte.text: **Hafez al-Assad** came to power through a coup in 1970. He ruled Syria until his death in 2000. After that his son **Bashar al-Assad** took over the presidency. The government hardly allowed any criticism. Anyone who opposed it could expect to be arrested.

In 2011 there were protests in many Arab countries; this is called the **Arab Spring**. In the town of **Daraa** in southern Syria, young people were arrested for writing slogans critical of the government on walls. The protests against this spread across the whole country. The government cracked down hard. This developed into a long **civil war** with many groups and foreign powers.

Millions of people fled. For many years **Turkey** hosted more than three million Syrians. In small **Lebanon**, at times there was about one refugee for every four to five inhabitants. In **Jordan** the **Zaatari** camp opened in 2012, one of the largest refugee camps in the world. Many people also fled within Syria.

abschnitte.titel: Europe and the end of Assad
abschnitte.text: In 2015 many refugees came via the **Balkan route** to Austria and Germany. At that time Chancellor **Angela Merkel** said “We can do this”. The sentence was much debated. In March 2016 the EU and Turkey concluded an **agreement** to slow down the movement of refugees across the Aegean. In December 2024 rebels captured Damascus, and **Assad** fled to Russia. Since then many refugees have been wondering whether they can go back.

gewusst: Talks on a solution for Syria were held several times in Geneva under UN leadership.
Switzerland has also taken in people from Syria and supported aid on the ground.

teile.einleitung: Caritas Switzerland is a large aid organisation based in Lucerne. Since 1901 it has helped people who live in poverty or have fallen into need, in Switzerland and abroad.
wichtigste: Caritas Switzerland was founded in 1901 and is one of the oldest aid organisations in Switzerland.
Its headquarters is in Lucerne.
The Latin word “caritas” means love of one's neighbour.
Together with 16 regional Caritas organisations, Caritas helps people affected by poverty in Switzerland.
Abroad, Caritas provides emergency aid and development cooperation in about 20 countries.
Caritas Switzerland belongs to the worldwide network Caritas Internationalis.

abschnitte.text: Caritas Switzerland was founded in **1901** and is based in **Lucerne**. The name comes from Latin: **caritas** means love of one's neighbour or charity. The organisation grew out of the Catholic Church. But it helps all people in need, no matter where they come from or what they believe.

In Switzerland there are **16 regional Caritas organisations**. They are independent but work closely with Caritas Switzerland. In the **Caritas markets**, people with little money can buy food and everyday items cheaply with a shopping card. The **KulturLegi** gives discounts for museums, courses, sports clubs and much more. In this way people on low incomes can also take part in social life.

Many cantons give Caritas contracts. These are often about **looking after asylum seekers and refugees**. This includes, for example, accommodation, advice and help with **integration**, that is, with settling into the new surroundings. Caritas also offers advice on debts or money worries.

Caritas Switzerland also helps abroad, in **about 20 countries**. After disasters such as earthquakes or floods, it provides **emergency aid**. In **development cooperation** it supports projects that help people out of poverty in the long term. Caritas Switzerland is a member of **Caritas Internationalis**, a network in more than 160 countries, and of Caritas Europa.

Every year Caritas publishes the **Social Almanac**. In it, it describes the social situation in Switzerland, especially poverty. Many people think there is no poverty in rich Switzerland. Caritas shows that here too, families, single parents or older people sometimes hardly have enough money to live on.

gewusst: There are Caritas organisations in more than 160 countries around the world.
With the KulturLegi you can go to museums, courses or sports clubs more cheaply in many regions of Switzerland.
Caritas Switzerland is older than the First World War.

teile.einleitung: The European Court of Human Rights, ECtHR for short, is an international court in Strasbourg. It examines whether member states of the Council of Europe have violated the European Convention on Human Rights. People from Switzerland can also turn to this court.
wichtigste: The ECtHR examines whether member states of the Council of Europe have violated the Convention on Human Rights.
Its seat is in Strasbourg in France.
It was set up in 1959.
It belongs to the Council of Europe and not to the European Union.
Each member state of the Council of Europe provides one judge.
Individual people can also lodge an application.
Switzerland ratified the Convention on Human Rights in 1974.

abschnitte.text: The **European Court of Human Rights** is a court of the **Council of Europe**. It watches over the European Convention on Human Rights, ECHR for short. This Convention was signed in 1950 and protects rights such as the right to life, freedom of expression and the ban on torture. The court was set up in 1959 and has worked as a permanent court since 1998.

Anyone who feels their human rights have been violated in a member state can lodge an **application**. First, however, they must have gone through the courts in their own country. In Switzerland this usually means that the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne must have decided first. Countries can also bring cases against other countries.

The court has its seat in the **Human Rights Building** in Strasbourg. There is one judge for each of the 46 member states of the Council of Europe. They are elected for nine years by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. Every year the court receives tens of thousands of applications.

If the court finds a violation, the country concerned must comply with the **judgment**. Often it has to pay compensation or change laws. A well-known judgment against Switzerland came in 2024 in the case of the **KlimaSeniorinnen** (Senior Women for Climate Protection). The court ruled that Switzerland had not protected older women enough from the effects of climate change.

The ECtHR is often confused with the EU's **Court of Justice**. That court has its seat in Luxembourg and is responsible for the law of the European Union. The ECtHR in Strasbourg, on the other hand, belongs to the Council of Europe, which also includes countries outside the EU. That is why Switzerland is part of the ECtHR but not of the EU's Court of Justice.

begriffe.erklaerung: Basic rights that every person has, for example the right to life and freedom.
A treaty between many countries.
An official request to a court to review a decision.
To make an international treaty officially valid.

gewusst: The Human Rights Building in Strasbourg was designed by the British architect Richard Rogers.
The ECtHR is one of the few international courts that individual people can turn to directly.

teile.einleitung: The European Parliament is the elected representation of the people of the European Union. Its members are elected directly by the people in the EU countries every five years. It meets mainly in Strasbourg and Brussels.
wichtigste: The European Parliament is the only directly elected institution of the EU.
It meets mainly in Strasbourg and Brussels.
Since 1979 it has been directly elected every five years.
After the 2024 election it has 720 members.
Together with the Council of the EU it passes the EU's laws.
The members join together in political groups according to their political views.
Since 2022 Roberta Metsola from Malta has been President of Parliament.

abschnitte.text: The **European Parliament** represents the roughly 450 million people of the EU. Its members are called **Members of the European Parliament** (MEPs). Since 1979 they have been elected directly every five years; the latest election took place in June 2024. Large countries such as Germany have more seats than small countries such as Malta, but small countries get more seats in relation to their population.

Parliament has several places of work. The large **plenary sessions** usually take place twelve times a year in Strasbourg, in the Louise Weiss building. The committees and additional sessions meet in Brussels. The administration, the General Secretariat, is partly based in Luxembourg.

Together with the Council of the EU, Parliament passes the **laws** that the Commission proposes. It can amend or reject proposals. It also has a say in the budget, meaning the EU's money. It elects the President of the Commission and can force the whole Commission to resign with a vote of no confidence.

In Parliament the members do not sit by country but by political views. Such groups are called **political groups**. For many years the largest group has been the European People's Party, followed by the Social Democrats. There are also, for example, Liberals, Greens and several right-wing and left-wing groups.

In Parliament every member may speak in one of the EU's 24 **official languages**. Interpreters translate the speeches into all the other languages at the same time. That is why Parliament is one of the largest employers of translators and interpreters in the world. Switzerland is not represented, because it is not an EU member.

begriffe.erklaerung: Elected people who represent the people in a parliament.
A session that all the members take part in.
A group of members with similar political views.
A person who translates spoken language straight away.

gewusst: Because Parliament moves between Brussels and Strasbourg every month, files and equipment are regularly transported in lorries.
The plenary chamber in Strasbourg is one of the largest parliamentary chambers in the world.
Since 1988 Parliament has awarded the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought every year.

teile.einleitung: The European single market is a shared market of the EU countries. Within it, goods, people, services and money can move almost as freely as within a single country.
wichtigste: The single market has officially existed since 1 January 1993.
It is based on four fundamental freedoms.
These are the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital.
Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein take part through the EEA.
Switzerland rejected the EEA in 1992 and chose the bilateral agreements.
The CE mark shows that a product meets the EU rules.

abschnitte.text: The single market started on **1 January 1993**. Since then there have in principle been no **customs checks** on goods at the EU's internal borders. Even before that there was a **customs union**. This means that there are no customs duties between the members, and they all charge the same external duties towards other countries.

The single market is based on **four fundamental freedoms**. These are the free movement of **goods**, **persons**, **services** and **capital**, meaning money. **Free movement of persons** means that EU citizens may live and work in any member state. Thanks to an agreement, it also applies between Switzerland and the EU.

Through the **European Economic Area**, EEA for short, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein also take part in the single market. On **6 December 1992** the people and the cantons in Switzerland narrowly said no to the EEA. After that Switzerland chose the path of **bilateral agreements**. With them it has access to the single market in certain areas.

So that goods can be sold everywhere, shared rules apply. Many products such as toys or electrical appliances carry the **CE mark**. With it, the manufacturer declares that the product meets the EU's requirements, for example on safety. You can also see the mark on many products in Switzerland.

gewusst: Liechtenstein is part of the single market through the EEA; Switzerland is not.
The CE mark is not a seal of approval from an authority but a declaration by the manufacturer.

teile.einleitung: A diplomatic representation is an office of a state abroad. The most important forms are embassies and consulates. They maintain relations with the host country and help their own nationals.
wichtigste: The embassy is a state's most important representation in the capital of another state.
Consulates help their own nationals, for example with lost passports.
Honorary consuls represent a country on a voluntary basis.
An embassy is inviolable: the authorities of the host country may not enter it without permission.
New ambassadors present their letter of credence to the head of state.
In 2024 more than 800,000 Swiss people lived abroad.

abschnitte.text: The **embassy** is a state's most important representation. It is usually in the **capital** of the host country and is headed by an **ambassador**. The embassy talks to the government of the host country, observes its politics and promotes business and culture. The Swiss embassy in **Berlin** is special: its building survived the Second World War and today stands right next to the German **Federal Chancellery**.

A **consulate** deals mainly with people. It helps its own nationals, for example with a lost **passport** or in an emergency, and issues documents. There are often consulates in large cities outside the capital too. Where there is no embassy, **honorary consuls** sometimes help. They are not career diplomats; they usually work in another profession and represent the country **on a voluntary basis**.

The rules are in the **Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations** of 1961. An embassy is **inviolable**: the police and authorities of the host country may only enter it with the consent of the head of mission. The host country must also protect it. At the start of her term of office, a new ambassador presents her **letter of credence** to the head of state. With it, her country confirms that she officially represents it.

In 2024 **more than 800,000** Swiss nationals lived abroad, most of them in Europe. They are called **Swiss abroad** or the **Fifth Switzerland**.
