For them and for travellers, the **FDFA** runs a network of embassies and consulates. With the **Travel Admin** app you can read travel advice and register your trip with the FDFA. In this way the FDFA can reach travellers better in a crisis.

gewusst: Contrary to what many people believe, an embassy is not territory of the country that runs it. It lies in the host country but is protected by special rules.
At international organisations such as the UN in Geneva, states have their own representations called “permanent missions”.

teile.einleitung: The European Free Trade Association, EFTA for short, is a free trade association of European countries outside the EU. Today it has only four members: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. Together they make trade agreements with countries all over the world.
wichtigste: EFTA is a free trade association of European countries outside the EU.
It was founded in Stockholm in 1960.
Switzerland is a founding member.
Today EFTA has four members: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.
The seat of the Secretariat is in Geneva.
EFTA has made free trade agreements with many countries around the world.
Unlike the EU, EFTA has no shared government and no shared parliament.

abschnitte.text: EFTA stands for European Free Trade Association. Its members want to trade goods without customs duties among themselves and with other countries. This is called **free trade**. Unlike the EU, however, EFTA does not want to be a political union.

EFTA was founded in 1960 with the Stockholm Convention. The founding members were Denmark, Great Britain, Norway, Austria, Portugal, Sweden and Switzerland. At the time they formed a counterweight to the European Economic Community. Later Iceland, Finland and Liechtenstein joined.

Many countries left EFTA again to join the **European Community**. Great Britain and Denmark left in 1973, Portugal in 1986, and Austria, Finland and Sweden in 1995. Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland were left. Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway are also members of the European Economic Area; Switzerland is not.

The EFTA countries negotiate **free trade agreements** together with countries outside Europe. Partners include, for example, Canada, Mexico, South Korea, Singapore and many other countries. In 2024 EFTA signed a trade agreement with India. Such agreements are important for the Swiss economy, because it exports a lot abroad.

The EFTA Secretariat has its seat in **Geneva**. The most important body is the EFTA Council, in which every member country is represented. For the EEA countries there is also a Surveillance Authority and the **EFTA Court** in Luxembourg. Decisions in EFTA are usually taken unanimously.

begriffe.erklaerung: Trade between countries without customs duties and with as few obstacles as possible.
A charge you have to pay when goods are brought across a border.
Selling goods abroad.
A treaty between countries.

gewusst: Of the seven founding members of EFTA, only Norway and Switzerland are still part of it today.
With Liechtenstein, one of the smallest countries in the world belongs to EFTA.

teile.einleitung: The European Commission is something like the government of the European Union. It has its seat in Brussels, where most of the EU's other important institutions are also based. Its most important task is to propose new laws and to make sure that the EU's rules are kept.
wichtigste: The European Commission is the executive body of the EU.
Its seat is in Brussels, where the most important EU institutions are based.
The Commission proposes laws; Parliament votes on them together with the Council of the EU.
Each member state provides one member of the Commission, so 27 in total.
Ursula von der Leyen has been President of the Commission since 2019.
The Commission is also called the guardian of the treaties.
Its main building in Brussels is called the Berlaymont.

abschnitte.text: The **European Commission** is one of the most important institutions of the EU. It is often compared to a government, because it plans and carries out the EU's policies. Its members are called **commissioners**; each is responsible for an area such as the environment, trade or transport. They are meant to be independent and represent the interests of the whole EU, not those of their home country.

Almost all new EU laws start with a proposal from the Commission. This right is called the **right of initiative**. The proposal is then discussed by the European Parliament and the Council of the EU, in which the countries' ministers sit. Only when both agree does the proposal become law.

The Commission checks whether the member states keep to the EU's rules. That is why it is called the **guardian of the treaties**. If a country does not keep to the rules, the Commission can take it to the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg. It also makes sure that large companies do not distort competition, and it can impose large fines.

At the top is the **President of the Commission**; since 2019 this has been Ursula von der Leyen from Germany. She is proposed by the European Council and elected by the European Parliament. The Commission is appointed for five years. For its work it has tens of thousands of staff, most of them in Brussels.

The Commission's headquarters is the **Berlaymont building** in Brussels, a large building with four wings arranged in a star shape. The European Council, the Council of the EU and many offices of Parliament are also in Brussels. That is why Brussels is seen as the unofficial capital of Europe. For Switzerland, the Commission is the most important negotiating partner for agreements with the EU.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body with fixed tasks within an organisation such as the EU.
A member of the European Commission who is responsible for a particular area.
The right to propose new laws.
A penalty paid in money.

gewusst: Ursula von der Leyen is the first woman to head the European Commission.
The Berlaymont building had to be renovated for years because of asbestos and stood empty from 1991 to 2004.

teile.einleitung: A diplomat represents their own country abroad. Diplomats keep up good relations with other countries and try to settle disputes through talks.
wichtigste: Diplomats represent their country in other countries.
Diplomacy means settling disputes through talks and negotiations.
Good speaking and listening skills, and often several languages, are important.
Swiss diplomats work for the FDFA.
They travel with a diplomatic passport.
Many move to a different country every few years.

abschnitte.text: A **diplomat** works for their country in another country. They talk to the government there, explain their country's position and keep up good relations. They often work in an **embassy**. Diplomats negotiate treaties, promote trade and help with problems. Settling disputes between countries through talks is called **diplomacy**.

Diplomats must be good at **speaking** and good at **listening**. They should stay calm and polite even in difficult situations. Many speak **several languages**, often including the language of the host country. In the past **French** was long the most important language of diplomacy in Europe. Today English is mostly spoken, but French is still important.

Swiss diplomats work for the **FDFA**, the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs. Switzerland is known for its **good offices**: it mediates between countries that are in dispute and organises peace talks. Sometimes it takes on a **protecting power mandate**; it then represents one country in another when the two have no direct relations. An especially large number of diplomats from all over the world meet in **Geneva**.

Diplomats travel with a **diplomatic passport**. It shows that they are travelling on behalf of their country. Under the **Vienna Convention** of 1961 they enjoy **immunity**: the host country may not simply arrest them. In this way they can do their work without pressure. If they do not keep to the laws, however, the host country can expel them.

Many diplomats change their **place of work** every few years. Then they move to another country with their family. That is why diplomats' children often go to school in different countries. Large meetings at which representatives of many countries negotiate are called **conferences**. In everyday life, we say someone is **diplomatic** when they say things in a friendly and skilful way.

gewusst: Since 1980 Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran, because the two countries have no direct relations.
The word “diplomat” comes from the Greek “diploma”, a folded document of the kind that envoys used to carry.

teile.einleitung: **Argentina** is a large country in the south of South America. It stretches from hot regions in the north to icy areas in Patagonia. It is known for the tango, football and the huge grasslands of the Pampas.
wichtigste: The capital of Argentina is Buenos Aires.
Buenos Aires means “good airs”.
People in Argentina speak Spanish.
The presidential palace is called the Casa Rosada, the pink house.
The tango comes from Buenos Aires and Montevideo.
People pay with the Argentine peso.

abschnitte.text: The capital and largest city is **Buenos Aires**. The name is Spanish and means “good airs” or “good winds”. The city lies on the **Río de la Plata**. This estuary is so wide that you can hardly see the other shore. **Pope Francis**, who was Pope from 2013 to 2025, was also born in Buenos Aires.

Argentina used to be a **colony of Spain**. That is why **Spanish** is spoken there. In 1816 the country declared its independence. Later many people emigrated there from Europe, especially from Italy and Spain. Many families from Switzerland also moved to Argentina in the 19th century.

Argentina is a **republic**. The people elect a **president**, who leads the country. He works in the **Casa Rosada**, the pink-painted presidential palace in Buenos Aires. People pay with the **Argentine peso**. Other countries in Latin America also have a currency with this name.

The **tango** began more than 100 years ago in Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Today it is danced all over the world. Almost as famous is **football**. Argentina has been world champion three times: in 1978, 1986 and 2022. Many children play football in the street and dream of a great career.

Argentina is one of the largest countries in the world. In the west lie the **Andes** with **Aconcagua**, the highest mountain in America. In the middle stretch the flat **Pampas**, where many cattle graze. In the far south lies **Patagonia**, with glaciers and penguins. On the border with Brazil, the mighty Iguazú Falls plunge into the depths.

gewusst: The city of Buenos Aires was named after a patron saint of sailors who was supposed to bring good winds.
Aconcagua in Argentina is almost 7000 metres high.

teile.einleitung: Bern is Switzerland's federal city, where the Federal Council and Parliament meet. Because the government is based here, many foreign states also have their embassies in Bern. The medieval Old City on the River Aare is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: The Swiss government, the Federal Council, meets in Bern.
In 1848 Bern was chosen as the seat of the federal authorities.
Officially Bern is called the federal city, not the capital.
The Federal Council, the National Council and the Council of States meet in the Federal Palace.
Many states have an embassy in Bern.
The Universal Postal Union, a UN organisation, is based in Bern.

abschnitte.text: After the federal state was founded, Bern was chosen as the seat of the government and Parliament in November 1848. Switzerland has no official capital, which is why Bern is called the **federal city**. Other tasks were deliberately shared out among other towns; for example, the Federal Supreme Court is in Lausanne. In this way not all offices were to be in one place.

The **Federal Palace** was opened in 1902 and has a large green dome. The National Council and the Council of States meet here, and the Federal Council holds its meetings here. In front of the building is the Federal Square with a fountain display. During state visits, guests from abroad are often welcomed in front of the Federal Palace.

Because the government is in Bern, many countries have their **embassy** here. An ambassador is received by the Federal Council and presents a letter of credence. The **Department of Foreign Affairs**, Switzerland's foreign ministry, is also based in Bern. Switzerland's foreign policy is planned from here.

Since 1874 the **Universal Postal Union** has been based in Bern. It makes sure that letters and parcels can be sent between almost all the countries of the world. Today it belongs to the UN family. However, most of the other international organisations in Switzerland are in Geneva.

Bern was founded around 1191 by Duke Berthold V of Zähringen. The Old City lies in a loop of the River Aare and has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1983. Its arcades, the Zytglogge tower with its astronomical clock and the Bear Park are well known. Albert Einstein lived here during the years when he developed the theory of relativity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The seat of Switzerland's government and Parliament.
The building in Bern where the Federal Council and Parliament work.
The representation of one country in another country.
Places that UNESCO protects as especially valuable for all of humankind.

gewusst: The Swiss Federal Constitution names no capital; in laws Bern is only called the federal city.
In summer many people from Bern swim in the Aare right past the Federal Palace.

t1hsq4np.t: Official languages of the United Nations

teile.einleitung: The United Nations, UN for short, has six official languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish. Important documents are published and speeches interpreted in these languages. In this way delegates from all over the world can understand each other.
wichtigste: The UN has six official languages.
They are Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.
English and French are the working languages of the UN Secretariat.
At many international conferences, French is often spoken as well as English.
Interpreters translate speeches into all six languages at the same time.
Arabic was the last official language to be added, in 1973.

abschnitte.text: When the UN was founded in 1945, five languages were chosen: Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish. In 1973 **Arabic** was added as the sixth language. These languages are spoken by a great many people or are official languages in many countries. All the UN's important decisions are available in each of these six **official languages**.

In the day-to-day work of the UN administration, the Secretariat, English and French are used most. They are called the **working languages**. French was long the most important language of diplomacy. That is why it is still often heard at conferences today, especially in Geneva, where a lot of French is spoken.

When someone speaks in the General Assembly, **interpreters** translate the speech straight away into the other languages. They sit in small booths and speak almost at the same time as the speaker. The listeners wear headphones and choose their language. This technique is called **simultaneous interpreting** and became well known after the Second World War at the Nuremberg trials.

Besides interpreting, there are many translators who translate written documents. Every year huge amounts of reports and decisions are translated. German is not an official language of the UN. However, the German-speaking countries pay for their own translation service, which translates important documents into German.

Switzerland has been a member of the UN since 2002, and Geneva is its second most important seat after New York. Of Switzerland's four national languages, only French is a UN official language. The University of Geneva has a well-known Faculty of Translation and Interpreting. That is why many Swiss people who speak several languages work for international organisations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A language used officially by authorities and for documents.
The language used in the everyday work of an organisation.
A person who translates spoken language orally.
Translating almost at the same time as someone is speaking.

gewusst: For each of the six official languages, the UN celebrates its own language day every year.
Chinese is the official language with the most native speakers, and English is the most learned foreign language.

teile.einleitung: Eleanor Roosevelt was an American politician, writer and human rights campaigner. She was First Lady of the USA and later led the UN group that drew up the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
wichtigste: Eleanor Roosevelt lived from 1884 to 1962 and was born in New York.
In 1905 she married Franklin D. Roosevelt, who later became the 32nd President of the USA.
From 1933 to 1945 she was First Lady.
From 1935 to 1962 she wrote the newspaper column “My Day” almost every day.
From 1945 to 1952 she represented the USA at the UN.
She chaired the UN Commission on Human Rights.
President Harry Truman called her “First Lady of the World”.

abschnitte.text: Eleanor Roosevelt was born in **New York City** in **1884**. She lost her parents early and grew up with her grandmother. As a teenager she went to a school in England, which gave her self-confidence. In **1905** she married **Franklin D. Roosevelt**, a distant relative. Her uncle **Theodore Roosevelt** was President of the USA at the time.

Franklin D. Roosevelt was President of the USA from **1933 to 1945**. He led the country through the **Great Depression** and the **Second World War**. During this time Eleanor was **First Lady**. She used this role more actively than anyone before her. She travelled around the country, visited poor people and workers and reported back to her husband. She even held **press conferences for women journalists only**, so that women could also find work at newspapers.

From **1935 to 1962**, Eleanor Roosevelt wrote the newspaper column **“My Day”** almost every day. In it she told of her experiences and gave her opinion on important questions. Many newspapers across the country printed the column. She also wrote books and gave many talks.

After her husband's death in 1945 she became a **US delegate to the UN**, until 1952. She chaired the UN **Commission on Human Rights**. This group wrote the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights**, which the UN adopted in Paris on 10 December 1948. All her life, Eleanor Roosevelt stood up for the rights of **women**, poor people and the disadvantaged. That is why President Harry Truman called her the **“First Lady of the World”**.

gewusst: To this day, 10 December is celebrated every year as Human Rights Day.
Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the USA, because her husband was elected president four times.

teile.einleitung: The Dublin Regulation is a rule of the European Union. It lays down which country is responsible for examining an asylum application. Switzerland has applied it since December 2008.
wichtigste: The first Dublin Convention was signed in 1990 in Dublin, the capital of Ireland.
It came into force in 1997.
Often the responsible country is the one a person entered first.
Fingerprints are compared in the Eurodac database.
Switzerland has applied the Dublin rules since 12 December 2008.
In Switzerland, the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) is responsible.

abschnitte.text: The Dublin rules are named after **Dublin**, the capital of **Ireland**. The first **Dublin Convention** was signed there in **1990**. It came into force in **1997**. Later it was replaced by EU regulations: the **Dublin II Regulation** of 2003 and the **Dublin III Regulation** of 2013. A **regulation** applies directly in all member states.

Each asylum application should be examined **only once**, by one clearly defined country. Often this is the country a person **entered first**. But there are exceptions, for example when **family members** already live in another Dublin country. If another country is responsible, the person can be taken there. This is called a **Dublin transfer**.

For the system to work, a shared database is needed: **Eurodac**. The **fingerprints** of asylum seekers are stored and compared there. This lets the authorities see whether someone has already made an application in another country or entered it.

Switzerland is not an EU member, but it takes part in Dublin through an agreement. The people voted in favour in 2005, and on **12 December 2008** **Schengen and Dublin** came into effect in Switzerland. The **State Secretariat for Migration (SEM)** is responsible. It decides on asylum applications and checks whether another Dublin country is responsible. The advantage for Switzerland: anyone who has already applied in another Dublin country is usually sent back there. Critics, on the other hand, point out that countries on the external borders have to examine a particularly large number of applications.

gewusst: Although the rules are named after the Irish capital, they also apply in countries outside the EU, such as Switzerland and Norway.
Schengen and Dublin came into effect in Switzerland on the same day, 12 December 2008.

teile.einleitung: An embassy is the official representation of one country in another country. It helps two states to talk to each other and keep up good relations.
wichtigste: An embassy is headed by an ambassador.
Embassies are usually in the capital; in Switzerland that means in Bern.
The flag of the country it represents flies at the embassy.
The police of the host country may only go in with permission.
Even so, the ground an embassy stands on remains part of the host country.
Switzerland has about 170 representations abroad (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: When two countries have **diplomatic relations**, they often open embassies in each other's country. In this way they can talk to each other directly. The staff are called **diplomats**. They negotiate, keep their government informed and look after the economy and culture. The head is the **ambassador**.

Embassies are **specially protected**. This is set out in an international treaty, the **Vienna Convention** on Diplomatic Relations of 1961. The police of the host country may only go in with the ambassador's **permission**. Even so, the ground still belongs to the **host country**. So a foreign embassy in Bern stands on Swiss soil.

Embassies are usually in a country's **capital**. In Switzerland that is the federal city of **Bern**. There are many foreign embassies there. The ambassador often lives in a **residence**, where receptions for guests are also held. The **flag** of the country it represents flies at every embassy.

According to the **FDFA**, Switzerland has about 170 representations abroad (as of 2026). They include embassies, **consulates** and cooperation offices. The embassy in France is in **Paris**, and consulates help in other towns too. The Swiss embassy in **Berlin** is an old building in the middle of the government quarter, right next to the **Federal Chancellery**.

gewusst: Switzerland sometimes acts as a protecting power, representing the interests of a country that has no direct relations with another.
Consulates mainly help their own citizens, for example when someone has lost their passport.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Europe shows a circle of twelve golden stars on a blue background. It is the best-known symbol of the European Union and of the Council of Europe. You can see it on public offices, number plates and euro notes.
wichtigste: The flag shows twelve golden stars in a circle on a blue background.
The Council of Europe introduced the flag in 1955.
Since 1986 the European Community, today the EU, has also used this flag.
The number twelve has nothing to do with the number of member states.
Twelve is seen as a symbol of perfection and unity.
The circle stands for solidarity and harmony between the peoples of Europe.

abschnitte.text: The **flag of Europe** is a blue rectangle with twelve golden-yellow, five-pointed stars. The stars form a circle, rather like the numbers on a clock face. Each star stands upright with one point at the top. The blue is meant to recall the sky above Europe.

The flag was introduced in 1955 by the **Council of Europe** in Strasbourg. Arsène Heitz and Paul Lévy, who examined many designs, are seen as its designers. In 1985 the heads of state and government of the European Community decided to adopt the same flag. Since 1986 it has officially flown in front of the European institutions.

Many people believe the stars stand for the member states, but that is not true. Since ancient times the number **twelve** has been seen as a sign of perfection and completeness; think of twelve months or twelve hours on a clock face. That is why the number stays the same even when new countries join. The **circle** stands for unity and solidarity.

The flag flies in front of the EU buildings in Brussels and Strasbourg and in front of many public offices in the member states. On the **number plates** of many EU countries you can see a small circle of stars with the country code. You can also find it on the euro banknotes and on many projects paid for by the EU. In Switzerland you see it, for example, in connection with the Council of Europe, of which Switzerland is a member.

Besides the flag, the EU has other **symbols**. The European anthem is a melody from Ludwig van Beethoven's 9th Symphony, the Ode to Joy. The EU's motto is “United in diversity”. On 9 May the EU celebrates **Europe Day**; the Council of Europe celebrates its Europe Day on 5 May.

begriffe.erklaerung: A piece of cloth with colours and signs that stands for a country or an organisation.
An organisation of European countries for human rights and democracy, which Switzerland also belongs to.
A sign that stands for an idea or a community.
A solemn song that represents a country or an organisation.

gewusst: The flag of Europe is older than the European Union itself, because it was introduced back in 1955.
Even when the EU got more than twelve members, the number of stars on the flag stayed the same.

teile.einleitung: The **Bank for International Settlements**, **BIS** for short, is based in **Basel**. It is not a bank for ordinary people but the bank of the central banks. It helps the world's central banks to work together.
wichtigste: The BIS was founded in 1930.
It is called the “bank of the central banks”.
It is based in Basel on the Rhine.
The Swiss National Bank is also a member.
It is regarded as the oldest international financial organisation in the world.
Private individuals cannot open an account at the BIS.

abschnitte.titel: The bank of the central banks
abschnitte.text: Every country has a **central bank**, which looks after the country's money. These central banks have their accounts at the BIS. That is why it is also called the “**bank of the central banks**”. In Switzerland the central bank is the **Swiss National Bank**, which is also a member of the BIS. The heads of the central banks meet regularly at the BIS to talk about the world economy.

The BIS was founded in **1930**. At that time it dealt, among other things, with payments that Germany had to make after the First World War. Today it is almost 100 years old. It is regarded as the **oldest international financial organisation** in the world. Other large organisations such as the International Monetary Fund were only founded later.

The BIS is based in **Basel**. The city lies on the **Rhine**, where Switzerland, Germany and France meet. The best-known BIS building is a tall, **round tower**. It was built in the 1970s and can easily be seen in Basel.

A child cannot open a **savings account** at the BIS. Adults cannot either. Only **central banks** and **international organisations** may put money there. So the BIS is a very special bank that you hardly notice in everyday life.

gewusst: Important rules for banks all over the world are prepared at the BIS in Basel, which is why some of them are called “Basel III”.
The BIS was founded long before the euro existed.

teile.einleitung: ASEAN is an association of states in South-East Asia. The members work together on the economy, politics, security and culture. The association was founded in 1967 and has had eleven members since 2025.
wichtigste: ASEAN stands for Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
ASEAN was founded in Bangkok on 8 August 1967.
The Secretariat is based in Jakarta.
Its members include, for example, Vietnam and the city state of Singapore.
In October 2025 East Timor became the eleventh member.
China, Japan and South Korea are important partners but not members.
In 2021 Switzerland voted on an economic agreement with Indonesia.

abschnitte.text: ASEAN stands for “**Association of Southeast Asian Nations**”. The members want to work together for **peace**, **prosperity** and **trade** in their region. Two principles are important: decisions are usually made by **consensus**, that is, when everyone agrees. And the states try not to interfere in each other's internal affairs.

ASEAN was founded on **8 August 1967** in **Bangkok**, the capital of Thailand. That is why its founding declaration is also called the **Bangkok Declaration**. Five states signed: **Indonesia**, **Malaysia**, the **Philippines**, **Singapore** and **Thailand**. The permanent **Secretariat** is in **Jakarta**, the capital of Indonesia. Cooperation is organised there.

Bit by bit other countries joined: **Brunei** in 1984, **Vietnam** in 1995, **Laos** and **Myanmar** in 1997 and **Cambodia** in 1999. For a long time ASEAN therefore had ten members. In October **2025** **East Timor** became the **eleventh member**. The members also include the **city state of Singapore**. East Asian countries such as **China**, **Japan** and **South Korea** are important partners but not members.

Several hundred million people live in South-East Asia. The ASEAN states have created a **free trade area** among themselves. Many customs duties have been removed so that goods can cross borders more easily. ASEAN also regularly holds **summits**, attended by guests from many countries. Difficult topics include, for example, disputes in the **South China Sea**.

Through **EFTA**, Switzerland has concluded agreements with several ASEAN countries. On **7 March 2021** Swiss voters voted on the economic agreement with **Indonesia** and narrowly approved it. Trade in **palm oil** was particularly controversial. Opponents feared damage to the rainforest. Supporters pointed out that the agreement contains rules for sustainable palm oil.

gewusst: The ASEAN logo shows a bundle of ten rice stalks, which stands for the community of the countries of South-East Asia.
8 August, the founding day, is celebrated in the member countries as ASEAN Day.

teile.einleitung: Elizabeth II was Queen of the United Kingdom from 1952 to 2022. With around 70 years on the throne, she reigned longer than any British king or queen before her.
wichtigste: Elizabeth was born in London in 1926.
In 1952 she became queen at the age of 25, when her father King George VI died.
She was queen for around 70 years.
She had four children: three sons and a daughter.
She loved corgis and horses.
In 2022 Britain celebrated her Platinum Jubilee.
She died in 2022 at the age of 96 at Balmoral Castle in Scotland.

abschnitte.text: Elizabeth was born in **London** on **21 April 1926**. She was the elder daughter of King **George VI**. At first nobody expected her to become queen. But in 1936 her uncle gave up the throne, and her father became king. This made Elizabeth next in line to the throne. In the Second World War, as a young woman, she served in an auxiliary unit of the army and learnt to drive and repair lorries.

In 1947 Elizabeth married **Prince Philip**. When her father died in **1952**, she became queen at the age of **25**. The ceremonial **coronation** took place in Westminster Abbey in 1953 and was shown on television. Elizabeth and Philip had **four children**: **Charles**, Anne, Andrew and Edward. Charles, her eldest son, succeeded her as King Charles III.

Elizabeth II had many **corgis** in her life. These are small dogs with short legs and big ears. They almost became a trademark of the Queen. She also loved **horses**. She was still riding at over 90 and also owned **racehorses**, which won many races.

In 2022 Britain celebrated the **Platinum Jubilee**: 70 years on the throne. For four days there were parades, concerts and street parties. No British monarch had ever reigned so long. On **8 September 2022**, Elizabeth II died at the age of **96** at **Balmoral Castle** in Scotland. She was queen until the very end. Many people around the world mourned her.

gewusst: During her reign, Elizabeth II was queen of more than 30 different countries in total; many of them later became republics.
During her reign, Britain had 15 different prime ministers.

teile.einleitung: 10 Downing Street is one of the best-known addresses in the world. The British Prime Minister lives and works in this house in London. The black front door with the white number 10 is familiar from many news pictures.
wichtigste: 10 Downing Street is in London, near Parliament.
It is the official residence and home of the British Prime Minister.
The front door is black and has no keyhole on the outside.
On the door hangs a door knocker with a lion's head.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer has his official residence in number 11.
The street is named after George Downing.
Larry the cat has lived in the house since 2011 and catches mice.

abschnitte.text: **Downing Street** is a small street in **London**, very close to **Parliament**. In the house with the number 10, the **British Prime Minister** has his **official residence** and his home. Here he meets guests from all over the world, and here the government meets. From the outside the house looks rather modest. Inside, however, it is much bigger, because several buildings are joined together.

The famous **front door** is **black** and bears a white **10**. On it hangs a **door knocker** with a **lion's head**. A special feature: the door has **no keyhole** on the outside. It is always opened from the inside, because someone is always there. Prime Ministers often give speeches in front of this door, for example on their first day in office. Today there are security gates at the entrance to the street.

The street is named after **George Downing**. He had the houses built around **1680**. In the 18th century the king gave the house at number 10 to the politician **Robert Walpole**. Walpole is regarded as the first Prime Minister of Great Britain. However, he did not want to keep the house for himself but for everyone who would hold this office after him. Since then it has been the official residence of Prime Ministers.

Right next door, at **11 Downing Street**, the **Chancellor of the Exchequer** has his official residence. That is what the **finance minister** is called in Great Britain. The houses are connected inside. Sometimes the Prime Minister and the Chancellor even swap flats, because the flat in number 11 is bigger. More government staff work in number 12.

For a long time, cats have lived in the house again and again to catch **mice**. The best known is **Larry** the cat. He has lived in Downing Street since **2011** and has the title “**Chief Mouser**”. Larry has already seen several Prime Ministers. He is very popular with photographers.

gewusst: The door of 10 Downing Street cannot be unlocked from the outside, because it has no keyhole at all.
Since 2011, Larry the cat has seen several Prime Ministers come and go.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Chancellery is the official seat of the German Federal Chancellor in Berlin. The large, modern building stands on the River Spree, very close to the Reichstag building.
wichtigste: The Federal Chancellery stands right on the Spree in Berlin.
It is about eight times as big as the White House in Washington.
Because of its round windows, some Berliners call it the “washing machine”.
A bridge leads across the Spree to the Chancellor's Park.
Nearby stands the Reichstag building, where the Bundestag meets.
Since May 2025 Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz has worked there (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: The Federal Chancellor and many staff work in the **Federal Chancellery**. Here the government's work is prepared and coordinated. The building is huge: it is about **eight times as big** as the **White House** in Washington. It was moved into in 2001, after the government had moved from Bonn to Berlin. The chancellor also receives state guests here.

The building has a light-coloured façade with large **round windows**. That is why some Berliners jokingly call it the **“washing machine”**. There are other nicknames too. The Chancellery stands in the **government quarter**, which is also called the “Federal Ribbon”. These buildings are arranged in a long row and connect the two banks of the Spree.

The **Spree** flows right through the middle of Berlin. The Chancellery stands directly on its bank. On the other side lies the **Chancellor's Park**. A bridge, the **Chancellery footbridge**, leads from the Chancellery across the river to it. Only a few steps away stands the **Reichstag building** with its glass dome. The **Bundestag**, the German parliament, meets there.

In May 2025 the Bundestag elected **Friedrich Merz** as Federal Chancellor. Before him, **Angela Merkel** governed for 16 years, from 2005 to 2021, followed by Olaf Scholz. The neighbouring country of **Austria** also has a **Federal Chancellor** as head of government. Its Federal Chancellery is in **Vienna** on the Ballhausplatz. In Switzerland, on the other hand, there is no single head of government.

gewusst: The Swiss embassy in Berlin is right next to the Federal Chancellery.
In Switzerland the Federal Chancellery works in the Federal Palace in Bern.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background. It is square, which is very rare for national flags. Its history goes back to the old banner of the canton of Schwyz.
wichtigste: The Swiss flag is red with a white cross.
It is square, like only the flag of Vatican City.
The cross has four arms of equal length.
Each arm is one sixth longer than it is wide.
The cross on red comes from the banner of Schwyz.
The Red Cross is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss flag is a **square**. In the middle is a **white cross** on a **red background**. Almost all other countries have rectangular flags. Only **Vatican City** also has a square national flag. That is why you recognise the Swiss flag straight away.

The **Swiss cross** has **four arms of equal length** that start from the middle. Each arm is **one sixth longer than it is wide**. The cross does not touch the edge of the flag. This shape was laid down exactly by the Confederation in the **19th century**. The same cross can also be found in the **Swiss coat of arms** and on many Swiss products.

The roots of the flag lie in the canton of **Schwyz**. It had a **red banner** early on; later a small white cross was added. The **name Switzerland** also comes from Schwyz. Over time the white cross on red became the shared sign of the Confederates. Since the founding of the federal state in **1848**, it has been the official sign of the whole country.

The **Red Cross** was founded in **Geneva** in the **19th century**. An important founder was the Genevan **Henry Dunant**. In honour of Switzerland, the movement chose as its sign the **Swiss flag with the colours reversed**: a red cross on white. Today this sign protects helpers and hospitals in war zones all over the world.

There is one exception to the square shape. **Ships** that sail under the Swiss flag on the **high seas** fly a **rectangular** flag. Rectangular flags are usual at sea. On **1 August**, the **National Day**, you see the Swiss flag everywhere: on houses, on paper lanterns and on boats on the lakes.

gewusst: The canton of Schwyz still has a small white cross in the top corner of its red flag today.
Anyone who wants to advertise with the Swiss cross must keep to strict rules, so that it stands only for genuine Swiss products.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Australia is dark blue and shows the Union Jack and six white stars. It tells of the country's history and of its place in the Southern Hemisphere.
wichtigste: The background colour of the flag is blue.
In the top left is the Union Jack, the flag of Great Britain.
In the bottom left is the large Commonwealth Star with seven points.
On the right is the constellation of the Southern Cross.
In total the flag has six white stars.
The flag was chosen through a competition in 1901.

abschnitte.text: In the top left of the dark blue flag is the **Union Jack**. This is the flag of the United Kingdom. It is a reminder that Australia used to be made up of **British colonies**. Even today the country is closely linked to Great Britain.

Below the Union Jack is a large white star. It is called the **Commonwealth Star** and stands for the joining of Australia into a **federation** in 1901. The star has **seven points**. Six stand for the states and one for the country's territories.

On the right of the flag is the constellation of the **Southern Cross**, with five white stars. Australia lies in the **Southern Hemisphere**. There this constellation can be seen clearly in the night sky. Together with the Commonwealth Star, the flag has **six stars**. All the stars are **white**.

In 1901 there was a **competition** for the new flag. Tens of thousands of people sent in designs. The flag of the neighbouring country, **New Zealand**, looks similar. It is also blue with the Union Jack and shows the Southern Cross. But its stars are **red** with a white border.

gewusst: In 1901 tens of thousands of people sent in designs for the flag of Australia.
Australia and New Zealand have very similar flags; only the colour of the stars is different.

teile.einleitung: Buckingham Palace stands in the middle of London. It is the official residence of the British king and one of the best-known palaces in the world. The guards with their tall hats are especially famous.
wichtigste: Buckingham Palace is in London.
It is the official residence of the British king.
The palace has about 775 rooms.
The guards wear tall black bearskin hats.
At the **Changing of the Guard**, new soldiers take over the guard with music.
When the king is in the palace, the Royal Standard flies on the roof.

abschnitte.text: **Buckingham Palace** has about **775 rooms**. Among them are 19 state rooms and 78 bathrooms. It was originally a large town house that came into the royal family's possession in the 18th century. Since **Queen Victoria** in the 19th century it has been the official residence of British monarchs. Here the king receives state guests and holds celebrations.

Soldiers of the King's Guard stand in front of the palace. They wear tall black **bearskin hats**. In summer they usually have **red tunics**, and in winter grey greatcoats. At the **Changing of the Guard**, new soldiers take over the guard. This happens with music and marching, and many tourists watch.

A flag flies on the roof of the palace. When the king is in the palace, the **Royal Standard** flies there. This is his personal flag. When he is not there, you usually see the British flag, the **Union Jack**. In this way people outside can tell whether the king is at home.

From the **balcony** at the front, the royal family waves to the crowd on big occasions, for example at weddings or jubilees. Behind the palace lies a **large garden** with a lake. It is one of the largest private gardens in London. In summer **garden parties** with many guests are held there. Some rooms of the palace can be visited in summer.

gewusst: Hundreds of people work at Buckingham Palace, from cooks to clockmakers.
In front of the palace stands a large memorial to Queen Victoria.

teile.einleitung: A member of parliament is an elected member of a parliament. Members of parliament represent the people of the country and help decide, for example, on laws. They have a slightly different name in every country.
wichtigste: Members of parliament are elected by the people and sit in parliament.
They represent the interests of the population, which is why they are also called representatives of the people.
They are often elected in a particular area, the constituency.
In Great Britain a member of the House of Commons is called an MP; the House of Commons has 650 members.
In the USA a member of the Senate is called a senator.
In Germany the pay of members of parliament is called “Diäten”.
Anyone who does not belong to a party is independent.

abschnitte.text: In a **democracy**, the people elect individuals to represent them in **parliament**. These people are called **members of parliament**. They are meant to represent the interests of the **population**, which is why they are also called **representatives of the people**. In parliament they debate **laws**, decide on the state's money and keep a check on the government. After a few years, elections are held again.

For elections, a country is often divided into areas. Such an area is called a **constituency**. In some countries exactly one person is elected per constituency. Most members of parliament belong to a **party**. In parliament they often work together in a **parliamentary group**. Some members of parliament do not belong to any party. They are called **independent**.

In **Great Britain** a member of the House of Commons is called an **MP**, which stands for “Member of Parliament”. There are **650** MPs in the British **House of Commons**, each representing a constituency. In the **USA** a member of the Senate is called a **senator**. A **governor**, on the other hand, leads a state and is not a member of parliament. In **Germany** the members of the Bundestag sit in the **Bundestag** in Berlin.

Members of parliament receive money for their work. In Germany this pay is called **“Diäten”**. Here the word has nothing to do with food or dieting. It comes from the Latin word for “day”, because in the past members were paid per day of sitting. The pay is meant to make sure that not only rich people can become members of parliament. How high it should be is debated again and again.

The Swiss parliament is called the **Federal Assembly**. It has two chambers: the **National Council** has **200** members, and the **Council of States** has **46**. The members are called **National Councillors** and **Councillors of States**. The constituencies are the **cantons**. Switzerland has a **militia parliament**: many members have another job besides their office.

gewusst: In the British House of Commons there are fewer seats than members, so at busy sittings some have to stand.
The members of the National Council and the Council of States are elected every four years.

teile.einleitung: Desmond Tutu was a South African clergyman of the Anglican Church. He fought non-violently against apartheid, the state system of racial segregation in South Africa, and received the Nobel Peace Prize for it in 1984.
wichtigste: Desmond Tutu was born in Klerksdorp in South Africa in 1931.
He worked non-violently against apartheid.
In 1984 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
In 1986 he became the first Black Archbishop of Cape Town.
From 1996 he led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
He coined the term “Rainbow Nation”.
He died in Cape Town on 26 December 2021 at the age of 90.

abschnitte.text: Desmond Tutu was born in **Klerksdorp** in **1931**. He grew up at a time when Black people in South Africa were heavily disadvantaged. At first he worked as a teacher. Later he became a **priest** of the **Anglican Church**, a church that began in England. He also studied in London and then became a bishop.

**Apartheid** was a system of state **racial segregation**. Black people were not allowed to vote or to live everywhere, and they had hardly any rights. Tutu demanded again and again that this injustice should end. In doing so he rejected **violence**. He called on other countries to put economic pressure on South Africa's government. In **1984** he received the **Nobel Peace Prize**, which made his struggle known worldwide.

In **1986** Tutu became **Archbishop of Cape Town**. This put him at the head of the Anglican Church in southern Africa. Before him, only white people had held this office. He used his voice to stand up for justice and spoke out bravely even when it was dangerous.

In the early 1990s apartheid came to an end. In 1994 **Nelson Mandela** became the first Black President. From **1996** Tutu led the **Truth and Reconciliation Commission**. It heard victims and perpetrators in order to uncover the crimes of apartheid. The aim was not revenge but for the country to find **reconciliation**.

Tutu coined the expression **Rainbow Nation**. By this he meant that people of all skin colours together form one country, just as the colours of a rainbow belong together. The term became very popular in South Africa. Tutu was known for his cheerful laugh and his sense of humour. He died in Cape Town on **26 December 2021**.

gewusst: Desmond Tutu and Nelson Mandela both received the Nobel Peace Prize, Mandela in 1993.
Tutu was often affectionately called “The Arch”, short for archbishop.

teile.einleitung: The Andean Community is an association of states in South America that lie along the Andes. The members want to work together more closely on the economy and make trade between them easier. It was founded in 1969 as the Andean Pact.
wichtigste: The Andean Pact was founded in 1969 with the Cartagena Agreement.
The full members are Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia and Peru (as of 2025).
Chile left in 1976, and Venezuela announced its withdrawal in 2006.
The General Secretariat is in Lima, and the Court of Justice in Quito.
Since the Trujillo Protocol of 1996, the Andean Pact has been called the Andean Community.
The judgements of the Andean Court of Justice are binding on the members.

abschnitte.text: The **Andes** are the longest mountain range in the world. They run along the western side of South America. Several countries along the Andes have joined together to strengthen their economies. On **26 May 1969** they signed the **Cartagena Agreement**. This is how the **Andean Pact** came about. The members wanted to remove customs duties and appear stronger together.

Over the decades several members have left. **Chile** left the pact as early as **1976** under Pinochet's military government. It wanted to follow a more liberal economic policy with lower customs duties. In **2006** **Venezuela** announced its withdrawal. President Hugo Chávez gave as his reason the free trade agreements of Colombia and Peru with the USA. Today **Bolivia**, **Ecuador**, **Colombia** and **Peru** are full members (as of 2025), and other states are associated.

With the **Trujillo Protocol** of **1996**, the Andean Pact was given the name **Andean Community**, in Spanish **Comunidad Andina**. The protocol reformed the institutions and created the **Andean Integration System**. The **General Secretariat** is the executive body and is in **Lima**, the capital of Peru. The **Court of Justice** of the Andean Community is in **Quito**, the capital of Ecuador. It interprets community law, and its judgements are binding.

Through **EFTA**, Switzerland has concluded free trade agreements with several countries of the Andean Community. The agreements with **Colombia** and **Peru** have applied since **2011**, and the one with **Ecuador** since **2020**. They make trade easier, for example in machines, medicines or watches from Switzerland and in coffee, flowers or fruit from South America.

gewusst: Citizens of the member countries can usually travel within the Andean Community with just their identity card.
The Andean Community is older than the European Union in its present form.

teile.einleitung: On 19 September 1946 the British politician Winston Churchill gave a speech about the future of Europe at the University of Zurich. It is regarded as an important impulse for European unification after the Second World War.
wichtigste: Churchill spoke in the great hall of the University of Zurich on 19 September 1946.
He addressed the “academic youth”, that is, students.
He called for a kind of “United States of Europe”.
As a first step he demanded a partnership between France and Germany.
He proposed founding a Council of Europe, which came about in 1949.
At that time Churchill was Leader of the Opposition in the British Parliament.
The speech ended with the call “Let Europe arise!”.

abschnitte.text: **Winston Churchill** had led Great Britain through the Second World War as Prime Minister. In 1945, however, his party lost the election. In 1946 he was therefore **Leader of the Opposition** in the British Parliament. In late summer 1946 he spent a holiday in Switzerland. On **19 September 1946** he spoke in the **great hall of the University of Zurich** to students, the “academic youth”.

After the war Europe lay in ruins. Churchill wanted to prevent the European countries from going to war with each other again. He called for the creation of a kind of **United States of Europe**. The peoples of Europe were to live together in peace, safety and freedom. He saw Great Britain as a friend and supporter rather than as a member.

One proposal was especially surprising: the first step, he said, must be a **partnership between France and Germany**. The two countries had fought each other in several wars. Only a year after the end of the war, that was a bold idea. Later the reconciliation of the two countries did indeed become the core of European unification.

As a first practical step, Churchill proposed a **Council of Europe**. It was founded in **1949** and is based in Strasbourg. The Council of Europe works for **human rights**, democracy and the rule of law. Switzerland has been a member since 1963. At the end of his speech Churchill called out: **“Let Europe arise!”**.

gewusst: The Zurich speech is one of the best-known speeches ever given in Switzerland.
Churchill became British Prime Minister once more in 1951.

teile.einleitung: The 2030 Agenda is a United Nations plan for a better future for everyone. It contains 17 goals for sustainable development, for example against poverty and hunger and for protecting the climate. All the countries of the world, including Switzerland, are meant to reach them by 2030.
wichtigste: The 2030 Agenda was adopted on 25 September 2015 at UN headquarters in New York.
It has applied since 1 January 2016 and is to be carried out by 2030.
It has 17 main goals with 169 targets.
Goal 1 is called “No poverty”, and Goal 13 concerns climate action.
Unlike the Millennium Goals, it applies to all countries, including rich ones.
Its guiding principle is “Leave no one behind”.
In Switzerland, the ARE and the SDC coordinate its implementation.

abschnitte.titel: A plan for the whole world
abschnitte.text: On **25 September 2015**, at a summit at **UN headquarters in New York**, the states of the world adopted the **2030 Agenda**. It has applied since **1 January 2016**. As the name says, its goals are to be reached by **2030**. It is about **sustainable development**. This means that people should be able to live well today without future generations suffering for it.

The agenda consists of **17 sustainability goals**, in English the Sustainable Development Goals. Goal 1 is “**No poverty**”, and Goal 2 concerns **hunger**. Goal 13 calls for **action to protect the climate**, and Goal 14 concerns life below water. The 17 main goals are divided into **169 targets**. Whether countries are making progress is measured with more than 200 **indicators**, that is, measurable values.

The goals are grouped into five core areas, the “**5 Ps**”. In English they are **People**, **Planet**, **Prosperity**, **Peace** and **Partnership**. The guiding principle is “**Leave no one behind**”. Even the poorest and most disadvantaged people should benefit from development.

Before this there were the **Millennium Goals**, which applied until 2015. They were aimed mainly at **developing countries**. The 2030 Agenda is different: it commits **all states**, including rich countries such as Switzerland. There are tasks there too, for example in energy use, waste or equality. However, the goals are not legally binding.

In Switzerland the **Federal Office for Spatial Development ARE** and the **SDC**, the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, coordinate implementation. For this, the **Federal Council** adopted the **Sustainable Development Strategy 2030**. **Cantons**, **municipalities**, companies and schools also take part. Switzerland regularly reports to the UN on how far it has got.

gewusst: Each of the 17 goals has its own colour and its own symbol; together they form a colourful grid.
The 2030 Agenda was adopted by all 193 member states the UN had at the time.

teile.einleitung: Blue Helmets are soldiers, police officers and experts who keep the peace on behalf of the UN. They get their name from their light blue helmets and berets.
wichtigste: Blue Helmets wear light blue helmets and berets.
The UN has no army of its own; the member countries send people.
Usually the **Security Council** decides on a mission.
Blue Helmets may only use weapons in self-defence.
The first peacekeeping mission began in the Middle East in 1948.
In 1988 the peacekeeping forces received the Nobel Peace Prize.

abschnitte.text: The UN has **no army of its own**. When it wants to keep the peace, the **member countries** voluntarily send soldiers, police officers and civilian experts. Together they form a **peacekeeping force**. You can recognise them by their **light blue** helmets and berets. Their vehicles also stand out: they are usually **white** and bear the black letters “UN”.

Blue Helmets are not meant to wage war. They monitor a **ceasefire**, for example, keep former enemies apart or protect the civilian population. Often they also help with elections or with rebuilding. They may only use their weapons in **self-defence**, that is, to protect themselves and their mission. It is important that they are **impartial**.

Usually the UN **Security Council** decides on a peacekeeping mission. It sets out what the Blue Helmets are to do and for how long. The first mission began in **1948**: the UN sent observers to the **Middle East** to monitor a ceasefire. Since then there have been many other missions on several continents. In 1988 the peacekeeping forces received the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

Switzerland also takes part in UN peacekeeping missions. The Swiss Armed Forces mainly send **unarmed military observers** and experts, for example for clearing mines. They help to monitor the peace. There are also police officers and civilian experts. For an armed mission, Parliament in Switzerland would have to agree.

gewusst: Many Blue Helmets come from countries in Africa and Asia.
The blue colour of the helmets matches the UN flag, which is light blue.

teile.einleitung: COVAX was a worldwide initiative during the coronavirus pandemic. It was meant to give all countries, including poorer ones, fair access to vaccines against COVID-19. It was wound up at the end of 2023.
wichtigste: The aim of COVAX was fair access to Covid vaccines for all countries.
COVAX was the vaccine pillar of the **ACT Accelerator**.
Through the **Advance Market Commitment**, 92 poorer countries received vaccine doses.
The first country to receive doses through COVAX was **Ghana**, in February 2021.
In spring 2021 doses were missing because **India** stopped exports.
COVAX ended on 31 December 2023.

abschnitte.text: When the **coronavirus pandemic** broke out in 2020, research into vaccines began all over the world. People feared that rich countries would buy all the doses and poorer ones would go without. That is why **COVAX** was set up. It was the vaccine pillar of the **ACT Accelerator**, an initiative from April 2020. That initiative also had pillars for tests, medicines and health systems. Those involved included the WHO and the vaccine alliance **Gavi**.

Richer countries bought their doses directly through COVAX and paid for them themselves. For poorer countries there was the **Advance Market Commitment** (AMC). Through it, donor countries and foundations financed doses for **92 countries** with low and middle incomes. These received the vaccines free of charge. In this way people in poor countries were also meant to be vaccinated early.

On **24 February 2021** the first doses arrived in **Ghana** through COVAX. There were about 600,000 doses of the AstraZeneca vaccine, made by the **Serum Institute of India**. Shortly afterwards came Côte d'Ivoire. In spring 2021 India stopped exports because of a severe wave of infections. Because COVAX depended heavily on this manufacturer, millions of doses were suddenly missing.

Originally COVAX wanted to provide **2 billion doses** by the end of 2021. This target was missed, partly because rich countries secured many doses directly for themselves. The first billion doses delivered was only reached in January 2022. On **31 December 2023** COVAX was wound up. By then just under 2 billion doses had been delivered to 146 countries and territories.

gewusst: The vaccine alliance Gavi and the World Health Organization WHO are both based in Geneva.
Since the end of COVAX, Covid vaccinations for poorer countries have run through Gavi's regular programmes.

teile.einleitung: CERN near Geneva is a research centre where countries study physics together. Here scientists investigate the smallest building blocks of matter. CERN is home to the world's largest particle accelerator, and the World Wide Web was also invented here.
wichtigste: CERN is a European research centre for particle physics in Meyrin near Geneva.
It was founded in 1954, and Switzerland is one of the founding states.
The Large Hadron Collider is a ring-shaped particle accelerator 27 kilometres long.
In 2012 the Higgs boson was discovered at CERN.
In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN.
The site lies on the border between Switzerland and France.

abschnitte.text: The name **CERN** comes from the French Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire, the European Council for Nuclear Research. The centre was founded in 1954 by twelve European states, including Switzerland. After the Second World War it was meant to bring researchers from different countries together peacefully. Today thousands of scientists from all over the world work there.

At CERN people study **particle physics**, that is, the tiniest building blocks that everything is made of. To do this, particles such as protons are made to collide at almost the speed of light. These collisions produce new particles, which are recorded by huge measuring instruments called **detectors**. In this way the researchers learn how the universe is built.

The **Large Hadron Collider**, LHC for short, is the largest particle accelerator in the world. It is a ring about 27 kilometres long and lies about 100 metres underground. It runs beneath Swiss and French soil. Its magnets are cooled to almost minus 271 degrees, which is colder than outer space.

In 2012 researchers at CERN announced the discovery of the **Higgs boson**. Physicists had predicted this particle decades earlier. It helps to explain why other particles have mass. Antimatter has also been produced and studied at CERN.

In 1989 the British computer scientist **Tim Berners-Lee** at CERN proposed a system with which researchers could share documents via links. This became the World Wide Web, which we use every day today. The world's first website ran on a computer at CERN. CERN made the technology freely available so that everyone could use it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that makes tiny particles extremely fast.
A small particle in the nucleus of an atom.
A measuring instrument that tracks and records particles.
A kind of mirror image of normal matter, which is very rare.

gewusst: The protons in the LHC go round the 27-kilometre ring about 11,000 times a second.
In front of CERN stands a large wooden sphere, the Globe of Science and Innovation.

teile.einleitung: AUKUS is a security pact between Australia, Great Britain and the USA. It was announced in September 2021. At its centre are nuclear-powered submarines for Australia and the joint development of modern military technology.
wichtigste: The name is made up of AU for Australia, UK for Great Britain and US for the USA.
AUKUS was announced in September 2021.
Australia is to receive submarines with nuclear propulsion but without nuclear weapons.
As a result France lost a large submarine contract and temporarily recalled ambassadors.
As a temporary solution, the USA is to supply Virginia-class submarines.
The second pillar concerns cutting-edge technologies such as artificial intelligence and quantum technology.

abschnitte.text: The name **AUKUS** is made up of the abbreviations of the three states: **AU** for Australia, **UK** for Great Britain and **US** for the USA. The three heads of government announced the pact in **September 2021**. It focuses on security in the **Indo-Pacific**, that is, the region between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. Many observers see it as a response to China's growing military weight. China criticises the pact.

Australia is to get **nuclear-powered submarines**. They are driven by a small nuclear reactor but carry **no nuclear weapons**, only conventional weapons. Such boats can stay under water for a very long time and operate far away. Australia's existing **Collins-class boats** are diesel-electric. From the 2030s the USA is to supply **Virginia-class** boats as a temporary solution. Later a jointly developed model is planned.

Before AUKUS, Australia had a contract for **conventional submarines** with a French shipyard. With the new pact, Australia cancelled this contract worth billions. **France** spoke of a **breach of trust**. It temporarily recalled its **ambassadors** from Washington and Canberra. That is a very unusual step between allies.

AUKUS consists of two parts, the so-called **pillars**. The first pillar concerns the submarines. In the second pillar, “**Pillar II**”, the three states want to develop **cutting-edge technologies** together. These include **artificial intelligence**, **quantum technology** and **hypersonic weapons**. Other partners such as **Japan** can take part in this second pillar.

The technology for nuclear-powered submarines is regarded as top secret. The USA already shared it with **Great Britain** from **1958**, based on a defence agreement. **Australia** is only the **second state** to receive this technology from the USA. Supporters see AUKUS as a contribution to stability. Critics fear a new arms race in the region.

gewusst: Nuclear-powered submarines do not have to surface to refuel and can stay at sea for months, limited mainly by the supplies for the crew.
Australia has no nuclear power stations and has still planned to build nuclear-powered submarines.

teile.einleitung: In an **extradition**, one state hands over a wanted person to another state. There the person is to stand trial or serve a sentence. Because it concerns people's freedom, strict rules apply.
wichtigste: An extradition is the handing over of a wanted person to another state.
Swiss citizens may only be extradited with their consent.
Nobody may be extradited to a state where they face torture.
The act must be a crime in both states.
As a rule, there is no extradition for purely political offences.
In Switzerland the Federal Office of Justice is responsible.

abschnitte.text: Sometimes a suspected or convicted person flees to another country. The state looking for them can then make an **extradition request**. If it is granted, the other state hands the person over. In Switzerland this is regulated mainly by the **Mutual Assistance Act**. There are also international treaties, for example the Council of Europe's European Convention on Extradition.

Article 25 of the **Federal Constitution** protects everyone. Nobody may be extradited to a state where they face **torture** or other cruel treatment. In addition, **Swiss citizens** may only be extradited with their **consent**. However, Switzerland can put them on trial itself instead.

According to the principle of **dual criminality**, the act must also be a crime under Swiss law. In this way nobody is prosecuted for something that is allowed here. Traditionally there is no extradition for purely **political offences**. This is meant to stop political opponents from being persecuted through criminal law. Because Switzerland rejects the **death penalty**, it demands a binding assurance that the person will not be executed.

In Switzerland the **Federal Office of Justice** deals with extradition requests. It belongs to the Federal Department of Justice and Police. **Interpol**, the international police organisation, often helps with the search. With a **red notice**, a state asks police worldwide to arrest a wanted person provisionally. It can then request their extradition.

gewusst: An Interpol red notice is not an international arrest warrant but a request for help.
Switzerland can punish its own citizens itself if they have committed a crime abroad.

teile.einleitung: The European Economic Area, EEA for short, connects the EU with Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway. It gives these three countries access to the European single market without being EU members. Switzerland rejected joining the EEA in a famous popular vote in 1992.
wichtigste: The EEA allows access to the single market without being an EU member.
It is made up of the EU countries and Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.
The EEA came into force in 1994.
Switzerland narrowly rejected joining on 6 December 1992.
The four freedoms of the single market apply in the EEA.
EEA countries adopt many EU rules but cannot take part in the decisions.
Farming, fishing and the euro are not part of the EEA.

abschnitte.text: The **European Economic Area** is an agreement between the EU and three EFTA countries. It turns these countries and the EU into one large shared market. The four freedoms apply there: goods, people, services and capital can move freely. This is called the **single market**.

The EEA countries Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway are not EU members. They have no vote in the European Parliament or in the Council of the EU. Even so, they have to adopt most of the rules for the single market. Important areas such as the common **agricultural policy**, the customs union and the euro are not part of the EEA.

The EEA Agreement was signed in Porto in 1992 and came into force on 1 January 1994. At that time more EFTA countries took part, but Austria, Finland and Sweden joined the EU as early as 1995. Liechtenstein joined in 1995. Since then the EEA has consisted of the EU and the three countries Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.

On **6 December 1992** Switzerland voted on joining the EEA. At almost 79 per cent, turnout was very high. With 50.3 per cent voting no, the people narrowly rejected it, and the majority of the cantons also said no. Afterwards Switzerland concluded **bilateral agreements** with the EU so as to have good access to the single market all the same.

So that the rules are kept, there are separate **institutions**. The EFTA Surveillance Authority in Brussels monitors the three EEA countries. In disputes, the **EFTA Court** in Luxembourg decides. New EU rules are added to the EEA Agreement in a joint committee.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shared market of several countries without customs duties and with the same rules.
The free movement of goods, persons, services and capital.
The European Free Trade Association, made up of Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.
The share of people entitled to vote who take part in a vote.

gewusst: Liechtenstein joined the EEA even though Switzerland had said no, and it had to adapt its agreements with Switzerland to do so.
The EEA vote of 1992 had one of the highest turnouts in the history of Swiss popular votes.

teile.einleitung: The EU can pass different kinds of legal acts. The two most important are the regulation and the directive. The difference lies in how they apply in the member states.
wichtigste: The kinds of EU legal acts are set out in Article 288 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (TFEU).
A regulation applies directly in all member states.
A directive sets a goal that the countries must put into their own law.
A decision is binding, often only on certain addressees.
Recommendations and opinions are not binding.
The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a well-known example of a regulation.

abschnitte.text: Under **Article 288 TFEU**, a **regulation** applies generally and **directly** in every member state. This means that as soon as it comes into force, it applies in the same way everywhere, without the countries having to make a law of their own. A well-known example is the **General Data Protection Regulation**, **GDPR** for short. It has applied in all member states since **25 May 2018** and replaced a data protection directive of 1995.

A **directive** works differently. It is binding only as to the **goal** that is to be reached. How the countries reach this goal, meaning the **form and methods**, they may choose themselves. Each country must **transpose** the directive **into national law** within a deadline. If a country makes stricter rules than required, this is called **gold-plating**.

abschnitte.titel: When a country does not transpose
abschnitte.text: If a country does not transpose a directive in time, the EU Commission can start **infringement proceedings**. They can end before the **Court of Justice of the European Union** (CJEU). Under Art. 260 TFEU, the court can impose lump sums or **penalty payments**. In the **Francovich** ruling of 1991, the court also decided that people affected can claim **compensation** from the state. Italy had failed to transpose a directive protecting employees when a company went bankrupt.

Besides regulations and directives there is the **decision**. It is binding in its entirety. If it is aimed at particular **addressees**, for example a company, it applies only to them. **Recommendations** and **opinions**, on the other hand, are **not binding**. But they show what the EU thinks is right.

Switzerland is not an EU member, so EU regulations and directives do not apply to it directly. Even so, they are very important. Swiss companies that do business in the EU must, for example, keep to the GDPR. Switzerland often adapts its own laws to EU rules voluntarily, so that trade stays simple. For example, a revised Swiss **Data Protection Act** came into force in 2023.

gewusst: The GDPR applies not only to companies in the EU but also to companies elsewhere that process data of people in the EU.
The expression “gold-plating” means covering something with a thin layer of gold, here adding extra rules on top.

teile.einleitung: Diplomatic immunity means that diplomats may not be arrested or put on trial in the host country like ordinary citizens. This special protection is meant to let them work for their country freely and without pressure. The rules for it are in the Vienna Convention of 1961.
wichtigste: Diplomats may not be arrested in the host country like ordinary citizens.
The rules are in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961.
The premises of an embassy are also protected, and the police may not enter them without permission.
Diplomatic mail may not be opened or seized.
Diplomats must still respect the laws of the host country.
For serious offences, the host country can expel a diplomat.

abschnitte.text: **Immunity** means something like inviolability or protection. Diplomatic immunity means that diplomats may not be arrested in the host country and usually may not be put on trial. This often also applies to their family members. The protection does not exist because diplomats are better people, but so that they can do their work.

abschnitte.titel: Where do the rules come from?
abschnitte.text: Even in ancient times, envoys were regarded as inviolable, so that it was possible to negotiate even with enemies. Today the rules are set out in the **Vienna Convention** on Diplomatic Relations of 1961. Almost all the states in the world have signed it. For consulates there is a separate convention from 1963, which gives somewhat less protection.

Not only the diplomats but also the **premises of the embassy** are protected. Police officers of the host country may only enter with the ambassador's permission. The **diplomatic bag**, in which documents are sent, may not be opened either. In this way a country can communicate safely with its embassy.

Immunity does not mean that diplomats may do anything they like. They must respect the laws of the host country, for example the traffic rules. For serious offences, the host country can declare them **persona non grata**, and then they must leave. Their home country can also lift their immunity so that they can be put on trial.

A great many diplomats live in Switzerland, especially in Bern and Geneva. You can recognise their cars by number plates with the letters **CD**, for Corps Diplomatique. The Department of Foreign Affairs issues them with special identity cards. Staff of international organisations in Geneva also enjoy certain privileges.

begriffe.erklaerung: Special protection from arrest and prosecution.
The country in which a diplomat works.
Protected consignments between a country and its embassy.
French for all the diplomats in a country, abbreviated CD.

gewusst: Diplomats sometimes get parking fines too, even if they often do not have to pay them.
An embassy is not territory of the foreign country; it remains the host country's soil but is specially protected.

t1sy1ux7.t: Switzerland's application to join the EU

teile.einleitung: In May 1992 the Federal Council submitted an application in Brussels for Switzerland to join the European Community, today's EU. After the no to the EEA in December 1992, the application was put on ice, and in 2016 it was officially withdrawn.
wichtigste: The Federal Council submitted the application in May 1992, a few months before the EEA vote.
On 6 December 1992 about 50.3 per cent of voters rejected the EEA.
The French-speaking cantons and the two Basels voted yes.
After that the application stayed “frozen” for decades.
In 2001 about 77 per cent rejected the initiative “Yes to Europe!”.
In 2016 Switzerland officially withdrew the application.
Joining the EU would need a yes from both the people and the cantons.

abschnitte.text: In the early 1990s Europe was changing a great deal. Switzerland was negotiating on the **European Economic Area**, **EEA** for short. In **May 1992** the Federal Council also sent an **application for membership** to the European Community in **Brussels**. This was a few months before the popular vote on the EEA. For many people, the EEA was an intermediate step on the way to possible membership.

abschnitte.titel: The narrow no to the EEA
