abschnitte.text: On **6 December 1992** the people voted on the EEA. The result was very close: **about 50.3 per cent no** against 49.7 per cent yes. A clear majority of the cantons also said no. All the **French-speaking cantons** and the two **Basels** voted yes, many German-speaking cantons no. This difference between the language regions was often called the **Röstigraben** (the “rösti ditch”).

After the no to the EEA, the Federal Council did not pursue the application any further. It lay **frozen** in Brussels for decades. Instead, Switzerland chose the path of **bilateral agreements**, meaning individual agreements with the EU. On 4 March 2001 the popular initiative **“Yes to Europe!”** was put to the vote. It wanted accession negotiations to start quickly. About **77 per cent** rejected it.

Parliament instructed the Federal Council to withdraw the old application. In summer **2016** the Federal Council informed the EU that the application was to be regarded as **withdrawn**. Supporters saw this as a clarification; others thought the step was purely symbolic. Joining would affect the **Constitution**. That is why it would need a **double majority** of the people and the cantons in a mandatory referendum.

gewusst: At almost 80 per cent, turnout in the EEA vote of 1992 was one of the highest in Swiss history.
The application lay in Brussels for about 24 years before it was withdrawn.

teile.einleitung: The **limitation initiative** wanted Switzerland to control immigration itself again and to end the free movement of persons with the EU. On **27 September 2020** the people clearly rejected it. The vote was important for relations with the EU.
wichtigste: The initiative was launched by the SVP and AUNS.
It demanded an end to the free movement of persons with the EU.
Because of the Covid-19 pandemic, the vote was postponed from May to September 2020.
61.7 per cent of voters said no.
Only four cantons voted yes, including Ticino.
Before that, since 2018, the obligation to report vacancies had applied to implement the mass immigration initiative.

abschnitte.text: On 9 February 2014 the people narrowly approved the **mass immigration initiative** with 50.3 per cent voting yes. It demanded quotas for immigration without directly terminating the free movement of persons. It was implemented from July 2018 with the **obligation to report vacancies**. In occupations with high unemployment, vacancies must first be reported to the regional employment centres. This solution was often called “domestic preference light”.

The **Swiss People's Party** and the **Campaign for an Independent and Neutral Switzerland**, AUNS for short, submitted the initiative in 2018. The Federal Council was to end the **Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons** by negotiation within **twelve months**. If this did not succeed, it would have had to terminate it within a further 30 days. The Federal Council and Parliament recommended rejecting it.

Originally the people should have voted on 17 May 2020. Because of the **Covid-19 pandemic**, the Federal Council cancelled this date. The proposal was then put to the vote on **27 September 2020**. Beforehand there was intense debate about jobs, wages and the Bilateral Agreements.

The people clearly rejected the initiative, with **61.7 per cent voting no**. The great majority of cantons also said no. Only **Schwyz, Glarus, Appenzell Innerrhoden** and **Ticino** voted yes. In Ticino, competition from cross-border commuters is an important issue. With the no, the free movement of persons and the Bilateral Agreements I remained in place.

gewusst: Because of a special clause, terminating free movement would also have ended the other agreements of the Bilaterals I.
On 17 May 2020 no federal vote was held at all because of the pandemic.

teile.einleitung: FIFA is the world governing body of football. It organises the FIFA World Cup and has its seat in Zurich.
wichtigste: FIFA was founded in Paris in 1904.
Since 1932 it has had its seat in Zurich.
Its headquarters, the “Home of FIFA”, stands on the Zürichberg.
Since 2016 the president has been Gianni Infantino from the Valais (as of 2025).
The 1954 World Cup took place in Switzerland.
At the 2026 World Cup, 48 teams played for the first time.

abschnitte.text: FIFA is the world governing body of **football**. Its members are the football associations of more than 200 countries and territories. It was founded in **Paris** in **1904**. Since **1932** it has had its seat in **Zurich**. Its headquarters is called the **“Home of FIFA”** and stands on the **Zürichberg**, at the edge of the woods above the city.

Since 2016 the President of FIFA has been **Gianni Infantino** (as of 2025). He was born in **Brig** in the Valais and is Swiss. He also has an Italian passport. Before him, Sepp Blatter, another man from the Valais, led FIFA.

FIFA's best-known tournament is the **FIFA World Cup**. National teams from all over the world play for the title there. The **World Cup trophy** is made of 18-carat **gold** and is hollow inside. The 2026 World Cup took place in the **USA**, Canada and Mexico. For the first time, 48 teams took part.

In **1954**, **Switzerland** hosted the World Cup. The final took place in the **Wankdorf Stadium** in Bern. There Germany beat Hungary. In Germany this victory is still called the “Miracle of Bern” today.

gewusst: FIFA has had its seat in Zurich for almost a hundred years.
A famous football match is named after a Swiss city: the “Miracle of Bern” of 1954.

teile.einleitung: The European Union's Europe Day is on 9 May. It commemorates a speech by Robert Schuman in 1950, with which European cooperation began.
wichtigste: On 9 May 1950 Robert Schuman presented the Schuman Declaration.
Schuman was Foreign Minister of France.
France and Germany were to manage coal and steel together.
The cooperation was above all meant to secure peace.
The Council of Europe celebrates its Europe Day on 5 May.
In Luxembourg, 9 May has been a public holiday since 2019.

abschnitte.text: On **9 May 1950**, **Robert Schuman** gave an important speech in Paris. He was **Foreign Minister of France** at the time. He proposed that the countries of Europe should work closely together. This proposal is called the **Schuman Declaration**. The EU's Europe Day commemorates this day.

Schuman proposed that France and Germany should manage their **coal** and **steel** together. Other countries could join in. At that time coal and steel were needed for weapons. If they are managed together, no country can secretly prepare for war. After the Second World War, this was a way to secure **peace**. In 1951 it led to the European Coal and Steel Community.

There are two Europe Days. The EU celebrates on **9 May**. The **Council of Europe** celebrates on **5 May**, because it was founded on a 5 May. The Council of Europe is a separate organisation, which Switzerland also belongs to. In **Luxembourg**, 9 May has been an official public holiday since 2019. In most other countries it is a normal working day.

Around Europe Day, many **EU buildings** open their doors. On open days you can visit them and find out how the EU works. The **flag of Europe** flies on many buildings. It shows a circle of twelve golden stars on a blue background. The number twelve stands for perfection, not for the number of members.

gewusst: The twelve stars on the flag of Europe have never had anything to do with the number of member states.
Europe has two Europe Days: the Council of Europe's on 5 May and the EU's on 9 May.

teile.einleitung: The **Arab League** is an association of states where Arabic is spoken. It was founded in 1945, even before the UN. Its aim is cooperation between the Arab countries in politics, the economy and culture.
wichtigste: The Arab League was founded by seven states in March 1945.
Today it has 22 members in North Africa and Western Asia.
Its headquarters is in Cairo, the capital of Egypt.
Its official language is Arabic.
From 1979 to 1990 the General Secretariat was in Tunis.
The Comoros joined in 1993 as the most recent member so far.

abschnitte.text: The Arab League was founded in **March 1945**. The founding members were seven states: **Egypt, Iraq, Transjordan, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Yemen**. Transjordan is now called Jordan. The League is one of the oldest associations of states in the world.

Today the League has **22 members** in North Africa and Western Asia. They include **Palestine**. Other states joined bit by bit, for example Mauritania in 1973, Somalia in 1974 and Djibouti in 1977. The most recent member so far was the **Comoros**, which joined in 1993; it is a group of islands in the Indian Ocean between Africa and Madagascar. What all members have in common is the **Arabic language**, which is also the League's official language.

The League has its headquarters in **Cairo**. The headquarters building is on the well-known **Tahrir Square**. Only once did the headquarters have to move. In 1979 Egypt concluded a peace treaty with Israel, which many other members rejected. As a result Egypt was suspended, and the General Secretariat moved to **Tunis**. In 1990 it returned to Cairo.

The League can exclude members from taking part. This happened, for example, with **Syria**. Because of the government's violence against demonstrators, the country was suspended in 2011. In May 2023 Syria was allowed to take part again. Decisions like these show that the members do not always agree.

gewusst: The Arab League is a few months older than the UN.
The Comoros lie far away from most of the other members, in the middle of the Indian Ocean.

teile.einleitung: The Rio Earth Summit was a large UN conference in 1992. Almost all the countries of the world discussed there how to protect the environment and fight poverty at the same time.
wichtigste: The Earth Summit took place in Rio de Janeiro from 3 to 14 June 1992.
Its guiding idea was sustainable development.
Agenda 21 was adopted there.
The Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention on Biological Diversity were signed.
Twelve-year-old Severn Suzuki gave a famous speech.
In 2012 there was the follow-up conference Rio+20.

abschnitte.text: The official name was the **United Nations Conference on Environment and Development**. It took place in June 1992 in Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. At its centre was **sustainable development**. This means that people today should meet their needs without taking away the basis of life from future generations. In this way Rio linked environmental protection and development.

The countries adopted **Agenda 21**, a programme of action for the 21st century. Later, many municipalities and cantons in Switzerland also developed their own “Local Agenda 21”. The **Framework Convention on Climate Change** and the **Convention on Biological Diversity** were opened for signature. Both are still foundations of worldwide environmental policy today.

Rio also laid the foundation for the **Convention to Combat Desertification**, which was signed in Paris in 1994. The UN founded the **Commission on Sustainable Development**. It was meant to check whether countries were carrying out the decisions. In 2013 it was replaced by a new forum.

The speech by the Canadian **Severn Suzuki** became especially famous. She was only twelve years old. She called on adults to protect the environment for her generation. Twenty years later, in June 2012, the countries met again in Rio. That is why this conference was called **Rio+20**.

gewusst: A twelve-year-old gave one of the best-known speeches of the whole conference in Rio.
The Rio Framework Convention on Climate Change is the basis for the later climate conferences.

teile.einleitung: The Eurovision Song Contest is a large singing competition. Artists from many countries each sing one song, and expert juries and the public vote on the winner.
wichtigste: The first contest took place in Lugano in 1956.
Switzerland won in 1956 with Lys Assia and the song “Refrain”.
In 1988 Céline Dion won for Switzerland.
In 2024 Nemo from Biel won with “The Code”.
ABBA won in 1974 with “Waterloo”.
The contest is organised by the European Broadcasting Union in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: In the Eurovision Song Contest, each country enters with **one song**. It is organised by the **European Broadcasting Union**, EBU for short. This is an association of radio and television broadcasters and has its seat in **Geneva**. Millions of people watch the contest on television every year.

The very first Eurovision Song Contest took place in **Lugano** in Ticino in **1956**. Switzerland itself won: **Lys Assia** sang the song **“Refrain”**. In 1988 the Canadian **Céline Dion** won for Switzerland with the song “Ne partez pas sans moi”. After that she became world-famous.

In 2024 **Nemo** from **Biel** won with the song **“The Code”**. It was Switzerland's third win. Because the winning country hosts the next contest, the 2025 Eurovision Song Contest took place in Basel.

Some winners later became world-famous. The Swedish band **ABBA** won in 1974 with **“Waterloo”**. There is also a contest for children: in the **Junior Eurovision Song Contest**, children and teenagers sing for their country.

gewusst: In 1956 Switzerland was both host and winner of the very first Eurovision Song Contest.
Céline Dion comes from Canada, but she sang for Switzerland in 1988 and won.

teile.einleitung: The Antarctic Treaty is an international agreement that sets out how Antarctica may be used. It states that the coldest continent on Earth may be used only for peaceful and scientific purposes. Military activity and nuclear weapons tests are banned there.
wichtigste: The Antarctic Treaty was signed in Washington in 1959 by twelve states.
It came into force in 1961.
Antarctica may be used only for peaceful and scientific purposes.
Military bases, weapons tests and nuclear waste are banned.
Territorial claims by individual states are frozen by the treaty.
Switzerland joined the treaty in 1990.

abschnitte.text: **Antarctica** is the continent around the South Pole. It is almost completely covered by a thick layer of ice and is much bigger than Europe. The lowest temperature on Earth was measured there, below minus 89 degrees. Apart from researchers, no people live there permanently, but there are many penguins, seals and whales.

Several states such as Great Britain, Norway, Argentina and Chile laid claim to parts of Antarctica. During the **Cold War**, people feared that disputes or even military conflicts might break out there. After a big international research year in 1957 and 1958, twelve states reached agreement. On 1 December 1959 they signed the **Antarctic Treaty** in Washington.

The treaty applies to the area south of 60 degrees south latitude. It allows only peaceful activities, especially research. Military installations, weapons tests and dumping **nuclear waste** are banned. All territorial claims are frozen, which means they still stand but may not be extended.

In 1991 an additional agreement on **environmental protection** was adopted in Madrid. It bans the mining of mineral resources such as ore, coal or crude oil. The animals and plants of Antarctica are given special protection. Tourists must also keep to strict rules so that nature is not damaged.

Many countries run **research stations** in Antarctica, for example the American McMurdo Station. Researchers there study the ice, the climate, the animals and the night sky. In ice cores you can read what the climate was like hundreds of thousands of years ago. Switzerland joined the treaty in 1990, and Swiss researchers often take part in other countries' projects.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ice-covered continent around the South Pole.
When a state says that a territory belongs to it.
A base where scientists live and do research.
A long cylinder of ice drilled out of the ice sheet that tells us about the climate in the past.

gewusst: The Antarctic Treaty was the first arms control treaty of the Cold War.
So much water is stored as ice in Antarctica that the sea level would rise by many metres if it all melted.

teile.einleitung: Lake Constance is one of the largest lakes in Central Europe. Three countries lie on its shores: Switzerland, Germany and Austria.
wichtigste: At Lake Constance, Switzerland, Germany and Austria border each other.
The Rhine flows through the lake.
Lake Constance consists of the large **Upper Lake** and the smaller **Lower Lake**.
The canton of Thurgau has the longest Swiss shoreline.
Because of its size it is also called the Swabian Sea.
A ferry connects Romanshorn with Friedrichshafen.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Constance** lies between Switzerland, Germany and Austria. It is so big that you can sometimes hardly see the other shore. That is why it is also called the **Swabian Sea**. The lake consists of the large **Upper Lake** and the smaller, western **Lower Lake**. Steckborn, for example, lies on the Lower Lake. Lake Constance supplies drinking water for millions of people.

The **Rhine** comes from the Alps. In the east, on the border between Switzerland and Austria, it flows into Lake Constance. At **Stein am Rhein** it flows out again and on towards the Rhine Falls. On the Swiss side, the cantons of **Thurgau** and **St Gallen** lie on the lake. Thurgau has the longest shoreline, with places such as Romanshorn and Arbon.

In Austria, **Bregenz** lies on the eastern shore. Every summer there is a festival there on a stage in the lake. In Germany, **Konstanz** lies right next to the Swiss town of **Kreuzlingen**; the border runs right between the two towns. The old town of **Lindau** is on an island. A **ferry** runs from **Romanshorn** to **Friedrichshafen**, carrying cars and bikes too.

The island of **Mainau** belongs to Germany and is famous for its many flowers. In Friedrichshafen, **Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin** built large airships. The first **Zeppelin** rose over the lake in 1900. Today a museum recalls this. The island of **Reichenau** with its old monasteries is also well known and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: In winter 1963 the whole of Lake Constance froze over; in Swiss German this is called a “Seegfrörni”.
On the Upper Lake, the border between the three countries has never been precisely fixed.

t1xsxwje.t: Relations between Switzerland and the European Union

teile.einleitung: Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe but is **not a member** of the European Union. Even so, it works closely with the EU. The rules for this are set out in many treaties, which the people often vote on too.
wichtigste: Switzerland is not a member of the EU.
On 6 December 1992 the people narrowly said no to the EEA.
In 2001 the people clearly rejected the initiative “Yes to Europe!”.
The EU is Switzerland's most important trading partner.
Cooperation is set out in the Bilateral Agreements.
Liechtenstein and Norway are not in the EU either.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland borders **Germany, France, Italy and Austria**. These countries are all members of the EU. Only one neighbouring country is not: **Liechtenstein**. **Norway** does not belong to the EU either; people there have said no twice in votes.

In Switzerland it is often **the people** who in the end decide on important treaties with the EU. In 1992 they voted on the **European Economic Area**, **EEA** for short. On 6 December 1992 they **narrowly said no**, with about **50.3 per cent**. On 4 March 2001 about 77 per cent rejected the initiative “**Yes to Europe!**”. It wanted quick negotiations on joining.

Instead of joining, Switzerland concluded **Bilateral Agreements** with the EU. “Bilateral” means between two sides. The first package, the **Bilaterals I**, was signed in 1999 and approved by the people in 2000. It includes, for example, the free movement of persons. Other agreements followed later, for example on **Schengen**. The future of the agreements is negotiated and debated again and again.

The EU is Switzerland's **most important trading partner**. Many goods go to the EU countries, and many come from there. People also feel this closeness. Swiss people can travel to EU countries **very easily**, for example on holiday to Italy. Thanks to Schengen, there are usually no fixed checks on people at the borders.

gewusst: In the EEA no of 1992, only a few tens of thousands of votes were missing for a yes.
Switzerland is not in the EU but is a member of the Schengen area.

teile.einleitung: For many centuries people were enslaved, bought and sold and forced to work. In the 18th and 19th centuries more and more people fought for the abolition of slavery. Today slavery is banned worldwide.
wichtigste: In 1804, after an uprising, enslaved people founded the free state of Haiti.
Great Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in almost all its colonies in 1833.
William Wilberforce fought against the slave trade in the British Parliament for decades.
Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863.
The 13th Amendment abolished slavery throughout the USA in 1865.
In 1981 Mauritania was the last country to officially abolish slavery.
23 August is the international day for remembering the slave trade and its abolition.

abschnitte.text: **Enslaved** people belong to another person like a thing. They have no rights and have to work without pay. From the 16th to the 19th century, European traders carried millions of people from **Africa** across the Atlantic to **America**. There they had to work mainly on **plantations**, for example for sugar, cotton or tobacco. This is called the **transatlantic slave trade**.

In the French colony of **Saint-Domingue** in the Caribbean, the enslaved people rose up from **1791**. The uprising began in the night leading into **23 August 1791**. After years of fighting, they founded the free state of **Haiti** in **1804**. It was the first state to come into being from a successful uprising of enslaved people. That is why 23 August is today **UNESCO**'s day for remembering the slave trade and its abolition.

In Great Britain the politician **William Wilberforce** fought against the **slave trade** for decades. Again and again he brought bills before Parliament. In **1807** Great Britain banned the trade in enslaved people. In **1833** Parliament passed the **Slavery Abolition Act**. The law came into force in 1834 and abolished slavery in almost all British colonies.

In the **southern states** of the USA, a very large number of enslaved people worked in the fields. The dispute about this led to the **Civil War** in 1861. In 1863 President **Abraham Lincoln** issued the **Emancipation Proclamation**. With it he declared the enslaved people in the southern states free. After the end of the war, the **13th Amendment** to the Constitution came into force in December **1865**. It bans slavery and forced labour throughout the USA, except as a punishment.

The last country in the world to abolish slavery by law was **Mauritania** in West Africa, in **1981**. But it was only made a criminal offence there in **2007**. The **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** of 1948 bans slavery everywhere. People and companies from **Switzerland** also once made money from the slave trade, for example as investors or traders. Today historians are researching this history.

gewusst: Haiti was the second independent state in the whole of America, after the USA.
In 1888 Brazil was the last country in America to abolish slavery.

teile.einleitung: The African Union is the association of all the countries of Africa. In it the states work together, for example for peace, security and trade. The organisation was founded in 2002 and is based in Addis Ababa.
wichtigste: The African Union, AU for short, was founded in 2002 in Durban in South Africa.
Its headquarters is in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia.
It has 55 member states (as of 2026).
Its predecessor was the Organisation of African Unity of 1963.
Africa Day is celebrated every year on 25 May.
The flag shows a map of Africa on a green background, surrounded by golden stars.

abschnitte.titel: An association for the whole of Africa
abschnitte.text: In the **African Union** the countries of Africa have joined together. It has **55 member states** (as of 2026). The members want to work together for **peace** and **security**, strengthen **trade** and make Africa's voice heard in the world. In conflicts the AU can mediate or send peacekeeping troops. Since 2023 the African Union has also been a member of the **G20**, a group of large economic powers.

As early as **25 May 1963**, many African countries joined together to form the **Organisation of African Unity**. At that time many states had only just become independent from the European colonial powers. The organisation supported the liberation of the remaining colonies. In memory of its founding, 25 May is celebrated every year as **Africa Day**. Later the organisation became the African Union.

The African Union was founded in **2002** at a summit in **Durban** in **South Africa**. It replaced the Organisation of African Unity. Its **headquarters**, however, is in **Addis Ababa**, the capital of **Ethiopia**. This is also where the **Commission**, which runs the daily work, is based. The **Pan-African Parliament** is based in South Africa.

The flag of the African Union has a **green** background. In the middle is a **map of Africa** in front of a **white sun**. Around it is a circle of **golden stars**. The stars stand for the member states. Green is regarded as the colour of hope.

Switzerland works with the African Union, for example on **peace promotion**. The Swiss embassy in Addis Ababa is also responsible for relations with the AU. Switzerland supports projects in several African countries, for example through the **SDC**. How well the cooperation works is judged differently in politics.

gewusst: Morocco was not a member for many years and only rejoined the African Union in 2017.
The main building of the African Union in Addis Ababa was built as a gift from China.

teile.einleitung: The Abraham Accords are agreements with which several Arab states normalised their relations with Israel from 2020. They were brokered by the US government under Donald Trump. Opinions on the accords differ.
wichtigste: On 15 September 2020 the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain signed the first accords.
The signing took place at the White House in Washington.
The name recalls Abraham, the forefather of Jews, Christians and Muslims.
Morocco joined in December 2020 and Sudan in January 2021.
In return, Israel suspended planned annexations in the West Bank for the time being.
Many Palestinians criticised the accords.

abschnitte.text: **Normalisation** means that states establish official relations, open embassies and trade with each other. For a long time most Arab states did not recognise Israel. Only **Egypt** in 1979 and **Jordan** in 1994 had made peace with Israel. On **15 September 2020** the **United Arab Emirates** and **Bahrain** signed the first **Abraham Accords** at the **White House**. They had been brokered by the government of **Donald Trump**.

**Abraham**, in Arabic **Ibrahim**, is regarded as the **forefather** of Jews, Christians and Muslims. He is honoured in **Judaism**, **Christianity** and **Islam**. That is why these three religions are also called the **Abrahamic religions**. The name of the accords is meant to emphasise their shared roots. It is meant to show that the peoples of the region have a lot in common.

**Morocco** joined in December 2020. In return, the USA recognised Morocco's sovereignty over the disputed **Western Sahara**. This territory is also claimed by the independence movement **Polisario**. In January 2021 **Sudan** signed a declaration on the accords. In return, the USA also removed it from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. Because of the later war in Sudan, putting it into practice remained open.

The Emirates justified the step by saying that Israel had suspended planned **annexations** in the **West Bank**. Annexation means that a state declares a territory part of its own territory on its own. Israel spoke of a postponement, not of giving them up for good. Many **Palestinians** criticised the accords. For a long time the **Arab League** had held the principle of recognising Israel only after a Palestinian state had been founded. Supporters, on the other hand, see more trade and stability in the accords.

Before October 2023 there were intensive negotiations on a rapprochement between Israel and **Saudi Arabia**. After the Hamas attack on Israel on **7 October 2023** and the **Gaza war** that followed, these talks stalled. Since then Saudi Arabia has demanded a credible path to a **Palestinian state**. The existing accords, however, remained in force.

gewusst: After the accords there were direct flights between Israel and the United Arab Emirates for the first time.
Bahrain is an island state in the Persian Gulf and one of the smallest countries in Asia.

teile.einleitung: There has been a civil war in Yemen since the mid-2010s. The Houthi rebel group is fighting against the internationally recognised government. The war has caused one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world.
wichtigste: Yemen lies in the south of the Arabian Peninsula.
North and South Yemen were united into one state on 22 May 1990.
In September 2014 the **Houthis** captured the capital **Sanaa**.
From March 2015 a coalition led by **Saudi Arabia** intervened.
The Houthis are supported by **Iran**.
The government used **Aden** in the south as a substitute capital.

abschnitte.text: For a long time **Yemen** was divided into two states: the Arab Republic in the north and a socialist People's Republic in the south. On **22 May 1990** they united. The old contrasts between north and south still shape the country today. In 2011, during the **Arab Spring**, there were large protests against the president of the time. After that, the situation became more and more unsafe.

The **Houthis**, officially **Ansar Allah**, come from the north. They belong to the Shiite **Zaidis**. In September 2014 they captured the capital **Sanaa** and drove out the internationally recognised government. The government moved its seat to **Aden** in the south. The separatist **Southern Transitional Council**, which is supported by the United Arab Emirates, is also strong there.

From March 2015 **Saudi Arabia** intervened with a coalition of Arab states to support the government. The Houthis, in turn, are supported by **Iran** with weapons and know-how. That is why the war is also regarded as a **proxy war** between Saudi Arabia and Iran. From the end of 2023 the Houthis attacked merchant ships in the **Bab el-Mandeb** strait. Many shipping companies therefore took the long detour round Africa.

The UN has repeatedly described the situation in Yemen as one of the **worst humanitarian crises** in the world. Millions of people suffered from hunger, and from 2016 **cholera** spread. A large part of the aid supplies came into the country through the port city of **Hodeidah**. In the **Stockholm Agreement** of December 2018, the warring parties agreed a ceasefire for the city with UN mediation.

gewusst: Negotiations on exchanging prisoners took place several times in Switzerland.
The old city of Sanaa with its tall mud-brick houses is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The **Iran nuclear deal**, **JCPOA** for short, was concluded in Vienna in 2015. It was meant to prevent Iran from building nuclear weapons. In return, sanctions against the country were to be lifted. The deal later came under heavy pressure.
wichtigste: The deal was concluded in Vienna on 14 July 2015.
Iran negotiated with the P5+1 group.
The UN Security Council endorsed it with Resolution 2231.
Iran was only allowed to enrich uranium up to 3.67 per cent.
The International Atomic Energy Agency monitored compliance.
In May 2018 US President Donald Trump announced the USA's withdrawal.

abschnitte.text: Iran negotiated with the **P5+1** group. These are the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, that is, the USA, Russia, China, Great Britain and France, plus **Germany**. The EU coordinated the talks. In April 2015 the main points were agreed in **Lausanne**. On **14 July 2015** the deal was concluded in **Vienna**.

Iran was only allowed to enrich uranium up to **3.67 per cent**. That is enough for power stations but not for atomic bombs, which need about 90 per cent. Inspectors from the **International Atomic Energy Agency** regularly checked the facilities on site. In return, sanctions were lifted. The UN Security Council unanimously approved the deal with **Resolution 2231**.

In May 2018 US President **Donald Trump** announced the USA's withdrawal. He considered the deal inadequate and relied on “maximum pressure” with new sanctions. From 2019 Iran also gradually stopped keeping to the limits. In the end it enriched uranium up to **60 per cent**.

The deal contains the **snapback** mechanism. With it, earlier UN sanctions can be brought back into force. Great Britain, France and Germany triggered it in August 2025, and at the end of September 2025 the sanctions applied again. Already in June 2025 the USA had bombed the **Fordo** facility. It lies deep inside a mountain near Qom and was supposed to be protected from attacks in this way.

gewusst: Since 1980 Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran as a so-called protecting power.
The main points of the deal were negotiated in Lausanne in April 2015.

teile.einleitung: A debate is an orderly exchange of opinions. In parliament, members discuss a topic from all sides in debates before they vote on it.
wichtigste: In a debate, speakers state their opinion and the reasons for it.
In parliament people usually speak from the lectern.
Each person has a set speaking time.
A heckle is a short remark made during someone else's speech.
Anyone who behaves badly can be called to order.
After the debate on a law there is usually a vote.

abschnitte.text: In a **debate**, several people talk about a question on which there are different opinions. Each side explains its position and gives **arguments**, that is, reasons. Good debates have rules: you let others finish speaking, stay factual and listen. In this way a topic can be looked at from all sides and a good decision can be made.

In parliament there are fixed procedures. Anyone who wants to say something asks to speak and then goes to the **lectern** with a microphone. That is how it is in the German Bundestag, and also in the Swiss **National Council**. In the **Council of States**, members usually speak from their seats. So that many people get the chance to speak, each person has only a set **speaking time**. The president chairs the sitting and gives people the floor.

Sometimes someone briefly calls out during another person's speech. This is called a **heckle**. It can be funny or critical and interrupts the speech for a moment. Anyone who behaves badly in a debate, for example by insulting others, can be **called to order**. This means they are given a warning by the chair.

In the **US Senate** there is a special tactic: the **filibuster**. Someone talks for hours so that a vote does not take place. The Senate's rules allow this under certain conditions. In most other parliaments, fixed speaking times prevent such endless speeches.

When a law has been discussed in detail, the **vote** comes. The members decide with yes or no. In Switzerland, votes in the National Council are electronic, and the results are public. By the way, you can debate at school too: in debating competitions, young people practise arguing convincingly and disagreeing fairly.

gewusst: In the US Senate, the longest filibuster speech by a single senator lasted more than 24 hours.
In many parliaments debates are written down word for word, including the heckles.

teile.einleitung: The European Convention on Human Rights, ECHR for short, is a treaty of the Council of Europe. In it, countries promise to protect important basic rights of all people.
wichtigste: The ECHR was signed in Rome on 4 November 1950.
It came into force on 3 September 1953.
It comes from the Council of Europe, not from the EU.
Article 2 protects the right to life; Article 3 bans torture.
Article 8 protects private life; Article 10 protects freedom of expression.
Additional protocols have abolished the death penalty.

abschnitte.text: The ECHR was drawn up within the **Council of Europe**. The Council of Europe is an organisation of European countries that works for human rights, democracy and the rule of law. The Convention was signed in Rome on **4 November 1950**. It came into force on **3 September 1953**, after enough countries had ratified it. To **ratify** means to make a treaty officially valid.

**Article 2** protects every person's right to life. **Article 3** bans torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, without any exception. **Article 8** protects private life, family life, the home and correspondence. **Article 10** protects **freedom of expression**. This includes receiving and passing on information and ideas.

The ECHR was later extended with **additional protocols**. The 6th Protocol banned the **death penalty** in peacetime. The 13th Protocol bans it in all circumstances. That is why there is no longer a death penalty in the member countries of the Council of Europe today.

Anyone who thinks their rights under the ECHR have been violated can turn to the **European Court of Human Rights** in Strasbourg. First, however, they must go through the courts in their own country. **Switzerland** is a member of the Council of Europe and ratified the ECHR in 1974. So people from Switzerland can also bring cases in Strasbourg.

gewusst: The ban on torture in Article 3 applies without any exception, not even in war.
The ECHR belongs to the Council of Europe, so it also applies to non-EU countries such as Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In the European Council, the heads of state and government of all 27 EU countries meet. At these summits they decide the direction in which the European Union should develop. It must not be confused with the Council of the EU or the Council of Europe.
wichtigste: The European Council brings together the heads of state and government of the EU countries.
In the Council of the EU, on the other hand, the ministers for particular areas meet.
The European Council sets the general aims and priorities of the EU.
It does not make laws itself.
Since 2009 it has had a permanent president.
The meetings usually take place in Brussels and are called EU summits.
The European Council is not the same as the Council of Europe.

abschnitte.titel: Who sits in the European Council?
abschnitte.text: The **European Council** is made up of the heads of state and government of the 27 member states, for example presidents or prime ministers. In addition there are the President of the European Council and the President of the European Commission. They meet at least four times a year in Brussels. These meetings are called **EU summits**.

The European Council decides the EU's big **aims**. For example, it decides on the EU's position in crises, wars or on climate protection. It also proposes who should become President of the Commission. But it does not pass laws itself; Parliament and the Council of the EU do that.

Since the **Treaty of Lisbon** of 2009, the European Council has had a permanent president. The president is elected for two and a half years and chairs the meetings. The first was Herman Van Rompuy from Belgium. Since December 2024 the Portuguese António Costa has held this office.

There are three bodies with similar names. The **Council of the European Union** is the meeting of ministers for particular areas, for example all the environment ministers, and it passes laws together with Parliament. The presidency of the Council of the EU passes from country to country every six months. The **Council of Europe** in Strasbourg is a completely separate organisation for human rights, which Switzerland also belongs to.

The European Council meets in the **Europa building** in Brussels. The building is known for its glass cube, inside which there is a lantern-like dome. At important summits the leaders often negotiate deep into the night. Decisions are usually taken by consensus, meaning when nobody objects.

begriffe.erklaerung: The person who leads a country or its government, for example a president or a chancellor.
A meeting of the most important politicians of several countries.
A decision that everyone agrees with or that nobody objects to.
An EU treaty of 2007, which came into force in 2009 and reorganised the way the EU works.

gewusst: The European Council has only officially been an institution of the EU since 2009, although the leaders had been meeting regularly since the 1970s.
Switzerland does not take part in the European Council, because it is not an EU member.

t85fmu9.t: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

teile.einleitung: The FAO is the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. It works to make sure that everyone in the world has enough healthy food.
wichtigste: FAO stands for “Food and Agriculture Organization”.
The FAO was founded in Canada on 16 October 1945.
Its headquarters has been in Rome since 1951.
World Food Day is held every year on 16 October.
Its logo shows an ear of grain and the words “Fiat panis”.
It also looks after fishing and forests.

abschnitte.text: FAO is short for **“Food and Agriculture Organization”**. Agriculture means farming. It is a **specialised agency of the UN**. Almost all the countries of the world are members, including Switzerland.

The FAO was founded in Canada on **16 October 1945**. Since 1951 it has had its headquarters in **Rome** in Italy. In memory of its founding, 16 October is **World Food Day** every year. It reminds us that not everyone has enough to eat. The logo shows an **ear of grain** and the Latin words “Fiat panis”. This means “Let there be bread”.

The FAO teaches farmers in poor countries **better growing methods**. For example, it shows how to water fields better, choose good seed and protect plants from pests. This lets families harvest more. The FAO's work also includes **fishing** and **forests**, because they provide food too.

The FAO explains how important **bees** are for our food. Bees carry pollen from flower to flower. This is called **pollination**. Only then can many plants form fruit. Without bees and other pollinating insects there would be much less fruit and vegetables.

gewusst: World Food Day on 16 October is the FAO's birthday.
Many kinds of fruit and vegetables need bees or other insects so that fruit can grow.

teile.einleitung: The Council of Europe is an independent organisation of European countries that works for human rights, democracy and the rule of law. It has more members than the European Union, and Switzerland is one of them. Its seat is in Strasbourg in France.
wichtigste: The Council of Europe is an organisation for human rights with more members than the EU.
It was founded in 1949.
Its seat is in Strasbourg.
It has 46 member states (as of 2026).
Switzerland has been a member since 1963.
Its most important treaty is the European Convention on Human Rights.
The Council of Europe is not part of the European Union.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Council of Europe?
abschnitte.text: The **Council of Europe** is an international organisation founded in London on 5 May 1949. It is the oldest political organisation of European countries after the Second World War. Its tasks are protecting **human rights**, democracy and the rule of law. Unlike the EU, it does not make laws for a shared market.

Today the Council of Europe has 46 **member states**, including all 27 EU countries. They are joined, for example, by Switzerland, Norway, the United Kingdom, Turkey and Ukraine. Russia was expelled in 2022 after the attack on Ukraine. Belarus is the only larger country in Europe that has never been a member.

The most important work of the Council of Europe is the **European Convention on Human Rights** of 1950. It protects rights such as freedom of expression, the right to a fair trial and the ban on torture. The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg watches over whether it is kept. The Council of Europe has also abolished the death penalty throughout Europe; all members must give it up.

In the **Committee of Ministers**, the foreign ministers of the member states meet. The Parliamentary Assembly is made up of members of the national parliaments, including from Switzerland. The administration is led by a Secretary General. The seat is the Palais de l'Europe in Strasbourg.

abschnitte.titel: Switzerland in the Council of Europe
abschnitte.text: Switzerland joined the Council of Europe in 1963. It only ratified the Convention on Human Rights in 1974, partly because before that women did not have the **right to vote** at federal level. Since then people in Switzerland have been able to turn to the court in Strasbourg. By the way, the Council of Europe uses the same blue **flag** with twelve stars as the EU.

begriffe.erklaerung: Basic rights that all people have, no matter where they come from.
A state in which everyone, including the government, must keep to the laws.
A treaty between many countries.
A country that belongs to an organisation.

gewusst: The Council of Europe introduced the flag of Europe with the twelve stars back in 1955, decades before the EU adopted it.
The Council of Europe celebrates its founding day, 5 May, as Europe Day.

teile.einleitung: With the Erasmus Programme, young people can study or learn in another country for a while. It is one of the best-known programmes of the European Union.
wichtigste: The Erasmus Programme began in 1987.
With it, students spend some time at a university abroad.
It is named after the scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam.
Erasmus died in Basel in 1536 and is buried in Basel Minster.
Since 2014 it has been part of the large programme Erasmus+.

abschnitte.text: With Erasmus, **students** can spend one or two semesters at a university in another country. The programme started in **1987**. Since then a great many young people have taken part. People who live abroad often get to know a **new language**, a different culture and new friends along the way.

The programme is named after **Erasmus of Rotterdam**. He was a famous **scholar**, meaning a very well-educated person who wrote and researched a lot. He came from Rotterdam in the Netherlands and travelled widely across Europe. That is why his name suits a programme for exchange so well.

Erasmus lived in **Basel** for several years. There he worked with printers who printed his works. He died in Basel in 1536 and is buried in **Basel Minster**. So the man the programme is named after has a close link to Switzerland.

Since 2014 the large EU programme for education and exchange has been called **Erasmus+**. It includes student exchange. But **apprentices** in vocational training, school pupils and teachers can also take part. Switzerland has its own exchange programme and wants to be fully part of Erasmus+ again from 2027.

gewusst: The scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam is buried in Basel Minster.
Erasmus is one of the oldest exchange programmes of the EU; it started back in 1987.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Denmark is called the Dannebrog. It shows a white cross on a red background and is seen as one of the oldest flags in the world. A famous legend is told about how it came to be.
wichtigste: The Danish flag is called the Dannebrog.
It shows a white Nordic cross on a red background.
According to legend, it fell from the sky during a battle in 1219.
The battle took place near today's Tallinn in Estonia.
On 15 June, Valdemar's Day, flags are flown in Denmark.
Denmark has the same colours as Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **Dannebrog** is red and carries a **white cross**. The cross is not exactly in the middle but moved closer to the flagpole. Such a cross is called a **Nordic cross**. The colours red and white are the same as on the Swiss flag. But the shape is different: the Danish flag is a rectangle.

An old **legend** tells how the Dannebrog came to be. In **1219**, the Danish king **Valdemar II** fought in the **Battle of Lyndanisse**. The place is near today's **Tallinn**, the capital of **Estonia**. When things were going badly for the Danes, a red flag with a white cross is said to have fallen from the sky. After that the Danes are said to have won the battle. Nobody knows whether this really happened; it is a legend.

The legend takes place on **15 June**. In Denmark this day is called **Valdemar's Day**. On this day many people raise the Dannebrog. About **800 years** have passed since the legend. That is why people often say that the Dannebrog is one of the **oldest flags in the world** still used by a country today.

The Dannebrog is very popular in Denmark. You see it not only on official buildings. Many families decorate **birthday cakes**, gardens and even the **Christmas tree** with it. Small paper flags are simply part of many celebrations. So the flag is a sign of joy and community.

gewusst: Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland took the Nordic cross from the Dannebrog, but in other colours.
The name Dannebrog is often explained as meaning “Danish cloth”.

teile.einleitung: Since it was founded, the European Union has grown from six to 27 member states. This admission of new countries is called the enlargement of the European Union. Any country that wants to join must meet strict conditions and go through a long procedure.
wichtigste: In 1957 six countries founded the European Economic Community, from which the EU developed.
Today the EU has 27 member states (as of 2026).
The biggest enlargement took place in 2004 with ten new countries.
New members must meet the Copenhagen criteria.
A candidate country meets the conditions for accession negotiations but is not yet a member.
In 2020 the United Kingdom became the only country so far to leave the EU.
In 2016 Switzerland withdrew its application for membership from 1992.

abschnitte.text: In 1957 Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands signed the **Treaties of Rome**. With them they founded the European Economic Community. These six countries are called the **founding states**. In 1993 the European Union grew out of this community.

In 1973 Denmark, Ireland and the United Kingdom joined, in 1981 Greece and in 1986 Spain and Portugal. In 1995 Austria, Finland and Sweden joined. The biggest **enlargement** followed in 2004 with ten countries, including Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the three Baltic states. In 2007 Bulgaria and Romania joined, and in 2013 Croatia became the most recent country so far.

Any country that wants to become a member must meet the **Copenhagen criteria** of 1993. These include democracy, the rule of law, and protecting human rights and minorities. The country also needs a working market economy and must adopt the rules of the EU. In the end, all the existing members must agree to the accession.

A **candidate country** is a country that is officially recognised as an applicant but is not yet a member. Candidates include Montenegro, Serbia, Albania, North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Turkey, Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia (as of 2025). Negotiations often take many years. With Turkey they have been on hold for quite some time.

In 2016 the United Kingdom voted to leave; this so-called **Brexit** was completed at the end of January 2020. Switzerland submitted an application for membership in 1992, but shortly afterwards the people rejected joining the European Economic Area. The application was then left untouched and was officially withdrawn in 2016. Instead, Switzerland governs its relations with the EU through **bilateral agreements**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A country that belongs to the European Union.
A country that officially wants to become a member and is negotiating, or may negotiate, with the EU.
The conditions a country must meet to join the EU.
The United Kingdom's departure from the EU, from the English words Britain and exit.

gewusst: As part of Denmark, Greenland belonged to the European Community, but it left in 1985 after a referendum.
Norway has voted twice on joining, in 1972 and 1994, and both times the majority said no.

teile.einleitung: The British royal family is one of the best-known families in the world. Its head is the king or queen of the United Kingdom. Since 2022 that has been King Charles III.
wichtigste: The royal family lives in the United Kingdom, made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Queen Elizabeth II reigned from 1952 to 2022, that is, for 70 years.
Her husband was Prince Philip; he died in 2021 at the age of 99.
Her eldest son Charles III has been king since 2022.
Prince William is married to Catherine, and they have three children.
Prince Harry is married to Meghan, and they have two children.

abschnitte.text: The United Kingdom is a **constitutional monarchy**. This means that the king is head of state, but politics is made by the elected **Parliament** and the government. The king mainly has ceremonial duties. He receives guests, opens Parliament and visits towns and organisations. Since 1917 the family has been called the **House of Windsor**.

**Queen Elizabeth II** came to the throne in 1952 and reigned for 70 years, longer than any British monarch before her. She died in September 2022. Her husband **Prince Philip** was married to her for more than 70 years and died in 2021 at the age of 99. They had four children: **Charles**, **Anne**, Andrew and Edward. Princess **Anne** was born in 1950 and is the only daughter.

After his mother's death, **Charles III** became king. In May 2023 he was crowned in London. His first wife was **Princess Diana**, who was very popular with many people. She died in a car accident in Paris in 1997. Today Charles is married to **Camilla**, who has the title of Queen.

Charles and Diana have two sons. **Prince William** is the heir to the throne. In 2011 he married **Catherine Middleton**, whom many people simply call Kate. They have three children: George, Charlotte and Louis. His younger brother **Prince Harry** was born in 1984. In 2018 he married the American actress **Meghan Markle**. They have two children and live in the USA.

gewusst: When the king is at Buckingham Palace, his personal flag, the Royal Standard, flies there.
The king is also head of state of other countries, for example Canada and Australia.

teile.einleitung: The Charter of the United Nations is the founding treaty of the UN. It is something like the organisation's constitution: it sets out its goals, its rules and its most important bodies.
wichtigste: The Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945.
It came into force on 24 October 1945; this day is now United Nations Day.
It begins with the words “We the peoples of the United Nations”.
The first goal is to maintain world peace and international security.
The Charter consists of a preamble and 111 articles in 19 chapters.
Force against other states is forbidden, except in self-defence.

abschnitte.text: The Second World War had cost countless lives. That is why many countries wanted to create an organisation to prevent future wars. In spring 1945 they met for a large conference in **San Francisco**. On **26 June 1945** they signed the Charter. On **24 October 1945** it came into force, and with that the UN was founded.

The Charter consists of a **preamble**, that is, an introduction, and **111 articles** in 19 chapters. It begins with the words “We the peoples of the United Nations”. This is meant to show that the Charter applies to all people, not just to governments. The **equal rights of men and women** are already mentioned in the preamble. In 1945 that was something special.

The UN's first goal is to maintain **world peace** and international security. Other goals are friendly relations between countries and cooperation, for example on poverty or human rights. States are to settle disputes **peacefully**. **Force against other states** is in principle forbidden. All members are regarded as equal, no matter how big or small they are.

**Article 51** allows a country that is attacked to defend itself until the Security Council acts. The **Security Council** has special responsibility for peace. Under **Chapter VII** it can decide on **sanctions** when peace is threatened, for example trade bans. As a last resort it can also authorise military measures. Its decisions are binding on all members.

Switzerland only joined the UN in **2002**, after voters had said yes in a vote. By joining, it accepted the Charter. It kept its **neutrality** in doing so. Long before that, **Geneva** was an important UN location; today it is the UN's most important seat after New York.

gewusst: Every year on 24 October the world celebrates United Nations Day, because the Charter came into force on that day in 1945.
Switzerland was one of the last countries in the world to join the UN.
The International Court of Justice in The Hague is also established in the Charter.

teile.einleitung: Diplomacy is the art of keeping up peaceful relations between states and settling conflicts through talks. Diplomats negotiate, mediate and represent their country abroad. Switzerland is known for its good offices and as the host of important peace talks.
wichtigste: Diplomacy means shaping relations between states through negotiations.
The Vienna Convention of 1961 regulates the privileges and immunities of diplomats.
An unwelcome diplomat is declared persona non grata.
Since 1980 Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran as a protecting power.
In 1985 Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met in Geneva.
With its good offices, Switzerland supported the Évian Accords, which ended the Algerian War in 1962.

abschnitte.text: **Diplomacy** is the way states deal with each other using words instead of weapons. Diplomats negotiate treaties, settle disputes and maintain friendships between countries. They work in embassies, in the foreign ministry and at international organisations. The word comes from the Greek diploma, a folded document that was once used as a pass.

The most important rules are in the **Vienna Convention** on Diplomatic Relations of 1961. Before a new ambassador comes, the host country must agree; this is called the **agrément**. Diplomats enjoy special privileges and immunity. But a state can declare a diplomat **persona non grata**, and then he must leave the country.

In **shuttle diplomacy**, a mediator travels back and forth between the parties to a conflict, as Henry Kissinger did in the Middle East in the 1970s. Sometimes unusual ways help too. In 1971 table tennis matches between players from the USA and China started a rapprochement, ping-pong diplomacy. The longest-serving ambassador in a country is called the doyen and represents the diplomatic corps.

Because Switzerland is neutral, it is often chosen as a mediator. This help is called **good offices**. It supported, for example, the negotiations that ended the Algerian War with the Évian Accords in 1962. As a **protecting power**, Switzerland represents states that have no direct relations with each other, for example the interests of the USA in Iran since 1980.

Geneva is one of the most important centres of diplomacy in the world. The UN, the Red Cross and many other organisations are based there. In 1985 the American President Ronald Reagan and the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met in Geneva. This summit was an important step towards the end of the Cold War.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who represents their country towards other states.
Latin for unwelcome person; a diplomat who has to leave the country.
A state that represents the interests of another state in a third country.
Help from a neutral state with negotiations between parties in a dispute.

gewusst: When you are diplomatic in everyday life, you say unpleasant things especially politely and carefully.
Switzerland has taken on many protecting power mandates; there were especially many in the Second World War.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, FDFA for short, is Switzerland's foreign ministry. It looks after Switzerland's relations with other countries and with international organisations. It also helps Swiss people who get into difficulties abroad.
wichtigste: The FDFA looks after Switzerland's relations with other countries.
It is one of the seven departments of the federal administration.
It is headed by a member of the Federal Council.
The FDFA has its seat in the West Wing of the Federal Palace in Bern.
Switzerland has about 170 embassies, consulates and other representations around the world.
The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) also belongs to the FDFA.
The FDFA advises travellers with travel advice on many countries.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland's federal administration is divided into seven **departments**, one for each member of the Federal Council. The FDFA is the department for **foreign policy**; in other countries it would be called the foreign ministry. Its headquarters is the West Wing of the Federal Palace in Bern. The head of the FDFA is a kind of foreign minister of Switzerland.

The FDFA represents Switzerland's interests towards other countries. It negotiates treaties, for example with the European Union, and represents Switzerland in the **UN** and other organisations. Important aims of Swiss foreign policy are peace, human rights, prosperity and protecting the environment. In doing so, Switzerland pays attention to its **neutrality**.

So that Switzerland is present in other countries, the FDFA runs a network of **embassies** and consulates. An embassy is the official representation in the capital of another country. Consulates mainly help people, for example by issuing passports. In total Switzerland has about 170 representations around the world (as of the 2020s).

More than 800,000 Swiss people live abroad (as of about 2024). For them and for travellers, the FDFA is an important point of contact. Anyone who loses a passport, falls ill or gets into an emergency can turn to a representation or to the **FDFA Helpline**. Before a trip, you can read the FDFA's travel advice to find out whether a country is safe.

Switzerland is known for its **good offices**. This means that it mediates between countries in dispute or organises talks. With protecting power mandates, Switzerland represents the interests of one country in another when the two no longer have direct relations. Since 1980, for example, Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the seven large ministries of the Swiss federal administration.
The official representation of one country in another country.
The art of finding solutions between countries through talks and negotiations.
A country that represents the interests of another country when that country has no representation of its own.

gewusst: Geneva is one of the most important places for international diplomacy; many UN organisations have their seat there.
Until 1979 the FDFA was called the Federal Political Department.
Switzerland has mediated between hostile countries many times and has organised numerous peace talks in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: The European Court of Auditors checks whether the European Union collects and spends its money properly. It is something like the EU's auditor.
wichtigste: The Court of Auditors has its seat in Luxembourg.
It checks the income and spending of the EU.
Each member state provides one member.
The term of office is six years.
It began its work in 1977.
It reports suspected fraud to the office OLAF.

abschnitte.text: The European Court of Auditors is the EU's **external auditor**. It checks whether the EU's money is used **lawfully** and **efficiently**. It has its seat in **Luxembourg**, in the European quarter on the Kirchberg. The Court of Auditors cannot impose penalties itself. In Switzerland, the Swiss Federal Audit Office does similar work for the Confederation.

Each member state provides **one member**. The members are appointed by the Council for **six years** after consulting Parliament, and they may be reappointed. The Court of Auditors was founded by a treaty of 1975 and began its work in **1977**. With the Maastricht Treaty it became an **institution** of the Community in 1993.

Every year the Court of Auditors publishes an **annual report**. It contains the **statement of assurance**. This says whether the EU's accounts are reliable and whether the spending was lawful. There are also many **special reports**, which examine individual areas closely, for example farm subsidies or coronavirus aid.

On the recommendation of the Council, the **European Parliament** grants the Commission **discharge** for the budget. With it, Parliament confirms that the money was managed properly. The reports of the Court of Auditors are the most important basis for this. If fraud is suspected, the Court of Auditors cannot investigate itself. It reports the case to the **European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF)**.

gewusst: The Court of Auditors may check, but it may not impose penalties.
The Court of Auditors has only been an official institution since the Maastricht Treaty.

teile.einleitung: Fair trade aims to make sure that farmers and workers in poorer countries get a fair wage for their products. In Switzerland the Max Havelaar label is especially well known.
wichtigste: The Max Havelaar Foundation was founded in Basel in 1992.
It was founded by six Swiss aid organisations.
The first product with the label was coffee.
The Fairtrade Minimum Price protects against low world market prices.
The Fairtrade Premium goes into community projects.
The first world shop opened in the Netherlands in 1969.

abschnitte.text: Many products such as coffee, cocoa or bananas come from poorer countries. The farmers often earn very little from them. Fair trade wants to change this. The **Fairtrade Minimum Price** is paid even when prices on the world market fall sharply. It is meant to cover the costs of production. On top of this comes the **Fairtrade Premium**. The farmers decide together how to use it, for example for schools, wells or health posts.

The first **world shop** opened in April 1969 in Breukelen in the **Netherlands**. World shops sell fairly traded goods and are often run by volunteers. Later people wanted to bring fair products into ordinary shops too. For this, **labels** were created, which you can recognise on the packaging.

The **Max Havelaar Foundation** was founded in Basel in 1992; since 2015 it has been based in Zurich. Its founders were six aid organisations: Bread for All, Caritas, Fastenopfer, HEKS, Helvetas and Swissaid. It is named after the main character of a Dutch novel from the 19th century. The first product with the label was **coffee**. Later came bananas, sugar, flowers and much more.

In 2014 more than every second **banana** sold in Switzerland carried the Max Havelaar label. According to the foundation, people in Switzerland spent about **107 francs** per person on Fairtrade products in 2021. This puts Switzerland among the world leaders. The international rules are set by **Fairtrade International**. They are checked by an independent body.

gewusst: In 2014 more than every second banana sold in Switzerland was fairly traded.
Max Havelaar is not a real person but the main character of a novel.

teile.einleitung: Development cooperation means that richer countries and organisations support poorer countries. The aim is to reduce poverty and give people better living conditions. Both sides are meant to work together as partners.
wichtigste: Development cooperation is the support of poorer countries by richer countries and organisations.
In the past it was mostly called development aid.
Important aims are less poverty, more education and better health.
In 2015 the UN adopted the 2030 Agenda with 17 Sustainable Development Goals.
In Switzerland the SDC is mainly responsible.
Aid organisations such as Helvetas, Caritas or Swissaid also carry out development cooperation.
The UN recommends that rich countries spend 0.7 per cent of their national income on it.

abschnitte.text: In **development cooperation**, countries, international organisations and aid organisations support poorer countries. In the past it was mostly called **development aid**. The new name is meant to show that the countries work together as partners. The people on the spot should have a say in what they really need.

Support goes, for example, to schools, wells, hospitals, farming and small businesses. An important principle is **helping people to help themselves**: people should learn to solve their problems themselves. This also includes training skilled people such as teachers, doctors or craftspeople. With **microcredits**, meaning very small loans, people can start their own business.

In 2015 all UN member states adopted the **2030 Agenda**. It contains 17 Sustainable Development Goals, for example zero hunger, quality education and clean water. These goals apply to all countries, including Switzerland. They are meant to be reached by 2030, although this is difficult for many of the goals.

In Switzerland, the **SDC** and SECO are mainly in charge of state development cooperation. There are also many aid organisations, such as Helvetas, Caritas, HEKS, Swissaid or Terre des hommes. They are funded by donations and partly by money from the Confederation. So far Switzerland has not reached the UN target of 0.7 per cent of national income.

Development cooperation is much debated. Critics say that aid sometimes makes people dependent or ends up in the wrong hands. Supporters stress that thanks to vaccinations, schools and water projects, millions of people have a better life. That is why good planning, monitoring and **fair trade** are important, so that poorer countries can sell their products at fair prices.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organisation that uses donations to help people in need.
A very small loan for people who cannot get money from ordinary banks.
Designed so that it is also good for future generations.
Trade in which farmers and workers receive fair prices and wages.

gewusst: Since 1990, the share of people living in extreme poverty worldwide has fallen sharply.
The organisation Helvetas was founded in 1955 as the first private Swiss organisation for development cooperation.

teile.einleitung: The 0.7 per cent target is an international promise made by rich countries. Every year they are supposed to spend 0.7 per cent of their gross national income on official development aid. The target is more than 50 years old, but only a few countries meet it.
wichtigste: The Pearson Commission recommended the target in 1969.
The UN General Assembly adopted it in 1970.
Official development aid is known internationally as ODA or APD.
The OECD's Development Assistance Committee DAC decides what counts as development aid.
In 2024 Switzerland spent just under 0.5 per cent of its gross national income.
In 2024 only 4 of the 32 DAC countries met the target, including Norway and Luxembourg.

abschnitte.text: In 1969 a commission working for the **World Bank** presented a report. It was led by the former Canadian Prime Minister **Lester Pearson**. That is why it is called the **Pearson Commission**. Its report “Partners in Development” proposed that rich countries should spend 0.7 per cent of their economic output on development aid. In 1970 the **UN General Assembly** set out the target in a resolution. Since then it has been confirmed many times.

It is measured against **gross national income**, GNI for short. This is roughly all the income that the people and companies of a country earn in a year. Official development aid is called **ODA** in English, Official Development Assistance, and **APD** in French, Aide publique au développement. In Switzerland the abbreviation APD is common. Which spending counts is decided by the OECD's **Development Assistance Committee DAC**. Switzerland is a member.

Only a few countries meet the target. In 2024 only **4 of the 32** DAC donor countries were at 0.7 per cent or above: **Norway**, **Luxembourg**, **Sweden** and **Denmark**. Norway and Luxembourg even reached about one per cent. **Germany** reached 0.70 per cent for the first time in 2016. However, a large part of this was spending on refugees in its own country.

Switzerland gives development aid mainly through the **SDC**, the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, and through **SECO**. In 2011 **Parliament** decided on its own target of **0.5 per cent**. In 2024 Switzerland spent just under 0.5 per cent of its gross national income. This puts it well below the 0.7 per cent target. It is a matter of political dispute: some want more money for poor countries, others want the federal government to save.

Under the DAC rules, countries may also partly count the **costs of asylum seekers** in their own country, during the first twelve months. This also applies to Switzerland. Critics complain that this money does not go to poor countries. Supporters say that looking after refugees is also important help. In this way a country can raise its share without sending more money abroad.

gewusst: The 0.7 per cent target was adopted as early as 1970, and most donor countries have never reached it to this day.
0.7 per cent means that of every 1000 francs of a country's income, 7 francs would go to development aid.

teile.einleitung: The **Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty** is meant to prevent nuclear weapons from spreading to more and more countries. It was opened for signature in 1968 and is one of the most important treaties in the world. Almost all states have joined it, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: The treaty was opened for signature in 1968 and came into force in 1970.
It recognises five official nuclear-weapon states.
It rests on three pillars: non-proliferation, disarmament and peaceful use.
In 1995 it was extended indefinitely.
North Korea declared its withdrawal in 2003.
Switzerland ratified the treaty in 1977.

abschnitte.text: In the Cold War many people feared that dozens of countries might soon have nuclear weapons. That is why the treaty was opened for signature on **1 July 1968**. It came into force on **5 March 1970**, after enough states had ratified it. Originally it was to apply for 25 years. In 1995 the states party to it decided that it should apply **indefinitely**.

The treaty rests on three pillars. First, **non-proliferation**: states without nuclear weapons do without them. Second, **disarmament**: the nuclear-weapon states are to reduce their weapons. Third, **peaceful use**: all states may use nuclear energy, for example for power stations or medicine. This bargain is regarded as the core of the treaty.

The treaty recognises as official nuclear-weapon states only those countries that had exploded a nuclear weapon before 1967. They are the **USA, Russia, Great Britain, France and China**. India, Pakistan and Israel have never joined the treaty. **North Korea** declared its withdrawal in 2003 and carried out nuclear weapons tests from 2006.

The **International Atomic Energy Agency**, IAEA for short, checks compliance. It is based in **Vienna** and carries out inspections in nuclear facilities. This is meant to make sure that no nuclear material is secretly used for weapons. Every five years the states party to the treaty meet for a review conference.

Switzerland signed the treaty in **1969** and ratified it in **1977**. With this it gave up its own nuclear weapons in a binding way. Today Switzerland works internationally for disarmament and non-proliferation. Geneva is an important place for disarmament negotiations.

gewusst: The treaty was originally meant to apply for only 25 years; today it applies without end.
Almost all the states in the world are members of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

teile.einleitung: **António Guterres** is a Portuguese politician and has been Secretary-General of the United Nations since 2017. Before that he was head of government of Portugal and led the UN Refugee Agency in Geneva for ten years. His second term ends at the end of 2026.
wichtigste: Guterres was born in Lisbon in 1949 and studied physics and electrical engineering.
From 1995 to 2002 he was Prime Minister of Portugal.
He belongs to the Socialist Party of Portugal.
From 2005 to 2015 he led UNHCR, which is based in Geneva.
He is the ninth Secretary-General of the UN.
In 2021 he was confirmed for a second term until the end of 2026.

abschnitte.text: António Guterres was born in **Lisbon** in 1949. He studied **physics and electrical engineering** at the Instituto Superior Técnico, the technical university of Lisbon. After that he worked briefly as an assistant professor. But he soon turned to politics.

Guterres is a member of Portugal's **Socialist Party**, the Partido Socialista. As its general secretary, he led it to election victory in 1995. From 1995 to 2002 he was **Prime Minister** of Portugal. From 1999 to 2005 he was also head of the **Socialist International**, a worldwide association of social democratic parties.

From 2005 to 2015 Guterres was UN **High Commissioner for Refugees**. In this role he led **UNHCR**, which is based in Geneva. The agency protects and supports people who have had to flee their homes. His time in office saw large movements of refugees, for example because of the war in Syria.

On 1 January 2017 Guterres became the **ninth Secretary-General** of the UN. Before him, Ban Ki-moon from South Korea had held the office. The Secretary-General leads the UN administration and mediates in conflicts. In 2021 the Security Council and the General Assembly confirmed him, with no rival candidates, for a **second term**. It began on 1 January 2022 and ends on 31 December 2026.

Guterres warns again and again about the **climate crisis**. When July 2023 was found to be the hottest month ever measured, he said the “era of global boiling” had begun. He also proposed a **Summit of the Future**. There, in September 2024 in New York, the General Assembly adopted the “Pact for the Future”. It is meant to modernise cooperation between states and the UN itself.

gewusst: As Refugee Commissioner, Guterres worked in Geneva for ten years.
Before he became a politician, Guterres taught briefly as an assistant professor.

teile.einleitung: The Broken Chair is a giant wooden chair in Geneva with part of one leg missing. It stands in front of the Palais des Nations and commemorates the people who have been injured by landmines.
wichtigste: The Broken Chair is about 12 metres high.
It is made of wood and weighs about 5.5 tonnes.
It was designed by the Geneva artist **Daniel Berset** and built by the carpenter **Louis Genève**.
The organisation **Handicap International** had it put up in 1997.
It stands on the Place des Nations, opposite the Palais des Nations.
The broken leg recalls the victims of landmines.
