abschnitte.text: The **Broken Chair** is a **sculpture made of wood** about **12 metres** high. That is as high as a house with four floors. About **5.5 tonnes** of wood were used for the chair, roughly as much as an elephant weighs. A large piece is missing from one of its four legs.

The chair was designed by the Geneva artist **Daniel Berset**. It was built by the carpenter **Louis Genève**. It was commissioned by the aid organisation **Handicap International**, which helps people with disabilities. The chair was first put up in **1997**.

**Landmines** are weapons hidden in the ground. They explode when someone steps on them, often many years after a war. Many victims lose a leg as a result. The broken chair leg recalls these people. In 1997 many countries negotiated a **ban on landmines**. In December 1997 the treaty was signed in Ottawa.

abschnitte.titel: In front of the Palais des Nations
abschnitte.text: The chair stands on the **Place des Nations** in Geneva. Opposite is the **Palais des Nations**, the UN's European headquarters. Diplomats from all over the world meet there. The chair is meant to remind them to think of the victims of war. Today it is a well-known landmark of Geneva and a popular subject for photos.

gewusst: Originally the Broken Chair was only meant to stay for a short time.
Switzerland has signed the ban on anti-personnel mines and supports mine clearance in many countries.

teile.einleitung: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is a document that lists the rights of every person in the world. It was adopted by the UN in 1948. Its first article says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
wichtigste: The UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948 in Paris.
The Declaration has 30 articles.
It applies to everyone, whatever their origin, skin colour, religion or sex.
Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the commission that drew up the Declaration.
10 December is now International Human Rights Day.
The Declaration is not a treaty, but it has shaped many later laws and treaties.

abschnitte.text: The **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** lists rights that belong to every person simply because they are human. These include the right to life, liberty and security. It bans slavery and torture. It also names rights such as education, work, freedom of opinion and freedom of religion.

After the Second World War, with its terrible crimes, the states wanted to make sure that nothing like it would ever happen again. The newly founded **UN** therefore set up a commission. It was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, the widow of the American President Franklin D. Roosevelt. People from different cultures worked on the text, for example the Frenchman René Cassin.

The UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration on 10 December 1948 in the Palais de Chaillot in Paris. 48 states voted for it, none voted against, and eight states abstained. That is why 10 December is today **Human Rights Day**. The Nobel Peace Prize is also awarded on this day.

The Declaration is a recommendation and not a binding **treaty**. But many treaties build on it, for example the UN human rights covenants of 1966. In Europe the European Convention on Human Rights was created, which Switzerland joined in 1974. Many countries have also written human rights into their constitutions, including Switzerland in its Federal Constitution.

Human rights also directly concern children and young people. The right to **education**, for example, means that all children may go to school. Freedom of opinion allows you to say what you think, even if others do not like it. For children there is also the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child of 1989.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rights that every person has from birth.
The worth that every person has, which must be respected.
The assembly in which all UN member states are represented.
When you vote neither yes nor no in a vote.

gewusst: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is thought to be one of the most translated documents in the world; it exists in several hundred languages.
In the 1948 vote, not a single state voted against the Declaration.

teile.einleitung: Brexit is the name for Great Britain's departure from the European Union. The word is made up of the English words Britain and exit. The United Kingdom left the EU at the end of January 2020 after almost 50 years of membership.
wichtigste: Brexit means Great Britain's departure from the European Union.
On 23 June 2016 a narrow majority of Britons voted to leave.
The United Kingdom had been a member of the European Community since 1973.
The departure took place on 31 January 2020.
A transition period applied until the end of 2020.
The question of the border between Northern Ireland and Ireland was especially difficult.

abschnitte.text: **Brexit** is the departure of the **United Kingdom** from the European Union. The United Kingdom is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It joined the European Community, which later became the EU, in 1973. So far it is the only country that has left the EU again.

Many Britons were unhappy with the EU, for example because of immigration and rules from Brussels. Prime Minister David Cameron therefore promised a **referendum**. On 23 June 2016 just under 52 per cent voted to leave. Cameron, who wanted to stay in the EU, then resigned.

After the vote, the British government negotiated a **withdrawal agreement** with the EU. Parliament in London rejected several drafts, so everything took a very long time. Prime Minister Theresa May resigned in 2019 and was followed by Boris Johnson. On 31 January 2020 the United Kingdom finally left the EU.

There is a land border between Northern Ireland, which belongs to the United Kingdom, and Ireland, which is in the EU. After a long conflict it was important not to introduce border checks there. That is why a special arrangement was agreed, the **Northern Ireland Protocol**. In 2023 it was adjusted by a new agreement, the Windsor Framework.

Since Brexit there have again been customs checks and more paperwork in trade between Great Britain and the EU. EU citizens may no longer simply live and work in Great Britain. Switzerland had regulated many of its agreements with Great Britain through the EU. That is why it concluded its own **agreements** with the United Kingdom in good time, so that trade and travel would keep working well.

begriffe.erklaerung: A popular vote on an important question.
A treaty that sets out how a country leaves an organisation.
A time when old rules still apply until new ones are ready.
A charge or check on goods brought across a border.

gewusst: Following the Brexit model, word games appeared such as Grexit for a possible Greek exit from the euro.
In the 2016 vote, Scotland and Northern Ireland mostly voted to remain in the EU, while England and Wales voted to leave.

teile.einleitung: Emissions trading is a tool for protecting the climate. Companies need permission to emit greenhouse gases such as CO2, and these permits can be bought and sold.
wichtigste: The principle is called “cap and trade”: an upper limit and trading.
One emission allowance permits the emission of one tonne of CO2.
The upper limit is lowered every year.
The EU's emissions trading has existed since 2005.
Since 2020, Swiss emissions trading has been linked to the EU's.
In Switzerland it is mainly large industrial plants that take part.

abschnitte.text: The state lays down how much greenhouse gas all the participating companies may emit together. This is the **upper limit**, or “cap” in English. For this it issues **allowances**, handing them out for free or auctioning them. One allowance permits one tonne of CO2. At the end of the year, every company must hand in as many allowances as it has emitted.

Anyone who emits less needs fewer allowances and can sell the ones left over. Anyone who emits more has to buy extra. This is the **trading**, or “trade” in English. This makes it worthwhile for companies to save energy and use cleaner technology. Because the upper limit falls every year, there are fewer and fewer allowances, and emissions go down overall.

The European Union started its **Emissions Trading System** in 2005. It is one of the largest systems of its kind in the world. It covers power stations, factories and also flights within Europe. Other countries have their own systems. **China** began nationwide emissions trading in 2021, at first for coal-fired power stations.

Switzerland also has emissions trading. It covers plants with high emissions, such as **cement works**, refineries and chemical factories. Since 1 January 2020 the Swiss system has been **linked** to the EU's. The allowances are recognised by both sides. Since 2020 aviation has also been included.

Article 6 of the **Paris Agreement** allows countries to work together on climate protection projects. In October 2020 Switzerland signed the world's first such agreement with **Peru**. Switzerland supports projects abroad and can count the greenhouse gases saved towards its own targets.

gewusst: In 2020 Switzerland and Peru signed the world's first agreement under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.
Instead of CO2, an allowance can also apply to an equally effective amount of another greenhouse gas.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Brazil is green with a yellow rhombus and a blue circle in the middle. The blue circle shows a starry sky and carries the motto “Ordem e Progresso”.
wichtigste: The background colour of the flag is green.
On it lies a yellow rhombus.
In the middle is a blue circle with 27 stars.
A white band carries the words “Ordem e Progresso”, meaning “Order and Progress”.
The stars show the sky over Rio de Janeiro on 15 November 1889.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Brazil has a **green** background. On it lies a **yellow rhombus**. A rhombus is a four-sided shape standing on one corner, like a diamond. In the middle is a **blue circle**. It shows the sky with stars. Green and yellow are often linked with the country's forests and gold.

A **white band** runs across the blue circle. On it, in green letters, are the words **“Ordem e Progresso”**. This means **“Order and Progress”**. The motto is in **Portuguese**. Portuguese is spoken in Brazil because the country used to be a **colony of Portugal**.

The flag has **27 stars**. Each star stands for a **state** or for the Federal District with the capital Brasília. The stars show the sky over **Rio de Janeiro** on the morning of **15 November 1889**. On that day Brazil became a **republic**. That is why the stars are arranged as they could be seen in the sky at that time.

gewusst: The stars on the flag of Brazil show a real starry sky from 15 November 1889.
If a new state is added, the flag gets a new star.

teile.einleitung: A developing country is a country that is less developed economically and socially than the rich industrialised countries. Many people there have little money, and schools, hospitals or roads are often lacking. But every country is different, and many developing countries are changing very quickly today.
wichtigste: A developing country is less developed economically and socially than rich industrialised countries.
Typical features are poverty, little education and weak health care.
Most developing countries are in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
The UN calls the poorest countries the least developed countries.
Countries that are catching up strongly are called emerging economies.
The Human Development Index measures income, education and life expectancy.
Today people often also speak of the Global South.

abschnitte.text: A **developing country** is a country with a low standard of living. Many people have a very small income and often work in farming. There is no single worldwide list, because different organisations use different standards. The term is disputed because it sounds as if all countries had to follow the same path.

A well-known measure is the UN's **Human Development Index**. It takes into account income, the number of years spent at school and life expectancy. The World Bank groups countries by their income per person. In such rankings, Switzerland is always among the countries right at the top.

Many developing countries lack clean **drinking water** or good health care. Many children cannot go to school for long because they have to work. Often there are also problems such as debt, corruption, wars or natural disasters. The effects of climate change, such as droughts, also hit these countries especially hard.

Some countries develop very quickly and catch up. They are called **emerging economies** (in German, “threshold countries”), because they stand on the threshold of becoming industrialised countries. Examples are China, India, Brazil and Mexico. South Korea was very poor in the 1950s and is a rich industrialised country today.

People used to speak of the **Third World**; this expression is now considered outdated. Today the term **Global South** is often used, because many poorer countries lie to the south of the rich industrialised countries. The UN calls the poorest countries the least developed countries; there are more than 40 of them, most in Africa. Rich countries such as Switzerland support these countries with development cooperation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rich country with many factories, services and well-developed infrastructure.
How many years people in a country live on average.
A country that is developing quickly and could soon be one of the industrialised countries.
A collective term for poorer countries, especially in Africa, Asia and Latin America.

gewusst: In the 19th century, Switzerland too was poor in many areas, and thousands of people emigrated to America because of it.
When it became independent in 1966, Botswana was one of the poorest countries in the world, and it has developed strongly since then.

teile.einleitung: The European Union, EU for short, is an association of 27 European countries that work closely together. They have shared rules for trade, travel, the environment and much more. Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe but is not a member of the EU.
wichtigste: EU stands for European Union.
The EU has 27 member states (as of 2026).
About 450 million people live in the EU.
Switzerland is not a member, but it works closely with the EU through bilateral agreements.
In the single market, goods, people, services and capital can move freely.
Most of the important EU institutions have their seat in Brussels.
In 2012 the EU received the Nobel Peace Prize.

abschnitte.text: The **European Union** is a community of countries that take many decisions together. It is more than an alliance, but it is not a country of its own either. Its members include, for example, Germany, France, Italy and Austria, meaning all of Switzerland's neighbours except Liechtenstein. The EU has 24 official languages.

After the Second World War, the countries of Europe wanted to prevent another war. In 1951 six countries founded the European Coal and Steel Community, followed in 1957 by the European Economic Community. With the **Maastricht Treaty**, the European Union was created in 1993. For its contribution to peace and reconciliation it received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012.

The EU has several important **institutions**. The European Commission proposes laws; the European Parliament and the Council of the EU pass them. In the European Council, the heads of state and government meet and set the overall direction. The Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg makes sure that EU law is applied correctly.

The heart of the EU is the **single market** with four freedoms: goods, people, services and capital may move freely. Many EU countries also have the **euro** as shared money. Thanks to the Schengen Agreement, there are no longer regular passport checks at many borders. EU citizens may live and work in any member state.

Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but the EU is its most important trading partner. In 1992 the Swiss people rejected joining the European Economic Area. Since then Switzerland has governed its relations with **bilateral agreements**, for example on the free movement of persons or on land transport. Since 2008 Switzerland has been part of the Schengen Area, and a new package of agreements with the EU is being debated in politics (as of 2026).

begriffe.erklaerung: A country that belongs to the EU.
A shared market without customs duties and with the same rules for all member countries.
Agreements between two partners, here between Switzerland and the EU.
An area in Europe where there are usually no passport checks at the borders.

gewusst: Switzerland is almost completely surrounded by EU countries; only Liechtenstein is not an EU member.
The EU also includes territories far from Europe, for example the French island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean.
In 2020 the United Kingdom became the only country so far to leave the EU.

teile.einleitung: **Labour migration** is when people move to another country to work there. Switzerland has been an important destination for decades. Labour migration brings opportunities but also causes political debate again and again.
wichtigste: Labour migrants move to another country to find work there.
Until 2002 Switzerland had the seasonal worker statute.
Since 2002 the free movement of persons has applied between Switzerland and the EU.
Cross-border commuters receive permit G.
Money that migrants send home is called remittances.
When highly qualified professionals leave, this is called brain drain.

abschnitte.text: Many people leave their country because they find **better work** and higher wages elsewhere. Some countries, on the other hand, urgently need workers, for example in construction, in hospitals or in restaurants and hotels. After the Second World War many workers came to Switzerland from **Italy**, and later also from Spain, Portugal and Yugoslavia. They helped to build roads, tunnels and houses.

For a long time many foreign workers were only allowed to work in Switzerland for a few months a year. This was regulated by the **seasonal worker statute**. Seasonal workers worked, for example, in construction or tourism and then had to leave the country again. They were not allowed to bring their families. The statute was abolished in 2002.

Switzerland often votes on immigration. In 1970 the **Schwarzenbach initiative** wanted to limit the share of foreigners sharply. About 54 per cent of voters rejected it. On 9 February 2014, however, the people approved the **mass immigration initiative** with about 50.3 per cent. It demanded that Switzerland control immigration on its own.

Since 1 June 2002 the **free movement of persons** with the EU has applied. It is part of the Bilateral Agreements I. Since then people from the EU with a work contract have been able to work in Switzerland more easily, and the other way round. Anyone who lives abroad and works in Switzerland receives **permit G**. The G stands for “Grenzgänger”, cross-border commuter. There are especially many in Geneva, Basel and Ticino.

abschnitte.titel: Effects on the countries of origin
abschnitte.text: Many migrants send money to their families. These **remittances** are an important source of income for some countries. Worldwide they are much larger than state development aid. But there are also disadvantages: when doctors or engineers emigrate, they are missing at home. This is called **brain drain**.

gewusst: Seasonal workers were not allowed to bring their children, so some children lived hidden in Switzerland.
Worldwide, migrants send more money home than states pay in development aid.

teile.einleitung: The Bretton Woods system was an order for money and exchange rates after the Second World War. It was created in 1944 at a conference in the USA and lasted until the early 1970s.
wichtigste: In July 1944 representatives of 44 states met at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire.
The dollar was tied to gold at 35 dollars per fine ounce.
The other currencies had fixed rates to the dollar.
The **International Monetary Fund** and the **World Bank** were founded.
In 1971 President Nixon ended the conversion of dollars into gold.
Since 1973 the rates of the major currencies have floated freely.

abschnitte.text: While the Second World War was still going on, representatives of **44 states** met in July 1944 at **Bretton Woods** in the US state of New Hampshire. They wanted to prevent currencies from falling into chaos as they had in the 1930s. The economist **John Maynard Keynes** negotiated for Great Britain. He proposed a neutral world currency called the “bancor”. But it was the American **Harry Dexter White** who got his way.

In the new system the **US dollar** became the **leading currency**. The USA promised to exchange dollars held by central banks for gold at **35 dollars per fine ounce**. The other currencies had **fixed exchange rates** to the dollar. In this way companies and states knew exactly what their money was worth abroad. This made trade easier after the war.

Two institutions were founded at the conference. The **International Monetary Fund** (IMF) was to safeguard the currency order and help countries in need. The **World Bank** was to finance reconstruction. Both are based in **Washington**. They still exist today, even though the system of fixed rates ended long ago.

In 1960 the economist **Robert Triffin** recognised a problem: the world needed more and more dollars, but the more dollars there were abroad, the less believable the gold promise became. This is called the **Triffin dilemma**. On 15 August 1971 President **Richard Nixon** suspended the conversion into gold. After the short-lived **Smithsonian Agreement**, the important countries gave up fixed rates in 1973. The **franc** too was allowed to float in January 1973.

gewusst: Switzerland only joined the IMF and the World Bank after a popular vote on 17 May 1992.
In the IMF, Switzerland leads its own voting group together with several other countries.

teile.einleitung: **BRICS** is a group of large emerging economies. The name is made up of the first letters of the first members: **Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa**. The group has since grown and represents almost half the world's population.
wichtigste: BRICS stands for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.
The economist Jim O'Neill coined the term BRIC in 2001.
The first summit took place in Yekaterinburg in Russia in 2009.
South Africa joined in 2010, and BRIC became BRICS.
At the beginning of 2024 and 2025 more countries joined, such as Egypt and Indonesia.
The group founded the New Development Bank, based in Shanghai.

abschnitte.text: The name is formed from the first letters. **B** stands for Brazil, **R** for Russia, **I** for India and **C** for China. The **S** at the end stands for South Africa. India and China together have almost three billion inhabitants.

In 2001 the British economist **Jim O'Neill** of the investment bank **Goldman Sachs** grouped Brazil, Russia, India and China under the abbreviation **BRIC**. He wanted to draw attention to fast-growing economies. Only later did the countries turn it into a political group. The first summit took place in June **2009** in **Yekaterinburg** in Russia. In 2010 South Africa joined.

At the beginning of **2024** the group was enlarged, among others with **Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran** and the **United Arab Emirates**. Argentina was also invited but decided not to join. In January **2025** **Indonesia**, the most populous country in South-East Asia, became a full member. Together the members account for almost half the world's population (as of 2025).

The BRICS states jointly founded the **New Development Bank**. It is based in **Shanghai** in China. The bank finances, for example, roads, power stations and other infrastructure. Many members want it to make them more independent of organisations in which Western states have a lot of influence.

gewusst: The term BRIC was invented by a bank economist long before the countries met.
With South Africa, a country from Africa joined the group for the first time in 2010.

teile.einleitung: Dag Hammarskjöld was a Swedish diplomat and, from 1953 to 1961, the second Secretary-General of the United Nations. He worked with great dedication for peace and died in a plane crash in Africa in 1961.
wichtigste: Hammarskjöld was born in Jönköping in Sweden in 1905.
In 1953 he followed Trygve Lie as the second UN Secretary-General.
During the Suez Crisis of 1956, the first armed UN peacekeeping force was created under him.
In September 1961 he died when his plane crashed near Ndola in what is now Zambia.
After his death he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1961.
His book “Markings” was published in 1963.

abschnitte.text: Dag Hammarskjöld was born in **Jönköping** in Sweden in **1905**. His father **Hjalmar Hammarskjöld** was Prime Minister of Sweden. Dag studied economics and law and later worked for the Swedish government. He was regarded as very well educated, hard-working and reserved.

In April **1953** Hammarskjöld became **Secretary-General of the UN**. He was the second, after the Norwegian **Trygve Lie**. At 47 he is still the youngest Secretary-General to this day. He saw his office as that of a neutral mediator between states. In the years of the **Cold War** this was especially difficult.

abschnitte.titel: The Suez Crisis and the Congo
abschnitte.text: In the **Suez Crisis of 1956**, troops fought over the Suez Canal in Egypt. Hammarskjöld helped to set up a neutral **UN force** quickly. It then monitored the ceasefire. It was the UN's first armed **peacekeeping force**. Later he worked for peace during the **Congo Crisis**. On the way to negotiations, his plane crashed at night in September 1961 near **Ndola** in what is now Zambia. The exact cause has still not been fully explained.

In 1961, after his death, Hammarskjöld received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. Today the Nobel Committee no longer awards the prize to people who have died. In 1963 his book **“Markings”** was published, with diary notes about faith and duty. At UN headquarters in New York, in 1957 he helped design the quiet **Meditation Room**, where people of all religions can find peace. The **Dag Hammarskjöld Library** was opened shortly after his death.

gewusst: Hammarskjöld is one of only a few people to have received the Nobel Peace Prize after their death.
He spoke several languages fluently and translated poems in his free time.
The UN Meditation Room in New York is decorated with a simple block of iron ore.

teile.einleitung: A federal asylum centre is a federal accommodation for people who ask for asylum in Switzerland. They are housed there, and their application is examined.
wichtigste: The federal asylum centres are run by the federal government; the **SEM** is responsible.
Switzerland is divided into six asylum regions.
Each region has a centre with a procedural function; for eastern Switzerland it is in Altstätten.
Asylum seekers may stay in a federal asylum centre for at most 140 days.
If a case needs more investigation, the person is assigned to a canton.
The distribution among the cantons is based on the size of their population.

abschnitte.titel: What a federal asylum centre is
abschnitte.text: Anyone who applies for **asylum** in Switzerland first goes to a **federal asylum centre**. Asylum means protection for people who are persecuted in their home country. The centres are a matter for the **federal government**. The **State Secretariat for Migration** (SEM) runs them and works with partners for care and security. People live in the centres, and their application is examined.

Switzerland is divided into **six asylum regions**. Each region has a federal asylum centre **with a procedural function**, where applications are examined. For eastern Switzerland this centre is in **Altstätten** in the St Gallen Rhine Valley. There are also other centres where people only live. For people who seriously disturb security or the running of a centre, there is a **special centre** with stricter rules.

The asylum procedure is meant to be **fast** and fair. Most cases are decided directly in the centre. The asylum seekers receive free **legal representation**. The law allows a stay of at most **140 days** in a federal asylum centre. If a case needs more investigation, it goes into the **extended procedure**. Then the person is assigned to a canton and lives there until the decision is made.

Asylum seekers are basically distributed among the cantons according to their **population**. Large cantons such as Zurich therefore take in more people than small ones. Children in the asylum procedure also have a right to **basic schooling**. This is often provided directly in the centres. In this way the children do not miss too much school.

gewusst: The accelerated asylum procedure with federal asylum centres has applied since 2019.
Asylum is often a subject of political debate in Switzerland, and opinions on it differ.

teile.einleitung: **Doctors Without Borders** is an international aid organisation. It helps people who are in need because of war, disease or disasters. Its important international office is in Geneva.
wichtigste: Doctors Without Borders helps sick and injured people in need.
The organisation was founded in France in 1971.
In French it is called “Médecins Sans Frontières”, MSF for short.
In 1999 it received the Nobel Peace Prize.
The international office is in Geneva.
Most of its money comes from private donations.

abschnitte.text: **Doctors Without Borders** was founded in **France** in 1971. Its founders included doctors who had previously helped during the war in **Biafra** in Nigeria, and journalists. One of them was **Bernard Kouchner**, who was later French Foreign Minister from 2007 to 2010. The founders wanted to help quickly and to be free to say openly what they saw in crisis areas.

The helpers **treat the sick and injured**, for example after earthquakes, in war zones or during epidemics. They set up hospitals and clinics, vaccinate people and provide clean water. Besides doctors, nurses, technicians and many other experts also work with them. Doctors Without Borders helps **all people in need**. Origin, religion or opinion make no difference.

In 1999 Doctors Without Borders received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. With it the Nobel Committee honoured the organisation's pioneering humanitarian work on several continents. At that time it was already active in more than 80 countries. The prize made its work even better known all over the world.

The **international office** of Doctors Without Borders is in **Geneva**. The Swiss section is also based there. Geneva is an important place for humanitarian aid; the International Committee of the Red Cross and many UN organisations are there too. Many people from Switzerland work for the organisation or support it with donations.

Most of the money comes from **private donations**. In this way the organisation stays **independent** of governments and can decide for itself where it helps. The logo shows a running figure in **red**. You can see it, for example, on the helpers' cars, tents and vests.

gewusst: The abbreviation MSF comes from the French name “Médecins Sans Frontières”.
Today Doctors Without Borders helps in many dozens of countries all over the world.

teile.einleitung: An oath of office is a solemn promise. Anyone who takes up an important office promises with it to carry out their duties well and to respect the constitution. Oaths of office exist in many countries, for example in the USA and in Switzerland.
wichtigste: An oath of office is a solemn promise made at the start of an office.
A new US President takes the oath on 20 January, usually in front of the Capitol.
The oath is normally administered by the Chief Justice of the United States.
Many US Presidents place their hand on a Bible when doing so, but this is not required.
In Switzerland you can make a solemn affirmation instead of an oath.
When swearing in Switzerland, you raise three fingers of your right hand.

abschnitte.titel: What an oath of office is
abschnitte.text: An **oath of office** is a **solemn promise**. Anyone who takes on an important office, for example as president, minister or judge, promises with it to carry out their duties well. It is usually about respecting the **constitution** and serving the country. The oath is taken in public and in a formal ceremony. It is meant to show that the person takes their office seriously.

A new **US President** takes the oath of office on **20 January** after the election. That is the day the term of office begins. The ceremony usually takes place outdoors in front of the **Capitol** in Washington. In 2025 it was so cold that it was held indoors in the Capitol. The **Chief Justice** of the Supreme Court says the oath first, and the President repeats it. Many Presidents place their left hand on a **Bible** while doing so, but this is not required.

Sometimes an oath of office has to be taken very quickly. In November 1963 President **John F. Kennedy** was assassinated in **Dallas**. Shortly afterwards, Vice-President **Lyndon B. Johnson** took the oath of office on board the **presidential aircraft**. In this way the USA immediately had a president again. The photo of this moment is very well known.

In Switzerland, too, elected people take an oath, for example new **Federal Councillors** before the United Federal Assembly. They may choose: with the **oath**, God is called upon; with the **solemn affirmation**, he is not. In this way everyone can decide according to their own beliefs. Members of the National Council and the Council of States and of many cantonal parliaments also take the oath or make the affirmation.

When swearing in Switzerland, you raise your **right hand** with the **thumb**, **index finger** and **middle finger**. That is **three fingers**. This gesture is also familiar from the **Rütli Oath**, as it is shown in many pictures. In the Federal Assembly the words of the oath are “I swear it”, and for the affirmation “I solemnly promise it”.

gewusst: The US President's oath of office is written word for word in the Constitution and is only one sentence long.
In 1789 in New York, George Washington was the first US President to take the oath of office.

teile.einleitung: The **asylum procedure** sets out how an asylum application is examined and decided. In Switzerland it was greatly speeded up in 2019. European rules such as the **Dublin Agreement** also play an important role.
wichtigste: Since 1 March 2019 the accelerated asylum procedure has applied in Switzerland.
Since then asylum seekers have received free advice and legal representation.
During the procedure they receive permit N.
Provisionally admitted persons receive permit F.
Since December 2008 Switzerland has applied the Dublin Agreement.
Appeals are decided by the Federal Administrative Court in St Gallen.

abschnitte.text: On **1 March 2019** a new asylum procedure came into force in Switzerland. Since then most decisions are meant to be made within a few months. The procedures take place in **federal asylum centres**, where everyone involved works under one roof. Because everything happens faster, asylum seekers receive **free** advice and **legal representation**. In this way the procedures are still meant to be fair.

Anyone who has made an asylum application receives **permit N**. It only applies while the procedure is under way. Anyone who is not granted asylum but cannot be sent back, for example because of war, is provisionally admitted and receives **permit F**. Recognised refugees usually receive a residence permit.

The **Dublin Agreement** sets out which European state is responsible for an asylum application. Usually it is the state that a person entered first. Switzerland has taken part since **December 2008**, even though it does not belong to the EU. Fingerprints are stored in the **Eurodac** database. In this way you can see whether someone has already made an application in another Dublin state.

The SEM can grant asylum, reject the application or order provisional admission. There is also a **decision not to consider the application**. In that case the authorities do not examine the reasons for fleeing at all, for example because another Dublin state is responsible. The person is then transferred to that state.

You can lodge an **appeal** against a negative decision. The **Federal Administrative Court** in **St Gallen** is responsible. In asylum matters it usually has the final say. Going on to the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne is generally not possible here.

gewusst: A permit N is not a right of residence; it only confirms that an application is under way.
Switzerland joined Schengen and Dublin on the same day in December 2008.

teile.einleitung: Some people are persecuted in their home country and have to flee. In another country they can ask for **asylum**, that is, for protection. Switzerland also grants people asylum when they are really in danger.
wichtigste: Asylum means protection in another country.
Someone who asks for asylum is called an asylum seeker.
In Switzerland the State Secretariat for Migration, SEM for short, decides.
Newly arrived asylum seekers first live in a federal asylum centre.
Anyone granted asylum is a recognised refugee.
Anyone who is not granted asylum but cannot safely return is provisionally admitted.

abschnitte.text: The word **asylum** means protection. Anyone persecuted in their own country, for example because of their opinions, religion or origin, can ask for protection in another country. As long as no decision has been made, the person is called an **asylum seeker**. The **Geneva Refugee Convention** of 1951 is important for protecting refugees. Switzerland has signed it too.

Anyone who applies for asylum in Switzerland first goes to a **federal asylum centre**. The people live there, and their application is examined there. The **State Secretariat for Migration**, **SEM** for short, is responsible. It belongs to the federal government and decides on every application.

An important part is the **interview**. The asylum seekers tell **why they fled** and what has happened to them. Often an interpreter helps. From the answers, the SEM checks whether the person really needs protection.

Anyone who is persecuted and granted asylum is a **recognised refugee** and may stay in Switzerland. Some people are not granted asylum but cannot go back because it is too dangerous there, for example because of war. They are **provisionally admitted**. Anyone who receives neither asylum nor protection must leave Switzerland again.

Those who may stay are later assigned to a **canton** and a **municipality**. Language is very important for settling in well. That is why many asylum seekers in German-speaking Switzerland attend **German courses**. Children go to school and often learn the language especially quickly there.

gewusst: The most important agreement for protecting refugees was adopted in Geneva in 1951.
The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, has its headquarters in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: The Dublin association is an agreement between Switzerland and the European Union. Through it, Switzerland takes part in the Dublin system even though it is not an EU member. The system decides which country examines an asylum application.
wichtigste: The Dublin system decides which country is responsible for an asylum application.
Each application should be examined in only one country.
Besides Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein also take part without being EU members.
Responsibility follows an order of priority: family members come before the place of first entry.
With the sovereignty clause, a country can choose to examine an application itself.
For a long time the basis was the Dublin III Regulation of 2013.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is not a member of the EU. Through a special agreement, however, it is connected to the **Dublin system**; this is called being **associated**. Swiss voters approved the agreements on **Schengen and Dublin** in 2005. Besides Switzerland, **Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein** also take part without being EU members. All four are also associated with Schengen. Switzerland adopts new EU rules on Dublin as **developments** of the agreement.

The Dublin system lays down **which country examines an asylum application**. This is meant to stop asylum seekers from making applications in several countries one after another. The criteria follow a fixed **order of priority**. First comes **family unity**: if family members already live in a Dublin country, that country is often responsible, especially for unaccompanied minors. Only further down the list comes the country the person **entered first**.

If another Dublin country is responsible, there is a **Dublin transfer**: the person is taken to that country, where the content of the application is examined. However, a country can also **choose to examine an application itself**, even though another country would be responsible. This is called the **sovereignty clause**. It is used for humanitarian reasons, for example for people who are seriously ill.

For a long time the basis was the **Dublin III Regulation** of 2013. It replaced the Dublin II Regulation of 2003. Switzerland adopted it as a development of the so-called Dublin acquis. In 2024 the EU agreed a major reform of its asylum system, which rewrites the Dublin rules. In Switzerland, the Dublin cooperation is debated again and again in politics, with different opinions about its advantages and disadvantages.

gewusst: For Dublin, the countries compare asylum seekers' fingerprints in a shared database called Eurodac.
Liechtenstein is the smallest country that takes part in the Dublin system.

teile.einleitung: A double taxation agreement is a treaty between two countries about taxes. It prevents people or companies from having to pay tax on their income in two countries at the same time. Switzerland has concluded such agreements with a great many states.
wichtigste: Double taxation agreements prevent income from having to be taxed in two countries at the same time.
They are often abbreviated to DTA.
Switzerland has concluded such agreements with more than 100 states.
They set out which country may levy which taxes.
They are especially important for cross-border commuters and companies working internationally.
Many agreements are based on a model agreement of the OECD.

abschnitte.text: Every country levies its own **taxes** on income and wealth. If someone lives in one country and works in another, both countries could demand taxes. This is called **double taxation**. Without rules, you would then have to pay twice for the same money, which would be very unfair.

A **double taxation agreement** sets out which country is responsible for which income. Often the country where someone works may tax it, or the country where someone lives. Sometimes both countries may levy a part, and the country of residence credits the tax already paid. Many agreements follow the **OECD Model Convention**, so that the rules are similar internationally.

Every day many people travel from France, Italy, Germany or Austria to work in Switzerland. They are called **cross-border commuters**. For them, the agreements set out exactly where they pay tax on their wages. With Italy, for example, Switzerland concluded a new cross-border commuter agreement that has applied since 2024.

Companies that are active in several countries also benefit from the agreements. On interest and **dividends**, Switzerland deducts a withholding tax of 35 per cent. Anyone living abroad can often reclaim part of it thanks to a DTA. In this way the tax burden is shared fairly between the countries.

Modern agreements also set out how tax authorities exchange information. This makes it harder to hide money from the state. Switzerland has greatly changed its rules on this since about 2009 and today takes part in the automatic exchange of information on bank accounts. The aim is that nobody pays tax twice, but also that nobody pays no tax at all.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money you have to pay to the state so that it can pay for schools, roads and much more.
A treaty between two or more states.
A person who lives in one country and regularly works in a neighbouring country.
A part of a company's profit that the shareholders receive.

gewusst: The double taxation agreement between Switzerland and Germany dates back to 1971 and has been amended several times since then.
In Switzerland a double taxation agreement must be approved by Parliament before it applies.

teile.einleitung: The German Bundestag is the parliament of Germany. Its members are elected by the people. It makes laws, passes the state budget and elects the Federal Chancellor.
wichtigste: The Bundestag is Germany's parliament elected by the people.
It is normally elected every four years.
In the 2025 election, 630 members were elected.
Until 1999 it met in Bonn; since then it has met in the Reichstag building in Berlin.
Members of the same party form a parliamentary group.
A large federal eagle hangs in the plenary chamber.

abschnitte.text: **Voters** in Germany aged 18 and over decide who sits in the Bundestag. A **legislative period** normally lasts **four years**. A new electoral law has fixed the number of seats at **630**. Exactly that many members were elected in the 2025 election. Before that, the Bundestag was often even larger because of special rules.

From **1949 to 1999** the Bundestag met in **Bonn** on the Rhine. After German reunification in 1990, **Berlin** became the capital again. In 1999 the Bundestag moved into the converted **Reichstag building**. On the roof is a large **glass dome**, which visitors can enter.

The large chamber where the sittings are held is called the **plenary chamber**. On the wall hangs the **federal eagle**, Germany's heraldic animal. Because of its round shape, some people jokingly call it the “fat hen”. Members of the same party join together in a **parliamentary group** and sit next to each other. The sittings are chaired by the President of the Bundestag.

The Bundestag passes **laws** and the **budget**, that is, what the state spends money on. It elects the **Federal Chancellor**, the head of the government. It also keeps a check on the government, for example with questions and inquiries. In many laws the German **Bundesrat**, in which the federal states are represented, is also involved.

In Switzerland, parliament consists of two chambers: the **National Council** and the **Council of States**, together the Federal Assembly. Be careful not to mix things up: in Switzerland the **Federal Council** (in German “Bundesrat”) is the government, with seven members. In Germany, on the other hand, the Bundesrat represents the federal states. Switzerland has no Federal Chancellor like Germany's.

gewusst: The glass dome on the Reichstag building is meant to show that politics should be open and transparent.
The Bundestag is one of the largest freely elected parliaments in the world.

teile.einleitung: Charles III has been King of the United Kingdom since 8 September 2022. He became king when his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, died. Before that he had been heir to the throne for longer than anyone before him.
wichtigste: Charles was born in London on 14 November 1948.
He is the eldest son of Queen Elizabeth II.
He has been king since 2022 and was crowned on 6 May 2023.
Before coming to the throne he held the title “Prince of Wales” for more than 60 years.
His wife is Queen Camilla, and he has two sons.
He is also King of Canada, Australia, New Zealand and other countries.
For many years he has worked for nature and the environment.

abschnitte.text: Charles was born in London in 1948. Even as a small child it was clear that he would one day be king. In 1958 he was given the title **Prince of Wales**, the traditional title of the heir to the throne. He held this title longer than anyone before him. On **8 September 2022** his mother died, and Charles became **king** at the age of 73. The formal **coronation** took place on 6 May 2023 in Westminster Abbey in London.

From his first marriage to Diana, Charles has two sons: **William** and **Harry**. William is the elder and therefore the next **heir to the throne**. Today he holds the title Prince of Wales. In 2005 Charles married **Camilla**. Since he became king, she has been called Queen Camilla.

Charles studied at Cambridge University. After that he served in the British navy, the **Royal Navy**, from 1971 to 1976. He learned to fly aeroplanes and helicopters. Finally he commanded a **minehunter**, that is, a ship that searches for sea mines.

Charles loves gardens and has been interested in the **environment and climate** for decades. He has spoken out for organic farming and protecting nature, long before many others did. Through foundations he also supports young people who are looking for training or work.

The British king does not govern himself. Politics is made by the government and Parliament. The king mainly has **ceremonial duties**: he receives guests, opens Parliament and signs laws. He is also **Supreme Governor of the Church of England**, which is led spiritually by the Archbishop of Canterbury. Charles is also king in several **Commonwealth** countries, for example Canada and Australia.

gewusst: No British heir to the throne has waited as long for the throne as Charles.
When he came to the throne, Charles was older than any British king or queen before him.
New British coins and banknotes now show the portrait of Charles III.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but it voluntarily adapts many of its own laws to EU law. This is called **autonomous adoption**. In this way Switzerland wants to avoid obstacles in trade with its most important partner.
wichtigste: In autonomous adoption, Switzerland voluntarily adapts its law to EU law.
No treaty obliges it to do so.
After the no to the EEA in 1992, the Swisslex programme followed in 1993.
Since 1 July 2010 the Cassis de Dijon principle has applied in Switzerland.
It is set out in the Federal Act on Technical Barriers to Trade.
In dynamic adoption of law, on the other hand, the adaptation is agreed by treaty.

abschnitte.text: In **autonomous adoption**, Switzerland takes EU rules into its own law even though no treaty forces it to. “Autonomous” here means by its own decision. The laws go through the normal Swiss procedures, that is, Parliament and, if necessary, a popular vote. In every case Switzerland decides for itself whether and how it adopts a rule.

The **EU** is Switzerland's most important trading partner. If different regulations apply in the two areas, products have to be tested twice. That costs time and money. Such obstacles are called **technical barriers to trade**. The same rules make exporting easier for Swiss companies.

abschnitte.titel: Swisslex after the no to the EEA
abschnitte.text: On 6 December 1992 the people rejected joining the **European Economic Area**. But many changes to the law had already been prepared for the EEA. With the **Swisslex** programme, the Federal Council made many laws EU-compatible anyway in 1993. Swisslex is regarded as an early example of autonomous adoption.

On **1 July 2010** Switzerland introduced the **Cassis de Dijon principle** on its own. Products that are lawfully sold in the EU or the EEA may in principle also be sold in Switzerland. This is meant to lower prices. The principle is set out in the **Federal Act on Technical Barriers to Trade**, TBTA for short. The name comes from a French blackcurrant liqueur that was the subject of a case at the European Court of Justice in 1979.

Critics point out that Switzerland adopts rules that it had **no say** in drawing up in the EU. Supporters stress that Switzerland can decide freely and keeps its democratic procedures. This must be distinguished from **dynamic adoption of law**. In that case Switzerland commits itself in an agreement to adopt new EU law in certain areas.

gewusst: The Cassis de Dijon principle is named after a liqueur made from blackcurrants.
Switzerland introduced the principle on its own; the EU does not grant it the same in return.

teile.einleitung: Amnesty International is a worldwide organisation that works for respect for human rights. It reveals where people are persecuted, tortured or unjustly imprisoned. Its symbol is a candle surrounded by barbed wire.
wichtigste: Amnesty International works worldwide for respect for human rights.
The organisation was founded in London in 1961 by the lawyer Peter Benenson.
It is independent of governments, parties and religions.
In 1977 Amnesty International received the Nobel Peace Prize.
One well-known method is writing letters to governments to help prisoners.
In Switzerland there is a separate section based in Bern.

abschnitte.text: **Amnesty International** is a **non-governmental organisation**, that is, an organisation not run by the state. The word amnesty means pardon or remission of punishment. The organisation is financed mainly by donations and membership fees. It does not accept money from governments so that it stays independent.

In 1961 the British lawyer **Peter Benenson** read about two students in Portugal who had been imprisoned for drinking a toast to freedom. He then wrote a newspaper article about forgotten prisoners. In it he called on people to stand up for them. This appeal quickly grew into a worldwide movement.

Amnesty sends experts to countries to investigate human rights violations and publishes reports. Members write letters and petitions to governments to get prisoners released. Every year around 10 December a large **Write for Rights** letter-writing marathon takes place. Often public attention alone helps people to be treated better.

Amnesty works for **prisoners of conscience**, that is, people who are imprisoned only because of their opinions or religion. The organisation fights against torture and against the death penalty in all cases. It also works for refugees, for women's rights and for fair trials. In doing so it examines governments in every country, including democratic states.

The Swiss section was founded in 1970 and is based in Bern. It looks after worldwide campaigns but also human rights in Switzerland. These include, for example, questions about the asylum system or police work. Many school classes take part in the letter-writing marathon and write letters for persecuted people.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organisation that does not belong to the state, often called an NGO.
A person who is in prison only because of their opinions, religion or origin.
When someone is deliberately caused great pain, for example to force a confession.
A punishment in which a state has a person killed.

gewusst: Amnesty International has several million members and supporters worldwide.
The candle in the logo recalls a proverb: it is better to light a candle than to curse the darkness.

teile.einleitung: In diplomacy, accreditation means that a state officially admits a diplomat. Only then may an ambassador, for example, work in the host country. Many fixed rules and special technical terms are part of it.
wichtigste: Before an ambassador is appointed, the host country's consent, the agrément, is needed.
A consul needs the host country's permission for his work, the exequatur.
With the letter of recall, a state calls its ambassador back.
An ambassador can be accredited to several states at the same time.
If there is no ambassador, a chargé d'affaires runs the embassy.
All the diplomats accredited in a country form the diplomatic corps.
The Pope's representative is called the Apostolic Nuncio.

abschnitte.titel: The road to becoming an ambassador
abschnitte.text: Before a state sends an **ambassador**, it asks the host country whether the person is welcome. This consent is called the **agrément**. The host country can refuse it without giving a reason. Once the agrément has been granted, the ambassador travels there. He hands his **letter of credence** to the head of state of the host country. Only then is he officially **accredited**. In Switzerland the **President of the Confederation** receives the new ambassadors.

Besides the ambassador, other diplomats work at an embassy. **Attachés** are experts in a particular field, for example military affairs, culture, science or the economy. If there is no ambassador in office at the time, a **chargé d'affaires** runs the mission. He is called chargé d'affaires ad interim, that is, temporary. A **consul** deals mainly with his own country's citizens abroad. He needs the host country's permission, the **exequatur**. The Latin word means “let him carry out”.

Many states do not have their own embassy in every country. An ambassador can therefore also be responsible for neighbouring countries from one capital. This is called **multiple accreditation**. At the end of the term of office, the sending state calls its ambassador back with a **letter of recall**. Often the successor hands over this letter together with his own papers. The most important rules are in the **Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations** of 1961.

All the diplomats accredited in a state together form the **diplomatic corps**. At official events, for example the New Year reception, it often appears together. The **Holy See**, that is, the leadership of the Catholic Church, also has diplomatic relations with many states. Its ambassador has the title **Apostolic Nuncio**. In **Bern** there is a **nunciature**, the Pope's embassy.

The word accreditation is not only used in diplomacy. **Journalists** also often need accreditation. With it they may, for example, report from parliament, from a summit or from large sporting events. In the **Federal Palace** in Bern there are accredited journalists who report regularly from Parliament.

gewusst: A host country can declare a diplomat “persona non grata”, that is, an unwelcome person, at any time and does not have to give a reason.
There are many foreign embassies in Bern, because that is where the Swiss government is based.

teile.einleitung: **Banking secrecy** forbids banks to pass on information about their customers to others. In Switzerland it was long a hallmark of the financial centre. Since 2009, however, it has changed a great deal under international pressure.
wichtigste: Banking secrecy protects bank customers' data.
Since 1934 breaching it has been a criminal offence under the Banking Act.
In 2009, under pressure from the USA, UBS handed over customer data.
The US law FATCA requires accounts of US persons to be reported.
Since 2017 Swiss banks have collected data for the automatic exchange of information.
Towards the Swiss tax authorities, banking secrecy largely still applies for people living in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Banking secrecy protects **financial privacy**. A bank may not reveal who has an account with it or how much money is in it. The duty of confidentiality had existed for a long time. In **1934** breaching it became a criminal offence under the **Banking Act**. Anyone who breaches banking secrecy can be punished with a fine or a prison sentence.

The big bank **UBS** had helped US customers hide money from the tax authorities. The USA therefore put great pressure on it. In **2009** customer data were handed over to the US authorities. This shook banking secrecy badly. In the same year Switzerland was briefly on a “grey list” of the **OECD**.

The USA passed the law **FATCA**, the “Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act”. Swiss banks too must report accounts of US persons to the US tax authorities. The **OECD**, based in Paris, also drew up a standard for the **automatic exchange of information**. Since 2017 Swiss banks have collected data for it, and in 2018 they were exchanged for the first time. In this way other countries find out about their citizens' accounts in Switzerland.

For people **living in Switzerland**, banking secrecy largely still applies towards the **Swiss tax authorities**. As a rule they cannot ask the bank directly for account data. In **criminal proceedings**, however, banks must provide information. So banking secrecy does not protect against the police or the courts.

gewusst: Banking secrecy does not apply in criminal proceedings; then banks must provide information.
In 2009 Switzerland was briefly on an OECD “grey list”.

teile.einleitung: In the European elections, people in the countries of the European Union elect the members of the European Parliament. The elections take place every five years, most recently in June 2024.
wichtigste: The European elections take place every five years.
A country has at most 96 and at least 6 seats.
Small countries have more seats per inhabitant than large ones.
All countries vote using a system of proportional representation.
In 2024 turnout across the EU was about 51 per cent.
In 2024 the European People's Party became the largest group.

abschnitte.text: The **European Parliament** is the elected representation of the EU's people. Together with the Council it passes laws and the budget. Since 1979 it has been elected directly by the citizens. The **parliamentary term** lasts five years. The latest election took place in June 2024. Switzerland is not in the EU and so does not take part.

abschnitte.titel: How the seats are shared out
abschnitte.text: Large countries have more seats than small ones, but not exactly in proportion to their population. This is called **degressive proportionality**. A member from Malta represents far fewer people than one from Germany. This way small countries are also well represented. Every country has **at least 6** seats, for example Malta, Luxembourg and Cyprus. The **maximum** is 96, which is how many Germany has.

All countries must use a system of **proportional representation**. Under it, parties get roughly as many seats as their share of the votes. But each country decides many details itself, for example the **voting age**. Germany lowered it from 18 to 16 for the 2024 European elections.

In the 2024 European elections, **turnout** across the EU was about 51 per cent, similar to 2019. The strongest force was the Christian Democratic **European People's Party** (EPP), ahead of the Social Democrats. In Parliament, members of similar parties from different countries join together in **political groups**.

gewusst: A seat from Malta stands for far fewer people than a seat from Germany.
In 2024, 16-year-olds in Germany were allowed to vote in the European elections for the first time.

teile.einleitung: On 1 January 2002, many people in Europe got new money in their hands: euro banknotes and euro coins. It was one of the biggest currency changeovers in history.
wichtigste: Since 1 January 1999 the euro had already existed as book money.
On 1 January 2002 twelve countries introduced euro cash.
One euro was fixed at 1.95583 German marks.
The banknotes show invented windows, gateways and bridges.
The 500-euro note has not been newly issued since 2019.
The euro sign is inspired by the Greek letter epsilon.

abschnitte.text: On 1 January 1999 the **exchange rates** of the old currencies to the euro were fixed irrevocably. From then on the euro existed as **book money**, meaning for transfers, accounts and on the financial markets. But there was no cash yet. In shops people went on paying with German marks, francs or lira.

On **1 January 2002** euro cash came into circulation. In 2001 **Greece** had joined the eleven founding states of the monetary union. So twelve countries issued the new money. Fixed rates applied for converting. For example, one euro was worth **1.95583 German marks**. In everyday life many people roughly worked with a factor of 2.

abschnitte.titel: What you can see on the money
abschnitte.text: The banknotes show **windows, gateways and bridges** in different architectural styles. They were deliberately invented, so that no country would be favoured. Windows and gateways stand for openness, bridges for connection. According to the EU Commission, the **euro sign** is inspired by the Greek letter **epsilon**. The two horizontal lines are meant to show stability. The largest note, 500 euros, has not been newly issued since 2019, but it is still valid.

abschnitte.titel: The euro outside the EU too
abschnitte.text: Some microstates use the euro on the basis of agreements with the EU, namely **Monaco**, **San Marino**, the **Vatican** and **Andorra**. Liechtenstein, on the other hand, pays with the **Swiss franc**. Switzerland has not introduced the euro either, but many shops near the border accept it.

gewusst: For three years the euro existed only in bank accounts, not in purses and wallets.
The buildings on the euro banknotes do not actually exist.

teile.einleitung: The European anthem is the melody “Ode to Joy” by Ludwig van Beethoven. It is played at celebrations of the Council of Europe and the European Union and stands for a united Europe.
wichtigste: The European anthem is called “Ode to Joy”.
The melody is by Ludwig van Beethoven.
It is the last part of his 9th Symphony.
The poem “Ode to Joy” was written by Friedrich Schiller.
The official anthem has no words, only the melody.
The Council of Europe chose it in 1972, and the EU adopted it in 1985.

abschnitte.text: **Ludwig van Beethoven** was a famous composer. He was born in Bonn and later lived in Vienna. His **9th Symphony** was performed for the first time in Vienna in 1824. In the last part, a choir and soloists sing the “Ode to Joy”. This melody is the European anthem today.

When Beethoven wrote the 9th Symphony, he was **almost deaf**. So he could hardly hear any more. Even so, he wrote this famous music. He heard the notes in his head and wrote them down. This shows how well he knew music.

The text that Beethoven set to music comes from the poem **“An die Freude”** (“Ode to Joy”) by **Friedrich Schiller**. Setting to music means writing music for a text. The poem is about **joy** and about all people being brothers. It expresses friendship and togetherness.

In 1972 the **Council of Europe** chose the melody as its anthem. In 1985 the **European Union** adopted it too. The official European anthem has **no words**. Europe has many languages, and everyone understands a melody without words. The anthem does not replace the countries' national anthems; it stands alongside them.

gewusst: Beethoven composed the melody of the European anthem when he could hardly hear anything any more.
The European anthem is an anthem with no official words.

teile.einleitung: In a direct democracy, citizens not only decide who represents them in parliament but also vote themselves on specific issues. Switzerland is the best-known example of this in the whole world. Several times a year the people here decide on new laws and changes to the constitution.
wichtigste: In Switzerland citizens can vote directly on laws and the constitution.
With a popular initiative, 100,000 signatures collected within 18 months can demand a change to the Federal Constitution.
Against a federal law, an optional referendum can be called with 50,000 signatures within 100 days.
Changes to the constitution need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
The Landsgemeinde now exists only in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden (as of 2026).
In 2007 Glarus was the first canton to introduce the right to vote and stand for election from the age of 16.
Direct democracy is an important difference between Switzerland and the EU.

abschnitte.text: In a **direct democracy** the people have the last word on specific issues. In a purely **representative democracy**, by contrast, people only elect representatives, who then decide for them. Switzerland combines both: the people elect parliament and may also vote on many proposals. That is why it is also called a semi-direct democracy.

With a **popular initiative**, citizens can put forward an idea themselves. To do this they must collect 100,000 valid signatures from people entitled to vote within 18 months. Parliament then discusses the initiative and makes a recommendation, often with a counter-proposal. In the end the people and the cantons decide at the ballot box.

The **optional referendum** is about laws that parliament has already passed. Anyone who is against one needs 50,000 signatures within 100 days; eight cantons can also call for a referendum. The law then goes to the people, and the majority of those voting decides. For changes to the Federal Constitution there is always a vote; this is called a **mandatory referendum**.

abschnitte.titel: Majority of the people and of the cantons
abschnitte.text: A change to the constitution needs two majorities. The **majority of the people** means that more than half of all those voting say yes. The **majority of the cantons** means that yes also wins in most of the cantons. The six former half-cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each count as half a cantonal vote. In this way small cantons have more weight than their population would suggest.

The **Landsgemeinde** is the oldest form of direct democracy in Switzerland. Those entitled to vote gather in the open air in a square and vote by raising their hands. Today it exists at cantonal level only in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden. At the Glarus Landsgemeinde in 2007 it was decided that young people aged 16 and over may vote and elect in the canton.

Other countries also hold popular votes, but usually much less often than Switzerland. In some states of the USA, citizens can vote on initiatives. There is also the **recall**, with which elected officials can be voted out before the end of their term. In the European Union there is the European Citizens' Initiative, but it is only a request to the EU Commission and does not lead to a vote.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to take part in votes and elections. In Switzerland you have it at federal level from the age of 18.
A proposal from the people to change the constitution. It needs 100,000 signatures.
A popular vote on a law or a change to the constitution that parliament has passed.
The majority of the cantons in a vote.
A container into which you put your ballot paper. Today most people in Switzerland vote by post.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are usually four voting Sundays a year, on which several proposals are often decided.
Women only received the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971; Appenzell Innerrhoden had to introduce it in 1990 on the orders of the Federal Supreme Court.
At the Landsgemeinde in Appenzell Innerrhoden, many men traditionally carry a sword or a bayonet as a sign of their right to vote.

teile.einleitung: **India** has risen in recent decades to become one of the most important powers in the world. It has the most inhabitants, a fast-growing economy and a successful space programme. In foreign policy, India likes to go its own way.
wichtigste: India became independent in 1947.
From 1991 India opened up its economy step by step.
According to UN estimates, India overtook China in 2023 as the country with the largest population.
In 2022 India became the fifth-largest economy in the world.
In August 2023 Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole.
In March 2024 the EFTA states signed a trade agreement with India.

abschnitte.text: After independence from Great Britain in 1947, India did not want to submit to any bloc. In 1961 Prime Minister **Jawaharlal Nehru** was one of the founders of the **Non-Aligned Movement**. These countries wanted to belong neither to the West nor to the Eastern bloc in the Cold War. Today's policy of “strategic autonomy” builds on this tradition.

In 1991 India fell into a serious **balance of payments crisis**. Under Finance Minister **Manmohan Singh**, the country then opened up its economy, lowered customs duties and cut regulations. This is regarded as the start of strong growth. In 2022 India overtook **Great Britain** in gross domestic product and became the fifth-largest economy in the world. Per head, however, India is still much poorer than most industrialised countries.

According to the UN, in spring 2023 India had more inhabitants than **China** for the first time, about 1.43 billion. China's population has been shrinking since 2022. Many people in India are young. This can help the economy, but it also needs a lot of schools and jobs.

In August 2023 the probe **Chandrayaan-3** was the first to land near the **Moon's south pole**. This made India the fourth country to achieve a soft landing on the Moon. In the same year India chaired the **G20**. At the summit in New Delhi, the **African Union** became a permanent member. India likes to present itself as the voice of the Global South.

There is a dispute with China over the border in the Himalayas. In June 2020 there were deadly clashes in the **Galwan Valley** in Ladakh. They were the first deaths on this border for decades. At the same time India is looking for new partners. In March 2024 the **EFTA states**, including Switzerland, signed a Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement with India. It came into force in October 2025.

gewusst: The agreement with EFTA set out the aim of EFTA companies investing 100 billion US dollars in India.
No firearms were used in the fighting in the Galwan Valley in 2020.

teile.einleitung: An ambassador represents their own country in another state. Ambassadors head the embassy, keep up relations with the government of the host country and protect the interests of their fellow citizens. Ambassadors are a country's highest diplomats abroad.
wichtigste: An ambassador represents their own country in another state.
He or she heads the embassy in the host country.
The host country must agree to the appointment; this is called the agrément.
On taking up office, the ambassador presents a letter of credence to the head of state.
Ambassadors enjoy diplomatic immunity.
In Switzerland ambassadors are appointed by the Federal Council.

abschnitte.text: The **ambassador** is the top representative of one country in another state. He speaks on behalf of his government with the government of the host country. He watches politics and the economy there and reports home. He also presents his country, for example through its culture, language and traditions.

Before a new ambassador arrives, his country asks the host country for its consent, the **agrément**. When he arrives, he presents a **letter of credence** to the head of state. In Switzerland this usually happens at a ceremony with the President of the Confederation in Bern. Only after that may he officially carry out his office.

The ambassador leads a team of diplomats and other staff. They deal with politics, the economy, culture and science. The **consular section** helps fellow citizens who, for example, need a new passport or are in difficulty. It also issues visas to people who want to travel to the country.

Ambassadors enjoy **diplomatic immunity** so that they can do their work without pressure. This means that they may not be arrested in the host country like ordinary citizens. Even so, they must respect the laws of the host country. These rules are in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961.

Switzerland has numerous embassies around the world, which belong to the Department of Foreign Affairs. The ambassadors are appointed by the **Federal Council**. They are often career diplomats who work in different countries for many years. Anyone in Switzerland who wants to become a diplomat must pass a demanding selection process and training.

begriffe.erklaerung: The host country's consent to a new ambassador.
A letter that confirms that someone is the official ambassador.
The country in which an ambassador works.
The part of the embassy that helps fellow citizens and issues visas.

gewusst: Ambassadors are traditionally addressed as Excellency.
The longest-serving ambassador in a country is called the doyen and speaks for all the diplomats there.

teile.einleitung: The Convention on Biological Diversity is a worldwide treaty for protecting nature. It was opened for signature in 1992 at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.
wichtigste: **Biodiversity** means the variety of life: species, habitats and genes.
The convention was signed in Rio in 1992 and came into force at the end of 1993.
It has three goals: to protect, to use sustainably and to share benefits fairly.
The Secretariat is in Montreal in Canada.
Almost all states take part; the USA has never joined.
The global biodiversity agreement of 2022 aims to protect 30 per cent each of land and sea areas by 2030.

abschnitte.text: **Biodiversity** means the variety of life. It includes all animal and plant species, but also the variety of **habitats** such as forests, moors and seas. The differences in **genes** within a species also count. The more varied nature is, the more resilient it is, for example against diseases or drought.

In 1992 many states met in **Rio de Janeiro** for the UN Conference on Environment and Development. The convention was opened for signature there. It came into force at the end of 1993. The **Secretariat** is in **Montreal** and organises the conferences of the parties. Almost all the states of the world take part. The **USA** did sign but never ratified the treaty.

The convention aims to **protect** diversity and to **use it sustainably**. The third goal is the **fair sharing of the benefits** from genetic resources. If, for example, a medicine is developed from a plant, the country of origin should also benefit. This is set out in more detail in the **Nagoya Protocol** of 2010, which came into force in 2014. The **Cartagena Protocol** of 2000 regulates the handling of genetically modified organisms.

In December 2022 the **Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework** was adopted. Its best-known goal is called **“30 by 30”**: by 2030, 30 per cent of land and sea areas are to be protected. Switzerland is a party to the convention. In September 2024 the people voted on the **biodiversity initiative**, which wanted more land and money for nature. About 63 per cent said no.

gewusst: 22 May is the International Day for Biological Diversity.
The UN climate convention was also opened for signature at the same Earth Summit in Rio.

teile.einleitung: The Bilaterals III is the name for the new package of agreements between Switzerland and the EU. Officially it is called the “Switzerland-EU package”. It is meant to develop the existing agreements further and to regulate new areas such as electricity and health.
wichtigste: Negotiations began in March 2024 and were concluded in substance on 20 December 2024.
The consultation ran from June to October 2025.
The agreements were signed on 2 March 2026.
On 13 March 2026 the Federal Council adopted its dispatch to Parliament.
New elements are an electricity agreement, a food safety agreement and a health agreement.
Disputes are to be settled by a joint arbitration tribunal.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland and the EU have long worked together through the Bilaterals I and II. With the new **Switzerland-EU package**, these agreements are to be secured and extended.
