This includes rules on how the agreements are adapted to new EU law. There are also **new agreements**. Negotiations began in March 2024 and were concluded in substance on 20 December 2024.

With the **electricity agreement**, Switzerland is to take part in the European internal electricity market. The **food safety agreement** creates a common area for safe food along the whole food chain. This includes taking part in the **European Food Safety Authority** (EFSA) in Parma. The **health agreement** is about cooperation on cross-border health threats, for example with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.

abschnitte.titel: Settling disputes and the safeguard clause
abschnitte.text: If there is a dispute, it is first negotiated in the **Joint Committee**. If no agreement is reached, a **joint arbitration tribunal** decides. Joint here means that both sides appoint the same number of members. A **safeguard clause** was also newly negotiated. It allows Switzerland to take measures if the free movement of persons causes serious economic or social problems.

The **consultation** ran from June to October 2025. During it, cantons, parties and associations could give their views. On 2 March 2026 the agreements were signed, and on 13 March 2026 the Federal Council adopted its **dispatch** to Parliament. Now the National Council and the Council of States are debating it. Supporters see secure relations with the most important trading partner; opponents fear too much influence from the EU. In the end the people are likely to have the last word.

gewusst: Before the new package, Switzerland had negotiated an institutional framework agreement, which the Federal Council broke off in 2021.
In Swiss politics, a dispatch is a report by the Federal Council that explains a proposal to Parliament.

teile.einleitung: Erasmus+ is the European Union's programme for education, youth and sport. It allows young people and teachers to learn or work abroad for a while.
wichtigste: Erasmus+ supports students, apprentices, teachers, youth work and sport.
From 2011 to 2013 Switzerland took full part in Erasmus.
From 2014 Switzerland counted as a third country again.
The replacement for students is the Swiss-European Mobility Programme.
The Swiss agency for exchange is called Movetia.
From 2027 Switzerland is to take full part again.

abschnitte.text: Erasmus+ is the large EU programme for **education, youth and sport**. It pays for stays abroad, for example a semester at another university. It is open not only to students but also to **apprentices** in vocational training, **teachers**, trainers and youth groups. Projects in sport are also supported.

From 2011 to 2013 Switzerland was **fully associated**. This means it took part like an EU country. In February 2014 Swiss voters approved the **mass immigration initiative**. After that, Switzerland did not sign the agreement on the free movement of persons with Croatia for the time being. The EU then stopped the negotiations on Erasmus+. Switzerland became a **third country** again, meaning a country that does not take full part.

So that exchanges are still possible, Switzerland pays for them itself. For students there is the **Swiss-European Mobility Programme**, SEMP for short. The agency **Movetia** is responsible. It supports exchange and mobility in schools, vocational training and universities.

As part of the new package with the EU, it was agreed that Switzerland will take full part in Erasmus+ again from **2027**. A new generation of the programme also begins then. Swiss universities and schools will then be able to take part directly in EU projects again.

gewusst: Erasmus+ is not only for students; apprentices in vocational training can take part too.
Since 2014 Switzerland has paid for its students' exchanges with its own money.

teile.einleitung: The European Coal and Steel Community, ECSC for short, is often called the Montan Union. It was the first European community and is seen as the forerunner of today's European Union.
wichtigste: The ECSC is also called the Montan Union.
The treaty was signed in Paris on 18 April 1951.
It came into force in 1952 and ran for 50 years until 2002.
There were six founding states; Great Britain was not one of them.
The High Authority had its seat in Luxembourg.
The European Parliament developed from the Common Assembly.

abschnitte.text: The word **“Montan”** refers to **mining**. Coal is extracted by mining, and steel is made from iron ore. That is why the ECSC is also called the Montan Union. The idea came from the Schuman Declaration of 1950. Coal and steel were important for industry and arms at the time. Countries that manage them together cannot secretly build up their weapons.

The founding states were **Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands**. Great Britain did not take part and only joined the European Communities in 1973. The treaty was signed in **Paris** on 18 April 1951 and is therefore also called the Treaty of Paris. It came into force on 23 July 1952.

The most important institution was the **High Authority**, with its seat in **Luxembourg**. It could take binding decisions for the member states. It is described as **supranational**, meaning above the individual states. It was a forerunner of today's EU Commission. Its first president was Jean Monnet. The **Common Assembly** was made up of members of the national parliaments. The European Parliament developed from it.

abschnitte.titel: A treaty for a fixed time
abschnitte.text: The treaty was concluded for **50 years**. It expired in July 2002, and its tasks passed to the European Community. The Montan Union is seen as the forerunner of the EU. For the first time, countries handed over powers to a shared European authority. Later communities built on this.

gewusst: From the start, the Montan Union was limited to exactly 50 years.
Ever since the Montan Union, Luxembourg has been the seat of European institutions.

teile.einleitung: Internally displaced persons are people who have had to leave their homes but have stayed in their own country. Worldwide there are many more internally displaced persons than refugees abroad.
wichtigste: Internally displaced persons flee within their own country.
The English abbreviation is **IDP**, for “internally displaced persons”.
The reasons are often war, violence or natural disasters.
Legally they do not count as refugees, because they have not crossed a national border.
In 1998 the UN published guidelines for their protection.
The monitoring centre IDMC is based in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: Sometimes people suddenly have to leave their village or town. The reasons are **war**, **violence** or **natural disasters** such as floods and earthquakes. Many do not flee abroad but to a safer area in their own country. These people are called **internally displaced persons**. The German word “Binnen” means “inside”.

abschnitte.titel: Not refugees in the legal sense
abschnitte.text: The **Geneva Refugee Convention** of 1951 protects people who are outside their home country. Internally displaced persons, however, have **not crossed a national border**. That is why they do not count as refugees in law. Their own state is first and foremost responsible for protecting them. This is difficult when it is that very state that is at war.

In 1998 the UN published the **Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement**. They are not binding but are regarded worldwide as an important standard. In 2009 the **African Union** adopted the **Kampala Convention** in Uganda. It is the first binding treaty for the protection of internally displaced persons. The states involved commit themselves to protecting and helping these people.

The **Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre** (IDMC) belongs to the Norwegian Refugee Council and is based in **Geneva**. Every year it collects figures from all over the world. According to UNHCR and the IDMC, most people flee within their own country. At the end of 2024 **Sudan** had the most internally displaced persons, more than 11 million people. The reason was the war that broke out there in 2023.

gewusst: Natural disasters also drive millions of people from their homes every year, but often only for a short time.
Geneva is an important place for humanitarian aid: UNHCR and the International Committee of the Red Cross are also based there.

teile.einleitung: The CO2 Act is a Swiss law for protecting the climate. It is meant to help reduce emissions of carbon dioxide. The first CO2 Act came into force in 2000.
wichtigste: CO2 stands for **carbon dioxide**, a gas produced when coal, oil and gas are burned.
The first CO2 Act came into force on 1 May 2000.
Since 2008 there has been a **CO2 levy** on heating oil and natural gas.
Since 2022 it has been 120 francs per tonne of CO2 (as of 2025).
A large part goes back to the population through health insurance premiums.
On 13 June 2021 the people narrowly rejected a revised CO2 Act.

abschnitte.text: **CO2** is the chemical formula for **carbon dioxide**. It consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. It is produced mainly when **coal, oil and gas** are burned, for example for heating or driving. CO2 is a **greenhouse gas**: too much of it in the air contributes to the warming of the Earth. That is why many countries want to reduce emissions.

The first **CO2 Act** was passed by Parliament in 1999 and came into force on **1 May 2000**. It set targets for reducing emissions. Since then it has been revised several times. On **13 June 2021** the people rejected a major revision with about 51.6 per cent voting no. Among other things, a **flight ticket levy** of 30 to 120 francs had been planned. After that, Parliament drew up a new proposal without new levies.

Since **2008** there has been a **CO2 levy** on **heating fuels** such as heating oil and natural gas. It began at 12 francs per tonne of CO2. Because the targets were missed, it was raised step by step. Since 2022 it has been **120 francs** per tonne, about 30 centimes for a litre of heating oil. **Motor fuels** such as petrol and diesel are exempt.

About two thirds of the income is **paid back** to the population and the economy. Each person receives the same amount, through lower **health insurance premiums**. So people who cause little CO2 benefit. Up to a third goes into the **Buildings Programme**. It supports, for example, better insulation and heating with renewable energy.

gewusst: The CO2 levy is an incentive tax: it is meant to change behaviour, not to bring money into the state's coffers.
In the 2021 vote the result was very close; opinions among the population differed widely.

tqxqgnt.t: Bilateral Agreements: Switzerland and the European Union

teile.einleitung: The bilateral agreements are a series of separate agreements between Switzerland and the European Union. Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but through these agreements it works closely with it in many areas. Bilateral means two-sided, so there are two partners: Switzerland and the EU.
wichtigste: The bilateral agreements are a series of separate agreements instead of EU membership.
In 1992 Swiss voters rejected joining the European Economic Area.
After that Switzerland negotiated separate agreements with the EU.
The Bilaterals I came into force in 2002; they include the free movement of persons.
With the Bilaterals II, Switzerland joined the Schengen area.
The EU is Switzerland's most important trading partner.

abschnitte.text: **Bilateral** means two-sided, so it is about agreements between two partners. Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe but is not a member of the **European Union**. Even so, it trades a great deal with the EU countries. That is why it has concluded many separate agreements with the EU that regulate particular areas.

As early as 1972 Switzerland concluded a **free trade agreement** with what was then the European Community. On 6 December 1992 the people and the cantons narrowly rejected joining the European Economic Area. After that the Federal Council looked for another way, which is called the bilateral way. Switzerland negotiated separate agreements that suited its needs.

The first seven agreements, the **Bilaterals I**, were signed in 1999 and approved by the people in 2000. They came into force in 2002. They include the **free movement of persons**, which allows people from Switzerland and the EU to live and work in each other's area. Other agreements concern land and air transport, agriculture, research and trade.

With the Bilaterals II of 2004, more agreements were added. The best known is joining the **Schengen area**, which the people approved in 2005. Since then there have usually been no systematic passport checks at the borders with neighbouring countries. In addition, the police authorities work more closely together, and there are shared rules for asylum applications.

The EU wanted to link the many agreements with shared rules, for example on how new EU law is adopted. In 2021 the Federal Council broke off the negotiations on a framework agreement. After that there were new negotiations, and at the end of 2024 a new package of agreements was negotiated. Parliament and probably also the voters will decide on these agreements.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two-sided, that is, between two partners.
The right to live and work in another country.
Countries in Europe between which there are usually no border checks.
Trade without customs duties or with very low ones.

gewusst: The Bilaterals I are linked by a so-called guillotine clause: if one agreement falls away, the others fall away too.
About half of Switzerland's exports go to EU countries.

teile.einleitung: The Commonwealth of Nations is a voluntary association of states. Most of them used to be part of the British Empire. Today they work together as equal, independent countries.
wichtigste: In 2025 the Commonwealth had 56 member states.
The most recent to join were Gabon and Togo in 2022.
Its head is the British monarch, today King Charles III.
The modern Commonwealth came about with the London Declaration of 1949.
The Secretariat is in Marlborough House in London.
The Commonwealth Games take place every four years.

abschnitte.text: Great Britain once ruled a huge **empire** with colonies on every continent. In the 20th century these territories gradually became independent. Many still wanted to stay connected. With the **London Declaration of 1949**, republics such as India were also allowed to remain members. Since then all members have been **free and equal** states.

In 2025 the Commonwealth had **56 members**. They are in Africa, Asia, America, Europe and Oceania. They include large countries such as **India** and **Canada** and small island states in the Caribbean and the Pacific. Some members were never British colonies: **Mozambique**, a former Portuguese colony, joined in 1995. In 2022 **Gabon** and **Togo** joined. Ireland left the Commonwealth in 1949.

The **Head of the Commonwealth** is the British monarch, since 2022 **King Charles III**. The role is mainly **symbolic**; he has no power over the member states. In some countries such as Canada or Australia he is also head of state. Day-to-day cooperation is organised by the **Commonwealth Secretariat** in Marlborough House in **London**.

Every four years athletes from the member countries meet at the **Commonwealth Games**. It is a big event with many sports, similar to the Olympic Games. In 2026 the Games took place in **Glasgow** in Scotland. Glasgow had already been the host city in 2014.

gewusst: Together about a third of all the people in the world live in the Commonwealth, most of them in India.
Mozambique and Rwanda are members even though they never belonged to the British Empire.

teile.einleitung: In the **automatic exchange of information**, AEOI for short (in German AIA), banks report the accounts of foreign customers to the country where those customers live. In this way tax authorities can check whether someone is paying tax on their money correctly. For Switzerland, the AEOI meant a big change in banking secrecy.
wichtigste: Banks report the account data of foreign customers to the country where they live.
Switzerland has collected data since 2017 and exchanged it for the first time in 2018.
The OECD's international standard is called the Common Reporting Standard.
In 2015 Switzerland signed an AEOI agreement with the EU.
For accounts of US taxpayers, the US law FATCA applies.
For people whose tax residence is in Switzerland, banking secrecy still applies.

abschnitte.text: Banks and other **financial institutions** record the accounts of people who pay tax abroad. They report these data to the **Federal Tax Administration**. It passes the information on to the **partner states** once a year. What is reported includes, for example, the account balance and the income. In return, the partner states send data about accounts of people who live in Switzerland.

In 2014 the **OECD** adopted the **Common Reporting Standard**, CRS for short. More than 100 states have joined it. Switzerland collected data from **1 January 2017** and exchanged them for the first time in autumn **2018**. For this it signed an agreement with the **EU** in May 2015. It replaced the savings tax agreement of 2004, under which Switzerland had anonymously withheld tax.

The USA went its own way. Its law **FATCA** of 2010, the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act, obliges banks worldwide to report accounts of US taxpayers to the US tax authority. Switzerland concluded an agreement on this with the USA in 2013. Anyone who does not take part must expect high deductions on payments from the USA.

Swiss **banking secrecy** has been set out in Article 47 of the **Banking Act** since 1934. Anyone who breaches it commits a crime. Because of the AEOI, it no longer applies towards foreign tax authorities. But for people with their **tax residence in Switzerland** there is no automatic exchange with the Swiss tax authorities. For them, banking secrecy still applies.

gewusst: The AEOI only applies between states that have committed themselves to exchanging data with each other.
Until 2017, instead of reporting names, Switzerland withheld an anonymous tax for EU customers.

teile.einleitung: The Southern African Development Community, SADC for short, is an association of countries in the south of Africa. It aims to strengthen the economy, secure peace and encourage cooperation.
wichtigste: Its forerunner, SADCC, was founded in Lusaka in 1980.
The SADC Treaty was signed in Windhoek in 1992.
The Secretariat has its seat in Gaborone in Botswana.
South Africa joined in 1994 after the end of apartheid.
The Comoros became the 16th member in 2017.

abschnitte.text: The forerunner was called the **Southern African Development Coordination Conference**, SADCC for short. It was founded in 1980 in Lusaka, the capital of Zambia. At its core were the **Frontline States**, for example Tanzania, Zambia, Botswana, Mozambique and Angola. They supported liberation movements and wanted to be less dependent on the apartheid state of South Africa. **Apartheid** was a system that separated people by skin colour and treated them unfairly.

On 17 August 1992 the countries signed the treaty for the new SADC in **Windhoek**, the capital of Namibia. Since then, 17 August has been SADC Day. The **Secretariat** is based in **Gaborone**, the capital of Botswana. The Community's programmes are coordinated from there.

After the first free elections in 1994, **South Africa** became a member. Later island states in the Indian Ocean also joined, such as Madagascar, Mauritius and the Seychelles. In 2017 the **Comoros** were admitted as the 16th member. The members are very different in size and in wealth.

SADC had its own court, the **SADC Tribunal**. It ruled against the seizure of farmers' land in Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe did not carry out the rulings, and in 2010 the heads of state suspended the court. From 2021 SADC sent a **military mission** to the province of Cabo Delgado in Mozambique. There it supported the government against rebels; the mission ended in 2024.

gewusst: 17 August, the day the treaty was signed in 1992, is SADC Day.
The apartheid regime in South Africa was an important reason for founding the forerunner organisation.

teile.einleitung: At the three-country corner in Basel, the borders of three countries meet: Switzerland, Germany and France. The exact point lies in the middle of the Rhine. Here you can get from one country to another in a few minutes.
wichtigste: At the three-country corner, Switzerland, Germany and France meet.
The exact border point lies in the middle of the Rhine.
A tall silver monument stands on the bank in Kleinhüningen.
The Three Countries Bridge links Weil am Rhein with Huningue, for pedestrians and bicycles only.
Tram 8 runs from Basel to Weil am Rhein.
The EuroAirport lies on French soil.

abschnitte.text: In the north of **Basel**, three countries meet: **Switzerland**, **Germany** and **France**. The exact point where the three borders meet lies **in the middle of the Rhine**. So you cannot stand on it. That is why a tall silver **monument** recalling the three-country corner stands on the bank of the Rhine in the Basel district of **Kleinhüningen**. Many day-trippers visit the place and look into all three countries.

Very close by, the **Three Countries Bridge** crosses the Rhine. It links **Weil am Rhein** in Germany with **Huningue** in France. You may only cross it **on foot or by bicycle**. Public transport crosses the borders too: **tram line 8** runs from Basel to Weil am Rhein. Another tram line runs to Saint-Louis in France.

Basel has a special station: the **Badischer Bahnhof**. It stands on Swiss soil but is run by **Deutsche Bahn**. Many trains to Germany leave from there. The **EuroAirport**, Basel's airport, on the other hand lies on **French** soil. It is run jointly by France and Switzerland.

The **Kleinhüningen Rhine port** lies by the three-country corner. Ships arrive here that have come up the Rhine from the large ports on the North Sea. They bring goods such as fuel, grain or containers to Switzerland. For Switzerland, which has no access to the sea of its own, this port is very important. Through the Rhine it is connected to the sea.

gewusst: At the three-country corner you can visit three countries on foot in one afternoon.
The EuroAirport has a Swiss and a French sector; you can reach it from Basel by a customs road.

teile.einleitung: The Camp David Accords of 1978 were an important step towards peace in the Middle East. Egypt and Israel, which had fought several wars against each other, reached agreement with the help of the USA.
wichtigste: The accords were signed in September 1978.
US President **Jimmy Carter** mediated in person.
**Anwar Sadat** negotiated for Egypt and **Menachem Begin** for Israel.
In 1979 Egypt and Israel made peace in Washington.
Israel gave back the **Sinai Peninsula** by 1982.
Sadat and Begin received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1978.

abschnitte.text: **Camp David** is a **country retreat of the US President**. It lies in the mountains of Maryland, not far from Washington. Presidents often receive guests there for confidential talks. In September 1978 President **Jimmy Carter** invited the leaders of Egypt and Israel there. The talks lasted almost two weeks and threatened to fail several times.

Egypt and Israel had fought several wars against each other. In the **Six-Day War** of 1967, Israel had captured Egypt's **Sinai Peninsula**. In November 1977 the Egyptian President **Anwar Sadat** took a surprising step: he was the first Arab head of state to travel to Israel. In Jerusalem he spoke before the **Knesset**, the Israeli parliament. With this he opened the way to direct negotiations.

On **17 September 1978** the accords were signed at the White House. For Israel, Prime Minister **Menachem Begin** signed. One part prepared peace between Egypt and Israel. Another part concerned the **West Bank** and the **Gaza Strip**. Self-government was planned there for a transition period of five years. However, this part was never carried out.

In March 1979 Egypt and Israel signed a **peace treaty** in **Washington**. Israel withdrew completely from the Sinai by 1982. Sadat and Begin jointly received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1978. In many Arab countries, however, the peace met with rejection. The treaty between Egypt and Israel still applies today.

gewusst: Jimmy Carter later also received the Nobel Peace Prize, in 2002.
Egypt was the first Arab country to conclude a peace treaty with Israel.

teile.einleitung: Big Ben is one of the best-known landmarks of London. Strictly speaking, Big Ben is the name of a large bell, but many people also use it for the whole clock tower at the British Parliament.
wichtigste: Big Ben is the largest bell in the clock tower of Parliament in London.
The bell weighs about 14 tonnes, more precisely about 13.7 tonnes.
The tower is about 96 metres high and has been called the Elizabeth Tower since 2012.
The clock has four dials, one on each side.
Every quarter of an hour, four smaller bells play the Westminster chimes.
From 2017 to 2022 the tower was renovated, and Big Ben was mostly silent.

abschnitte.text: Five bells hang in the tower. The largest and heaviest is called **Big Ben** and weighs about 13.7 tonnes. It strikes every hour on the hour. The bell was cast in the middle of the 19th century. Exactly where the name comes from is not completely certain. Today many people also use the name for the whole tower.

The clock tower belongs to the **Palace of Westminster**, where the British Parliament meets. It is about 96 metres high, roughly as tall as a building with 30 floors. For a long time it was simply called the Clock Tower. In 2012 it was renamed the **Elizabeth Tower** in honour of Queen Elizabeth II. At that time she was celebrating her 60th year as queen.

The clock has **four dials**, one on each side of the tower. In this way you can see the time from every direction. The clock is regarded as very accurate. Every quarter of an hour a short tune rings out, the **Westminster chimes**. Many church clocks in other countries also play this tune, perhaps even in your village.

From 2017 to 2022 the tower was thoroughly **renovated**. During this time it was covered in scaffolding, and Big Ben only rang on special occasions, for example at New Year. An interesting detail: the tower does not stand quite straight. It **leans slightly**, by about half a metre at the top. As far as we know today, this is not dangerous.

gewusst: The chimes of Big Ben are broadcast on British radio, especially at midnight on New Year's Eve.
The Palace of Westminster with the clock tower is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: Germany is Switzerland's northern neighbour and the country with the most inhabitants in the European Union. Its capital is Berlin, and the country is divided into 16 federal states.
wichtigste: The flag has three horizontal stripes: black, red and gold.
Germany lies to the north of Switzerland.
The capital is Berlin, and its landmark is the Brandenburg Gate.
Germany has 16 federal states, much as Switzerland has cantons.
Baden-Württemberg borders Switzerland, and the Rhine forms a large part of the border.
More than 80 million people live in Germany.

abschnitte.text: More than **80 million people** live in Germany, almost ten times as many as in Switzerland. No other neighbouring country of Switzerland has so many inhabitants. The capital is **Berlin**. Its best-known landmark is the **Brandenburg Gate**, a symbol of German unity. The **flag** has three horizontal stripes: black at the top, red in the middle and gold at the bottom. People pay with the **euro**.

Like Switzerland, Germany is a **federal state**. It is divided into **16 federal states**, for example **Bavaria** and **Baden-Württemberg**. The states have their own governments, a bit like our **cantons**. They are responsible, for example, for schools and the police. The government of the whole country is led by the Federal Chancellor.

Germany borders Switzerland in the **north**, for example the cantons of Basel-Stadt, Aargau, Schaffhausen and Thurgau. The German state on the border is **Baden-Württemberg**, with towns such as Lörrach and Waldshut. The **Rhine** flows between **Lake Constance** and Basel. For many kilometres it separates the two countries. One special case is **Büsingen am Hochrhein**: this German village is completely surrounded by Swiss territory and lies next to the canton of Schaffhausen.

In the north Germany borders the **North Sea** and the **Baltic Sea**, and in the south the Alps. In the south-west lies the **Black Forest**, a range of low mountains with dense forests. Its southern part reaches close to Basel. Besides the Rhine, other large rivers are the **Danube** and the **Elbe**.

The **Brothers Grimm**, Jacob and Wilhelm, came from Germany. They collected fairy tales such as “Hansel and Gretel” and “Little Red Riding Hood”. Composers such as Johann Sebastian Bach and Ludwig van Beethoven are also famous. Many people from Germany live and work in Switzerland, and every day many cross-border commuters cross the border.

gewusst: Because of its special location, some Swiss rules apply in Büsingen, for example for customs, and people there often pay with francs.
Germany has nine neighbouring countries, more than almost any other country in Europe.
The Danube rises in the Black Forest, not far from the Swiss border.

teile.einleitung: The European Central Bank, ECB for short, is the central bank for all the countries with the euro. It makes sure that the euro keeps its value as well as possible.
wichtigste: The ECB was founded on 1 June 1998.
Its most important aim is stable prices.
In the medium term it aims for inflation of 2 per cent.
Its most important tool is the key interest rate.
The Governing Council of the ECB decides on interest rates.
Since November 2019 the President has been Christine Lagarde (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: The ECB was founded on **1 June 1998** and has its seat in Frankfurt am Main. Shortly afterwards, at the start of 1999, the euro started as book money. The ECB's most important aim is **price stability**. So money should not lose its value too quickly. **Inflation**, meaning rising prices, of 2 per cent a year is seen as ideal.

The most important tool is the **key interest rate**. It decides at what interest rate banks borrow money from the central bank. If the key rate rises, loans become more expensive. People and companies then spend less, and prices usually rise more slowly. If it falls, borrowing becomes cheaper, and the economy is boosted.

The most important body is the **Governing Council**. It is made up of the six members of the **Executive Board** and the governors of the national central banks of the euro countries. The Governing Council decides on the key interest rates. The Executive Board consists of the President, the Vice-President and four other members. They are appointed for **eight years** and cannot be reappointed. This is meant to secure their **independence**.

The Frenchwoman **Christine Lagarde** has led the ECB since November 2019 (as of 2026). Before that she was head of the International Monetary Fund. Her predecessor was the Italian Mario Draghi. The President regularly explains the ECB's decisions at press conferences.

Switzerland is not part of the euro area. It has its own currency, the **franc**. The **Swiss National Bank** is responsible for it. It has a similar task to the ECB and also sets a key interest rate.

gewusst: Members of the ECB's Executive Board may serve only a single term of eight years.
Zero inflation is not the ECB's aim; it aims for 2 per cent.

teile.einleitung: The Chemical Weapons Convention is an international treaty that bans chemical weapons. States may not make, store or use such weapons, and they must destroy any existing stocks.
wichtigste: The convention was opened for signature in Paris in January 1993.
It came into force on 29 April 1997.
The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) in The Hague monitors it.
The OPCW received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013.
The Geneva Protocol of 1925 already banned the use of poison gas, but not making and storing it.
The Spiez Laboratory in the canton of Bern examines samples on behalf of the OPCW.

abschnitte.text: Chemical weapons are poisonous substances that can seriously harm or kill people. They are also called **chemical warfare agents**. One example is **sarin**, a nerve agent that is deadly even in tiny amounts. Because such weapons cause great suffering and hardly distinguish between soldiers and civilians, they are regarded as especially cruel.

In the **First World War**, poison gas was used on a large scale for the first time, with chlorine gas at **Ypres** in Belgium in 1915. After that several armies used poison gas. In response, the **Geneva Protocol of 1925** was created. It banned the use of poison gas in war but still allowed it to be made and stored. That is why the problem remained.

The **Chemical Weapons Convention** goes much further. It was opened for signature in **Paris** in January 1993 and came into force on **29 April 1997**. It bans the development, production, storage, transfer and use of chemical weapons. Existing stocks must be **destroyed**. Today almost all the states in the world are members.

The **Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons**, OPCW for short, is based in **The Hague** in the Netherlands. Its experts inspect factories and stores and monitor the destruction of weapons. In 2013 the OPCW received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. In the same year, after a poison gas attack near Damascus, **Syria** joined the convention under international pressure.

Switzerland also contributes to the checks. The **Spiez Laboratory** in the canton of Bern is recognised by the OPCW as a **designated laboratory**. There, experts examine samples, for example soil or water, for chemical warfare agents. Such analyses help to find out whether banned weapons have been used anywhere.

gewusst: The Chemical Weapons Convention bans a whole type of weapon of mass destruction and has the destruction of stocks checked by experts.
The Spiez Laboratory is one of the few laboratories in the world that the OPCW entrusts with such analyses.

teile.einleitung: Brussels is the capital of Belgium. Because important institutions of the European Union are based there, the city is often also called the capital of Europe.
wichtigste: Brussels is the capital of Belgium.
The European Commission, the Council of the EU and the European Council are based there.
The official languages are French and Dutch.
The **Atomium** was built for the 1958 World's Fair.
The **Grand-Place** has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.
The **Manneken Pis** is a small fountain figure of a boy.

abschnitte.text: Brussels is the capital of **Belgium**. Important parts of the EU work in the city. The **European Commission**, the **Council of the EU** and the **European Council** are based here. That is why Brussels is often called the unofficial **capital of Europe**. Switzerland also has a mission to the EU in Brussels. NATO's headquarters is here too.

In Brussels **French** and **Dutch** are the official languages. That is why street signs are often in two languages. Most people in the city speak French. Because many people from all over the world work here, you also hear many other languages. Like Switzerland, Belgium is a country with several national languages.

The **Atomium** was built for the **1958 World's Fair**. It consists of shiny spheres and looks like a giant, enlarged particle. The splendid main square is called the **Grand-Place**. It is surrounded by old, decorated guild houses and the Gothic town hall. Since 1998 it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

abschnitte.titel: A small figure and sweet specialities
abschnitte.text: The **Manneken Pis** is a small bronze figure of a boy on a fountain. He is often dressed in different costumes. Belgium is famous for **chocolate** and pralines, but also for waffles. Even a vegetable bears the city's name: the **Brussels sprout**, in French “chou de Bruxelles”, that is, Brussels cabbage.

gewusst: Brussels is also a city of comics: large comic pictures are painted on many house walls.
The spheres of the Atomium are connected by tubes that you can walk through.

teile.einleitung: With the **Foreign Policy Strategy**, the Federal Council sets out the goals Switzerland pursues in the world. Each strategy applies for four years, that is, for one legislative period. The current strategy covers the years 2024 to 2027.
wichtigste: The Federal Council adopted the 2024 to 2027 strategy on 31 January 2024.
It is drawn up by the FDFA.
Europe is the first geographical priority.
New focal points are the environment and democracy and governance.
Every year the Federal Council reports on implementation in the Foreign Policy Report.
Under Article 54 of the Federal Constitution, foreign policy is a matter for the federal government.

abschnitte.text: Under **Article 54** of the Federal Constitution, foreign affairs are **a matter for the federal government**. The article also names goals, such as relieving need and poverty, respecting human rights and the peaceful coexistence of peoples. Articles 173 and 185 oblige the **Federal Assembly and the Federal Council** to take measures to safeguard independence and **neutrality**. There is no separate article on neutrality in the constitution.

The **FDFA**, the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, draws up the strategy. It is adopted by the whole **Federal Council**. It adopted the 2024 to 2027 strategy on **31 January 2024**, shortly after the start of the new legislative period. Before that, the 2020 to 2023 strategy applied. On important plans, the Federal Council consults Parliament's **Foreign Affairs Committees**.

The strategy has four thematic focal points: **peace and security**, **prosperity and competitiveness**, the **environment** and **democracy and governance**. The last two are new. Geographically, **Europe** comes first. Switzerland aims for a stable and prosperous Europe, which includes developing its relations with the EU further.

Implementation takes place in three levels, like a **cascade**. Below the main strategy there are **follow-up strategies** for particular regions and topics. Below those come the departments' implementation plans. Every year the Federal Council presents the **Foreign Policy Report**. It shows how far the goals have been reached, and Parliament takes note of it.

gewusst: The Federal Constitution has no separate article on neutrality.
The strategy is always set for one legislative period of four years.

teile.einleitung: The Bilaterals II are the second large package of agreements between Switzerland and the EU. They were signed in Luxembourg in 2004 and go beyond the economy, for example to security, asylum and the environment.
wichtigste: The Bilaterals II were signed in Luxembourg on 26 October 2004.
The best-known agreement is **Schengen/Dublin**.
On 5 June 2005, 54.6 per cent voted yes to Schengen/Dublin.
Unlike the Bilaterals I, there is no guillotine clause.
Thanks to the environment agreement, Switzerland is a member of the European Environment Agency.
The statistics agreement links the Federal Statistical Office with Eurostat.

abschnitte.text: After the Bilaterals I, Switzerland and the EU went on negotiating. The result was the **Bilaterals II**, signed in Luxembourg on 26 October 2004. The package includes several agreements on very different topics. Importantly, the agreements are **not linked to each other**. If one falls away, the others remain in place.

**Schengen** regulates cooperation at the borders and between police forces. Between the Schengen states there are no longer any systematic checks on people. **Dublin** sets out which state examines an asylum application. A referendum was called against these agreements. On 5 June 2005 the people approved them with 54.6 per cent.

The agreement on **processed agricultural products** concerns factory-made foods, for example chocolate, coffee or biscuits. It lowered customs duties on these products. Under the **savings tax** agreement, Swiss banks deducted a withholding tax on the interest of people from the EU. In 2017 it was replaced by the **automatic exchange of information**.

Through the **environment agreement**, Switzerland is a member of the **European Environment Agency** in Copenhagen. It collects data on the environment throughout Europe. The **statistics agreement** makes sure that Swiss figures can be compared with those of the EU. For this, the Federal Statistical Office works closely with **Eurostat**, the EU's statistical office.

gewusst: The Bilaterals II also include an agreement on fighting fraud, for example in smuggling.
With the Schengen agreement you can travel to many neighbouring countries without passport checks, but you still have to carry your identity document.

teile.einleitung: The euro crisis was a serious crisis in several countries using the euro, starting in 2010. Some countries had such high debts that they could hardly borrow money any more and needed help.
wichtigste: In May 2010 Greece received a first aid package of about 110 billion euros.
The troika of the EU Commission, the ECB and the IMF monitored the aid programmes.
In 2012 the permanent rescue fund, the ESM, was set up.
In 2012 ECB President Mario Draghi promised to do whatever was necessary for the euro.
Ireland and Cyprus also needed help.
In 2011 the Swiss National Bank introduced a minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs per euro.

abschnitte.text: Greece had very high **national debts**. In May 2010 the euro countries and the International Monetary Fund (**IMF**) promised loans of about 110 billion euros. In return the country had to make strict **savings**. In 2012 private creditors gave up about 53.5 per cent of the face value of their Greek bonds. This **debt cut** was the largest restructuring of a country's debt up to that time.

The **troika** of the EU Commission, the European Central Bank and the IMF checked whether the countries were carrying out the agreed reforms. Only then were further loans paid out. In 2012 the **European Stability Mechanism (ESM)** was created, with its seat in Luxembourg. It is a permanent rescue fund and replaced a temporary solution.

In November 2010 **Ireland** asked for help. The state had rescued its banks after a property bubble burst, and it received a programme of about 85 billion euros. In 2013 **Cyprus** was rescued. There, for the first time, bank customers with savings of more than 100,000 euros had to bear part of the losses. Smaller savings stayed protected.

In July 2012, ECB President **Mario Draghi** said in London that the ECB would do everything necessary to save the euro: “whatever it takes”. After that, interest rates for the crisis countries fell clearly. In July 2015 about 61 per cent of voters in Greece voted against the savings conditions in a **referendum**. A few days later, the government accepted a third aid programme all the same.

Many investors fled into the **franc**, because it was seen as safe. This made the franc very expensive, which harmed Swiss companies when exporting. In September 2011 the **Swiss National Bank** set a minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs per euro. It defended it until January 2015.

gewusst: In 2012 a single sentence from Mario Draghi calmed the financial markets, even though at first the ECB hardly had to buy any bonds.
The euro crisis made the franc so strong that the National Bank defended a minimum exchange rate for more than three years.

teile.einleitung: A **letter of credence** is an official letter with which a state introduces its ambassador to another state. Only with it is the ambassador properly in office. The rules for this are in the **Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations** of 1961.
wichtigste: The letter of credence is issued by the head of state of the sending state.
In French it is called “lettre de créance”.
A copy usually goes first to the foreign ministry.
At the end of the mission comes the letter of recall.
Instead of a letter of credence, consuls receive an exequatur.
The rank of ambassadors depends on the date they took up office.

abschnitte.titel: A letter between heads of state
abschnitte.text: The letter of credence is a letter from the **head of state of the sending state** to the head of state of the **receiving state**. It confirms that the person officially represents their state. Because **French** was long the language of diplomacy, it is also called “**lettre de créance**”. That is why many technical terms in diplomacy come from French.

After arriving, the new ambassador first hands a copy to the **foreign ministry**. Depending on the country, he may then already take on certain tasks. Later the original is formally presented. In Switzerland new ambassadors present their letter to the **President of the Confederation**.

At the end of a mission, the **letter of recall**, in French “lettre de rappel”, informs the receiving state that the mission is over. Often the successor already hands it over together with his own letter. **Consuls** do not receive a letter of credence but a commission. Their admission by the receiving state is called the **exequatur**.

According to the Vienna Convention, diplomats should in principle have the nationality of the sending state. People from the receiving state may only be appointed with its **consent**. Within a class, rank depends on the **date of taking up office**. In this way the old dispute about powerful states having precedence was defused. The ambassador who has been accredited longest is often **doyen** of the diplomatic corps, but in many countries with a Catholic tradition it is traditionally the papal nuncio.

gewusst: In the past, diplomats argued fiercely about who was allowed to go first at ceremonies. Today the date simply decides.
The word doyen comes from French and means something like “the eldest”.

teile.einleitung: The Évian Accords ended the Algerian War between France and the Algerian independence movement in 1962. They were signed in the French town of Évian-les-Bains on Lake Geneva. Switzerland helped make the negotiations possible with its good offices.
wichtigste: Évian-les-Bains lies on the French southern shore of Lake Geneva.
The treaties were signed on 18 March 1962, and the ceasefire applied from 19 March.
On the Algerian side, the Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic negotiated.
The French President Charles de Gaulle pushed the negotiations through.
Switzerland provided good offices, and the Algerian delegation stayed in Switzerland.
In France about 90 per cent voted in favour in April 1962.
Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962.

abschnitte.text: **Algeria** in North Africa had been a French colony since the 19th century. From 1954 the independence movement **FLN** fought against France. The **Algerian War** lasted until 1962 and claimed a great many victims. In 1958 **Charles de Gaulle** came to power in France. In 1959 he recognised Algeria's **right to self-determination**. In 1961 some generals in Algiers staged a coup against his policy, but the coup failed.

Switzerland provided **good offices**. This means that, as a neutral country, it helped the opponents to talk to each other. It made contacts and organised secret meetings. A key figure was the Swiss diplomat **Olivier Long**. For security reasons, the Algerian delegation stayed in the **canton of Vaud**. A **Swiss Army helicopter** flew them to the negotiations in Évian and back again.

**Évian-les-Bains** lies on the French southern shore of **Lake Geneva**, opposite Lausanne. Being close to Switzerland was important for the negotiations. On the Algerian side, the **Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic**, GPRA for short, negotiated. This was the FLN's government in exile. The treaties were signed on **18 March 1962**. The **ceasefire** applied from **19 March 1962**.

On **8 April 1962**, about **90 per cent** of voters in France approved the treaties. In Algeria itself the vote was held on **1 July 1962**. On **5 July 1962** **independence** was declared. The date recalls 5 July 1830, when France had conquered Algiers. There was still violence even after the ceasefire, above all from the **OAS**. This underground organisation fought independence with terror.

gewusst: Évian is also known for its mineral water, which comes from the mountains above Lake Geneva.
Switzerland has often used its good offices since then to help enemy sides negotiate with each other.

txjiu7y.t: Bilateral Agreements between Switzerland and the European Union

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is not a member of the European Union. Even so, it works closely with it. For this there are many agreements, which are called the Bilateral Agreements.
wichtigste: “Bilateral” means two-sided: the partners are Switzerland and the EU.
The agreements regulate areas such as trade, transport, work and research.
The first package is called the Bilaterals I and the second the Bilaterals II.
On 21 May 2000 about two thirds of voters said yes to the Bilaterals I.
Thanks to the free movement of persons, Swiss people may live and work in the EU, and the other way round.
The EU is Switzerland's most important trading partner.

abschnitte.text: The word **bilateral** comes from Latin. “Bi” means two, and “lateral” means to do with sides. So a bilateral agreement is concluded by **two sides**. Here they are Switzerland and the EU. Each promises the other something so that they can work together well, for example in trade.

Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe and is surrounded by EU countries. It sells a great many goods to the EU. In 1992 the people rejected joining the **European Economic Area**. That is why Switzerland looked for its own way: it concluded agreements for individual areas. As early as 1972 there was an important **free trade agreement**.

The first package, the **Bilaterals I**, was signed in 1999. On 21 May 2000 about two thirds voted yes. Later the **Bilaterals II** of 2004 were added, for example with Schengen. Since 2024 there has been a new package, often called the **Bilaterals III**. Altogether there are well over a hundred agreements.

The **free movement of persons** allows people to live and work in another country. The **land transport agreement** regulates traffic by lorry and train through Switzerland. Thanks to the **air transport agreement**, Swiss airlines fly freely in Europe. And thanks to Schengen, there are no longer regular passport checks at many borders.

gewusst: The Swiss people have already voted many times on the agreements with the EU.
Many people from neighbouring countries work in Switzerland and cross the border every day; they are called cross-border commuters.

teile.einleitung: In spring 2014 Russia brought the Ukrainian peninsula of **Crimea** under its control and declared it part of Russia. Most states in the world, including Switzerland, regard this as an **annexation** that breaks international law. The conflict has a long history and its effects are still felt today.
wichtigste: In 1954, under Nikita Khrushchev, Crimea was transferred to the Ukrainian Soviet Republic.
The events were preceded by the Euromaidan protests in Kyiv.
On 16 March 2014 a referendum was held that is not recognised internationally.
Sevastopol is the main base of the Russian Black Sea Fleet.
With Resolution 68/262, the UN General Assembly declared the referendum invalid.
Russia was excluded from the G8, and the group met again as the G7.

abschnitte.text: Crimea lies in the Black Sea and belonged to the Russian Empire for a long time. In 1954, under the Soviet leader **Nikita Khrushchev**, it was transferred from the Russian to the Ukrainian Soviet Republic. Within the Soviet Union this was regarded as an administrative act. When the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, Crimea became part of independent Ukraine. In the **Budapest Memorandum** of 1994, Russia, the USA and Great Britain promised to respect Ukraine's borders. In return, Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons.

The port city of **Sevastopol** is the main base of the Russian **Black Sea Fleet**. Russia had already leased the port from Ukraine before 2014. The base is militarily very important because it secures access to the Black Sea. Many experts see this as an important motive for Russia's actions.

In November 2013 large protests began in Kyiv, the **Euromaidan**. They were triggered by the government putting an agreement with the EU on ice. In February 2014 President Yanukovych fled to Russia. Shortly afterwards, soldiers without insignia occupied important places in Crimea. On **16 March 2014** a referendum was held with them present, without independent observers. A few days later Russia declared that it was taking Crimea in.

In the UN Security Council a resolution failed because of Russia's **veto**. The **UN General Assembly** then adopted Resolution 68/262 on the territorial integrity of Ukraine in March 2014. It declared the referendum invalid. The leading industrial nations suspended cooperation with Russia, and the G8 became the **G7** again. Switzerland does not recognise the annexation either.

In 2018 Russia opened a bridge across the **Kerch Strait**. The Crimean Bridge is about 19 kilometres long and connects Crimea directly with the Russian mainland. Since Russia's attack on the whole of Ukraine in February 2022, the bridge has become an important target in the war. The question of who Crimea belongs to remains unresolved to this day.

gewusst: Since 2014 Russia has never returned to the group of leading industrial nations.
Crimea is connected to the rest of Ukraine by a narrow isthmus.
